Nandi realized that the Patriarch’s meaning was superior, and with a heart of humble submission, he said, "I wish to seek the Way and partake of the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and bestowed upon him the full precepts. He further told him:
He said: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it. Then he spoke this verse:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It reveals dharmas equal to empty space. When one realizes empty space, There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'."
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānandi, was a native of the country of Kāmala. His surname was Gautama, and he possessed a fleshly protuberance upon his crown.
He was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Initially, he encountered Vasumitra, from whom he left the household life and received instruction. Subsequently, he led his disciples on a journey.

Huizang traveled to the house of Viśāla in the kingdom of Tiqia. Seeing a white light ascending from the roof of the house, he said to his disciples, "There is a sage in this house who speaks no words;
he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He does not walk the four crossroads, for he knows that contact is defiling.
Having finished speaking, the elder came out to pay his respects and asked what was required. The Master replied, "I seek an attendant. The elder...
The man said, "I have a son named Puṇyamitra. He is already fifty years old; he has never spoken a word with his mouth, nor has he ever set foot upon the ground.
The Patriarch said, "If it is as you say, he is truly my disciple. Upon hearing this, Puṇyamitra rose immediately, prostrated himself, and spoke a verse:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my Way..."
"Who is the one who has attained the ultimate Way? The Patriarch answered with a verse: "What you say is more intimate than your own mind;
even your parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice is in accord with the Way; the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not what you need."
"I wish to know your original mind; it is neither joined nor separated. Having heard this verse, Vovada walked seven steps.

The Patriarch said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to part with, he remained silent and did not walk.
The elder then relinquished him to allow him to leave the household life. The Patriarch soon conferred upon him full ordination and further told him:
I now entrust to you the treasury of the Tathāgata’s eye of the true Dharma; do not let it be severed. Then he spoke in verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one thoroughly understands space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness."
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra:
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Ti-ga. His secular surname was Viśrāva.

Having received the entrustment of the Eighth Patriarch, he later traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma. At that time, there was an elder named Gandhacchattra who brought his son with him.
When he came to pay his respects, the Patriarch said, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years; therefore, he shall be named Nansheng (Difficult to Be Born).

He once met an immortal who declared that this boy was no ordinary man and would surely become a vessel for the Dharma. Now that he has encountered the Venerable One, you may cause him to leave the household life.
The Patriarch then shaved his head and conferred the precepts upon him, telling him: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you. You must protect it."
Reflecting upon this, he spoke in verse: "Ultimate truth is originally nameless; it is through names that ultimate truth is revealed.
Having received the true Dharma, it is neither real nor false."
The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Xie (脇), was a native of Central India. His original name was Nan-sheng (難生). Later, he encountered the Ninth Patriarch and served at his side, never once sleeping;
it was said that his ribs never touched the mat, and thus he was given the title "Venerable Xie. He first arrived in China...

He arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī. Resting beneath a tree, he pointed to the ground with his right hand and addressed the assembly, saying, "When this ground turns golden in color, a holy man shall enter this assembly.
As soon as he had finished speaking, it turned golden. At that time, there was a son of a householder named Pūrṇaśa.
He stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Yaśas replied, "My mind does not go. The Patriarch said, "Where do you dwell?
Yaśas replied, "My mind does not stay. The Patriarch said, "Is your mind then unsettled? Yaśas replied:

The Buddhas are likewise so. The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas. Yaśas replied, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]. (Dagui Zhi said: "The Patriarch asked one question and the youth gave one answer;

both are lacking in true understanding. How do you people understand this today? (Jingshan Gao said: "Even if you were to understand it right now, you must still study for sixty kalpas over three lifetimes.

Thereupon the Patriarch spoke a verse and immediately ordained him into the homeless life. He further conferred upon him the full precepts, and then told him: "The Great Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata is now..."
I entrust this to you; you must protect and keep it in mind. Then he spoke in verse: "The true essence is naturally true;
because it is true, its principle can be explained. Having realized the dharma of true truth, there is neither practice nor cessation."
The Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Punyayasas, was a native of the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Pārśva, he subsequently traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
There, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa came forward to greet him and pay his respects, asking: "I wish—"
“Do you wish to recognize the Buddha? asked the Patriarch. “That which cannot be recognized is it. Māng said, “If the Buddha cannot be recognized, how can one know that it is him?
The Patriarch said, “If the Buddha cannot be recognized, how can one know that it is not him? Māng said:
"This is the meaning of 'saw,'" [the Patriarch] said. The Patriarch replied, "That is the meaning of 'wood. The Patriarch asked, "What is the meaning of 'saw'?
Aśvaghoṣa said, "It emerges together with the Master. Aśvaghoṣa then asked in return, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? The Patriarch said, "You have been cut down by me.

At these words, Aśvaghoṣa attained sudden and complete enlightenment; he prostrated himself in refuge and requested ordination. The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "This Great Being, in the past..."
He became the king of the kingdom of Vaiśālī. In that country, there was a class of people who were as naked as horses. The king exercised his supernatural power and divided his body into silkworms;
they thus obtained clothing. Later, the king was reborn in Central India. The "horse-people" (aśvaka) were filled with longing and wailed piteously;
for this reason, he was called Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry). The Tathāgata prophesied, saying: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a worthy one."

"Aśvaghoṣa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, you shall subdue the heterodox and deliver immeasurable people. You shall succeed me in transmitting the transformation. Now is precisely the time. He then addressed him, saying:
"The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you. He then spoke this verse: "Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation;
clarity and darkness are not separate from one another. Now I entrust to you this dharma of concealment and manifestation—it is neither one nor two."
Second:
The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa.
As for the Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, he was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Having received the Dharma from Kāśyapa...
"Venerable One, later, while you were turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, a certain old man suddenly prostrated himself on the ground before your seat.
You said to the assembly, 'This is no ordinary person; he shall surely manifest extraordinary signs. As soon as you had finished speaking, he vanished.

A moment later, a golden-colored man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman. She pointed with her right hand toward you and spoke this verse: 'I bow my head to the Long [Lived One]...'"
"Venerable Elder, you shall receive the Tathāgata’s prediction. Now, upon this ground, you have proclaimed and disseminated the ultimate truth.
Having spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished. The Patriarch said, "A māra is about to come to compete with me in strength. After a short while, wind and rain arrived violently.
Heaven and earth grew dark and murky. The Patriarch said, "The arrival of Māra is indeed certain; I shall eliminate him.

He then pointed toward the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic spiritual power so that it shook the mountains and peaks. The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic disturbances were instantly extinguished.
After seven days had passed, there was a small insect, as large as a mayfly, that hid its form beneath the seat. The Patriarch took it up with his hand.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation wrought by a māra, who has come to eavesdrop upon my Dharma.
He then released it to depart, but the māra was unable to move. The Patriarch said to it, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers.
Thereupon, it returned to its original form, prostrated itself, and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name? How many followers do you have? It replied, "My name is..."
Kapimala had three thousand followers. The Patriarch asked, "Exerting all your supernatural powers, what kind of transformations can you perform?
He replied, "I could transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat. The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the Ocean of Nature?

He replied, "What is meant by the 'Ocean of Nature'? I have never known it. The Patriarch then explained the Ocean of Nature for him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it."
The three samādhis and six supernormal powers manifested from this. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra gave rise to faith and, together with three thousand followers, sought ordination.
The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts upon him. He further addressed him, saying:
"The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now to be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the very source.'"
The Dharma: light and darkness are fundamentally non-dual. Now, I entrust this Dharma of realization; it is neither grasped nor abandoned.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimora, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Initially, he was a follower of non-Buddhist paths and had many disciples.
[He traveled] three thousand [li], traversing various heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his disciples to Western India.
There was a crown prince there named Meghasvabhāva who, having heard the Venerable’s reputation, invited him to the palace to provide offerings. The Patriarch said:
The Tathāgata has taught that a śramaṇa must not associate with kings, ministers, or those of powerful families.
The Prince said, "To the north of my kingdom’s city there is a great mountain. On that mountain is a stone cave; may you practice dhyāna in seclusion there?
The Patriarch replied, "So be it," and immediately entered that mountain. After traveling several li, he encountered a large python. The Patriarch walked straight forward without hesitation.
He looked back and saw a python coiled around his body. The Master consequently conferred the Three Refuges upon it; once the snake had heard them, it departed.

As the Master was about to reach a stone cave, another elderly man appeared dressed in plain white robes. He joined his palms in greeting and paid his respects. The Master asked, "Where do you reside?
He replied, "In the past, I was often a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in solitude. There was a novice bhikṣu who frequently came to me..."

I requested instruction from you, but I grew weary of answering your questions and gave rise to thoughts of anger and resentment. When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have lived in this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the Precepts, I have come to express my gratitude.
The Patriarch asked, "Are there any other inhabitants dwelling on this mountain? He replied, "Ten li to the north, there is a great tree whose shade covers five..."

There were one hundred great dragons, and the king of those trees was named Nāga-druma (Dragon Tree). He constantly preached the Dharma for the assembly of dragons, and I too listened and received it with my own ears.
The Patriarch then went there with his disciples. Nāga-druma came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is solitary and remote, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons."

"O Virtuous and Most Honorable One, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet? Nāgārjuna said, "I am not the Most Honorable One; I have come to visit a worthy man. Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself:
"Has this master attained the nature of certainty and clarified the eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?"
The Patriarch said, "Although you spoke with your mind, I have already known it with my mind. Simply prepare yourself for ordination; why worry that I am not a sage?
Having heard this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately granted him ordination, as well as to five hundred dragon followers, and conferred the full precepts upon them all.
He spoke to him again, saying: "I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury. Listen attentively to these verses:
'The dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest—this is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). To awaken to this dharma of hiding and manifesting is neither ignorance nor wisdom.'"
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was a native of Western India. He was also named Nāgasena. He first received the Dharma from Venerable Māra.
Later, he traveled to South India. The people of that country were largely devoted to meritorious deeds; for their sake, the Patriarch...

He preached the Dharma. They said to one another, "Among all people, there is no one whose meritorious karma is greater than ours; yet we speak in vain of 'Buddha-nature. Who among us can truly perceive it?
The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride.

The men asked, "Is Buddha-nature large or small? The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small; neither broad nor narrow. It is without merit and without retribution; it neither dies nor is born."
Hearing that the principle was superior, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then manifested a body of sovereign mastery upon his seat, like a full moon disc;
the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and could not perceive the Patriarch’s physical form.

Among the crowd was the son of an elder named Kāṇadeva, who asked the assembly, "Do you recognize this phenomenon? The assembly replied, "We have never seen such a thing with our own eyes; how can we identify it?"
Devadatta said: "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to show us.
How do we know this? It is because through the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*), his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.
Having finished speaking, the wheel-mark vanished, and he returned to his original seat, whereupon he spoke this verse: "The body manifests the form of the full moon, To represent all..."
The essence of the Buddha’s body preaches the Dharma without form; its function is discernment, not sound or color.

When the assembly heard these verses, they suddenly awakened to non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life to seek liberation. The Patriarch immediately shaved their hair and commanded the holy ones to confer the full precepts upon them.
Previously, there had been more than five thousand followers of external paths in that country who practiced great illusory arts and were venerated by the masses; the Patriarch converted them all.
He caused them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. He further composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, which he bequeathed to the world.
Later, he addressed his chief disciple, Kāṇadeva, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to my verse:
'In order to clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, one speaks of the logic of liberation; yet within the Dharma, the mind does not find proof.'"
Without anger and without joy.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśāla. Initially...
Seeking to cultivate meritorious deeds while also delighting in debate, he later went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he was about to reach the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent an attendant with a bowl full of water and placed it before his seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable One immediately thrust a needle into it and proceeded inside.
They were delighted by their mutual accord. (Jin-su Wu remarked: "Kāṇadeva pierced his own brain to enter the lacquer basin; even now, there is no one who can save him.")
"If you can save it, return my head to me. Nāgārjuna then preached the Dharma for him; without rising from his seat, he manifested the form of a lunar disc.

Only his voice was heard, but his physical form was not seen. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This auspicious sign signifies that the Master has manifested his Buddha-nature, demonstrating that the preaching of the Dharma transcends both sound and form.
Having received the Dharma, the Patriarch later traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu. There lived an elder there.
He was named Brahmā Śuddhoda. One day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden; they were of exquisite flavor.
Only the elder and his second son, Rāhula, would gather and eat them. As soon as they were gathered, the mushrooms would grow back again.
None of the other relatives could see them. Knowing this to be the result of past causes, the grandfather went to their home, whereupon the elder asked him:
As for the reason, the Patriarch said: "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu. However, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Way was not yet clear;
because he had merely received the faithful offerings in vain, his retribution was to become a wooden fungus.

It is only because you and your son made offerings with such sincerity that you are able to enjoy it, whereas others could not. He then asked the elder how old he was, and the elder replied: "I am seventy-nine."
The Patriarch then spoke a verse, saying: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, they shall return to this body to repay the offerings of the faithful.

When you reach the age of eighty-one, this tree will no longer grow. Having heard the verse, the elder was filled with even greater admiration and submission, and said: "I, your disciple, am already advanced in years and infirm."
[The son] said, "I am unable to serve my teacher. I pray that you allow me to leave behind your second son so that I may follow you and renounce the householder's life.

The Patriarch said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this boy would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. Our meeting today surely accords with our past causes.

He immediately shaved his hair, took him as an attendant, and transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "To one who is destined to transmit the Dharma, I have explained the principle of liberation."
In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; it has neither end nor beginning.
The Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, was a native of Kapilavastu. While traveling to Śrāvastī to propagate the teachings, he arrived there.
In the city of Raṭa, there was a river called Suvarṇavālukā (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine. In its midstream, the reflections of the five Buddhas appeared.
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away; there dwells the holy one Saṃghanandin.
A thousand years after the Buddha’s passing, he shall succeed to the holy position. Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples up the current.

Ascending further, he arrived at the place where Saṃghanandi was sitting peacefully in meditative absorption. The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him; after twenty-one days had passed, Nandi finally arose from his concentration.
The Patriarch asked, "Is your body in concentration, or is your mind in concentration? Nandi replied, "Both body and mind are in concentration.
The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are in concentration, how can there be entering and emerging? Nandi replied, "Although there is entering and emerging..."
He did not lose the characteristic of meditative concentration. It was as if gold were in a well; the essence of the gold is eternally quiescent.

The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or whether the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself has neither motion nor stillness. What is it that enters and exits? Nan-ti said, "If one speaks of the motion and stillness of the gold, what is it that enters and exits?
If one speaks of the gold entering and exiting, the gold is neither moving nor still. The Patriarch said, "If the gold is in the well, what is this 'gold' that comes out? If...
"Gold comes out of the well. What is it that remains? Nanti said, "If the gold has come out of the well, then what remains is not gold.
If the gold is still in the well, then what has come out is not the object. The Patriarch said, "This principle is not so. Nanti said, "That principle is not established.
The Patriarch said, "This principle must fall. Nanti said, "That principle is not accomplished. The Patriarch said, "That principle is not accomplished; my principle [is]."
"It is accomplished. Nandi said, "Although my thesis is established, the Dharma is not 'I'. The Patriarch said, "My thesis is already established, for I am without 'I'.
Nandi asked, "Since I am without 'I', what further meaning is established? The Patriarch said, "Because I am without 'I'."
Thus, your argument is established. Nandi said, "Virtuous one, who is your teacher that you have attained this non-self?
The Master replied, "My teacher is Gaṇadeva; he realized this non-self. He then answered with a verse: "Since I am already without self, You must see my 'I.
If you take me as your teacher, Know that my 'I' is not a self. Nandi’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately requested ordination.
[The Sixth Patriarch] said, "Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me. Thereupon, the Patriarch charged Saṃghanandi with the transmission of the Dharma-eye, speaking this verse:
"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; Neither grasping nor abandoning. The Dharma has neither the mark of existence nor non-existence."
How did he arise from within and without?
The Seventeenth Patriarch,
Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of the city of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak, and constantly praised the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents with a verse, saying:
"I bow my head to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I pay homage to my Mother of flesh and blood. I now wish to leave the home-life; I pray you will have pity on me.
His parents tried to stop him firmly, so much so that he refused to eat for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the home-life while remaining at home, and he was given the name Seng.
Kāṇḍī further appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He often thought to himself, "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, as a divine light shone down upon him, he saw a path that was level and smooth.
Unconsciously, he walked slowly for about ten *li* until he reached a great cliff, where there was a stone cave.
Thereupon, he remained in quiet seclusion within. When the father lost his son, he immediately banished Śrīlāta from the country and went abroad to search for him, but did not know where he was.

After ten years had passed, the Patriarch, having received the Dharma and the prediction of his attainment, traveled through various lands to spread the teaching until he reached the kingdom of Mathurā.

Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of joy and physical well-being to their bodies and minds, yet they did not know its cause. The Patriarch said, "This is the Way..."
"This is the wind of virtue; surely a sage shall appear in this world to continue the lamp of the patriarchs.
Having spoken thus, he employed his supernatural powers to lead the great assembly through the mountains and valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak.

He said to the assembly, "Upon the summit of this peak there is a purple cloud shaped like a canopy; a sage dwells here. He then wandered with the great assembly for a long while until they beheld the mountain.
He left. A young boy holding a round mirror went straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? The boy said, "A hundred years.
The Patriarch said, "You are still quite young; why do you say you are a hundred years old? The boy said, "I do not understand the principle;
I am truly a hundred years old. The Patriarch said, "Are you skilled in wits? The boy said, "The Buddha said: 'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not comprehend the Buddhas...'"
[The Master said: "It is not as good as attaining decisive realization on the very day of one's birth. The Patriarch asked, "What does that which is in your hand signify?
The boy replied, "The great perfect mirror of all Buddhas; inside and out, it is free from flaw or obscuration. Two people see it together; their minds and eyes are alike.
When his parents heard the boy’s words, they immediately relinquished him so that he might leave the household life. The Patriarch took him to his own place and transmitted [the Dharma] to him.

Having completed his observance of the precepts, he was named Gayāśata. On another occasion, hearing the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells, the Patriarch asked, "Are the bells ringing, or is it the wind?
Śata replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that ring; it is my own mind that rings. The Patriarch asked, "And who is this mind?
Śata replied, "Because both are utterly tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! You are the one who shall succeed to my Way."
To whom did he entrust the Dharma-eye? He bestowed it upon Subhūti. The verse says: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth;
The ground arises from conditions. Condition and seed do not obstruct one another; Flower and fruit are likewise so."
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayasata.
The Venerable Gayasata was a native of the country of Mathura. His mother dreamed of a great deity holding a mirror.
Consequently, she became pregnant and gave birth after seven days. Her body was as translucent as lapis lazuli; she never required bathing, for she was naturally fragrant and pure.
From childhood, she delighted in solitude and her speech was unlike that of ordinary children. While out walking with a mirror in hand, she encountered the Venerable Nandī and received ordination.
Later, leading her disciples, she arrived at the kingdom of Mahācīna. There she perceived an extraordinary fragrance emanating from the house of a certain Brahmin. The Patriarch...
As he was about to enter the house, the master of the house, Kumāralata, asked, "Who are these followers? Bodhidharma replied, "They are disciples of the Buddha.
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, his spirit was suddenly stirred; he immediately closed the door. After a long while, Bodhidharma knocked on the door.
Ratna said, "There is no one in this house. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that says there is no one? Upon hearing these words, Ratna knew he was an extraordinary person;
he quickly opened the gate to welcome him. The Patriarch said, "In the past, the World-Honored One prophesied:

'A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a great being shall appear in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and flourish the profound transformation. Now you have encountered me; you are surely destined for this auspicious occasion."
Thereupon Kumāralata, having awakened the knowledge of his past lives, surrendered with sincerity to leave the household life. Once he had received full ordination, the Dharma was entrusted to him.

He spoke in verse: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, The causal conditions can cause the sprout to emerge. If these conditions do not obstruct one another, Then birth will surely arise; otherwise, it will not."

The Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Mo-zhi (Greater Yuezhi). In a former life, he was a deva of sovereign power (the sixth heaven of the desire realm);
upon seeing the jeweled necklaces of a Bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell [to be reborn] in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Lì (the second heaven of the Desire Realm) heard Kausika preach the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Because the Dharma is supreme, he ascended to the Brahma Heaven (the Form Realm).
Because his faculties were sharp, he skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma; the various deities honored him as their teacher.
When the time arrived to continue the ancestral lineage, he descended to the country of the Yuezhi. Later, he reached the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Great Being named Jayata.
Question: "The parents of my household have long placed their faith in the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by illness, and whatever they undertake never turns out as they wish.
Meanwhile, the neighbors next door have long followed the occupation of *caṇḍālas*, yet their bodies are always vigorous and healthy, and everything they do succeeds.
Why are they so fortunate while we are so guilty? The Patriarch said: "Why should you doubt this? Furthermore, regarding the retribution for good and evil—"

There are three periods [of time]. Ordinary people, seeing only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, and that the rebellious meet with good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune, claim that cause and effect do not exist and that sin and merit are empty.
They fail to realize, however, that shadow and echo follow one another without the slightest deviation;

even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they shall never perish. At that time, Śāṇakavāsin, having heard these words, was suddenly relieved of his doubts. The Patriarch said: "You..."

Although one has already gained faith in the three types of karma, one has not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion, that delusion exists because of consciousness, that consciousness depends upon non-awakening, and that non-awakening depends upon the mind.
This mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
"Tranquil and still; numinous and alert. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be one with all Buddhas. All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions.
Jñānagupta (Sha-ye-duo) received these words and grasped their meaning; his latent wisdom was immediately awakened, and he earnestly sought ordination.
Once he had received full precepts, the Master entrusted him with the Eye of the Dharma, saying in verse: "In the fundamental nature, there is originally no arising."
To those who seek [enlightenment], he said: "Since there is nothing to be attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts as to whether it is resolved or not?
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep; he transformed and guided [sentient beings].

[His lifespan was] immeasurable. Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the sudden teaching (dun-jiao). Among the assembly of students there, they exclusively esteemed dialectical debate.

Their leader was named Vāśpa (translated here as *Biànxíng*, "Universal Pervader"), who always ate only one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day, and was pure and free from desire;
thus, he was a refuge for the multitude. When the Patriarch [Bodhidharma] was about to convert him, he first asked that assembly: "This Universal Pervader..."
"Daowu, can one who practices the dhūtas attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly said, "Our master is diligent; why should he not be able to?
The Patriarch said, "Your master is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would all be the root of delusion.
The assembly asked, "What virtues does the Venerable One possess that you should disparage our master? The Patriarch said, "I do not seek the Way."
I am not inverted. I do not pay homage to the Buddha, nor do I treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, nor do I eat at irregular intervals. I am not content with little, yet I have no craving. My mind harbors no expectations.
"This is called the Way. When Vyāghrapāda heard this, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully offered praise.

The Patriarch again addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you understand my words? The reason I acted thus was because his desire for the Way was so intense; had the strings been too tight, they would have snapped.
Therefore, I did not praise him, but instead caused him to abide in the ground of peace and bliss and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas. He further told Vyāghrapāda:
Caryā said, "I have just rebuked you before the assembly; are you not troubled in your heart, O virtuous one?

Viśvāmitra replied, "I recall that seven kalpas ago, when I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Happiness, the Teacher and the wise Moon-Pure (Candraprabha) prophesied to me that before long I would realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin.
At that time, a Bodhisattva named Mahāprabha appeared in the world; because I was old, I [struggled]..."

I paid my respects with a staff in hand. The Master rebuked me, saying, "To honor a son while slighting a father—how vulgar this is! At that time, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to point it out to me.
The Master said, "When you prostrated before the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, you leaned your staff against the wall so that it struck the face of the painted Buddha.
Because of this arrogance, you lost two stages of fruition. Since I have taken this upon myself to repent, whenever I hear any harsh words, [I reflect on this]."
"It is like the wind and like an echo; how much more so now that you have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar—would you instead give rise to feverish affliction?
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said: "You have long planted manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage.
Listen to my verse: 'In a single word, one accords with the non-arising; it is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand in this way, one penetrates all phenomena.'"
The principle is concluded.
The Twenty-first Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (婆修盤頭), was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha. His father...
Guanggai’s mother was named Yan Yi. Her family was wealthy, yet she had no son. Her parents prayed at a Buddhist stupa, seeking an heir.
One night, her mother dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dark; upon waking, she found herself pregnant. Seven days later, there appeared an arhat.
The assembly of worthy sages arrived at his residence. Guanggai prepared the ritual offerings, and the assembly of sages sat upright to receive them.

When Yan stepped forward to bow, the assembly of sages rose from their seats and said, "Return the courtesy to the Great Being of the Dharma-body. Guanggai could not fathom the reason for this, so he took a precious jewel and knelt to present it.
The assembly of sages accepted it immediately, without any sign of declining or expressing thanks. Unable to restrain himself, Guanggai asked:
"I am a man of honor; I did not disregard your prostration. What virtue does my wife possess that you, Venerable One, would avoid her?

The assembly of noble ones replied, "We accepted your prostration and received your pearl; it was for the sake of your great merit. Your wife carries a holy child who, upon birth, shall become a lamp for the world and a sun of wisdom."
Therefore, I avoided them. The assembly of worthies spoke again, saying: "Your wife shall give birth to two sons. One shall be named Vāsava-bandhu, whom I hold in high esteem;
the other shall be named Cūḍapanthaka (which means 'Son of the Wild Magpie'). Long ago, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat, a magpie nested upon his head.
Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, the magpie received its karmic retribution by becoming the King of Nādi."
The Buddha had prophesied: "In the second five-hundred-year period, you shall be born into the family of Viśākhā in the city of Rājagṛha as a brother to a noble one;
now there is no discrepancy. One month later, she indeed gave birth to two sons.

When the Venerable Vāsudatta reached the age of fifteen, he paid homage to the Arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life. Moved by his sincerity, the Bodhisattva Vibhāṣa conferred the precepts upon him.
While traveling to transform [beings], he arrived at the kingdom of Nādi. Its king was named Constant Sovereignty (Nityeśvara). He had two sons:
the first was named Mahāla, and the second was named Maṇḍala. The king asked his grandfather, "How does the local custom of Rājagṛha differ from this? The grandfather replied:
"In that land, three Buddhas have appeared in the past; now, in this kingdom, there are two masters who provide guidance. The King asked, "Who are these two masters?

The Patriarch replied, "The Buddha prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two Great Beings of supernatural power who would leave the household life and succeed to the holy lineage."
"This is none other than the king’s second son, Maṇḍara. Although my virtue is meager, I dare to accept him as one.
The king said, "Truly as the Venerable One has spoken; I shall renounce this son to become a śramaṇa. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, Great King! You are able to follow the Buddha’s intent.
He then conferred the full precepts and transmitted the Dharma to him with this verse: "Like bubbles and illusions, they are equally unimpeded; how [can there be attachment]?"
Without realizing this, one fails to penetrate the Dharma within it; it is neither of the present nor of the past.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍarava, was the son of King Nityodyukta of the country of Nādi. He was [of such] age...
Thirty: He encountered the patriarch Vasu and left the household life to receive the transmission of the Dharma.

Upon arriving in Western India, he met the king named Deva, who was of the Gautama clan and had turned toward the Buddha Vehicle. The king practiced with diligent vigor; one day, while at his place of practice, [he saw the Master].
A small stupa appeared, and when the king wished to take it to offer worship, the assembly was unable to lift it.

The king immediately convened a great assembly of the three groups—the practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), those in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and those of incantations (*mantra*). He intended to ask about his doubts. At that time, the Patriarch also attended this assembly;

none of these three groups could discern [the cause], so the Patriarch extensively explained to the king the origin of the stupa and that its current appearance was due to the power of the king’s merit.
It was brought about by this. When the King heard these words, he said, "A Supreme Sage is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not lasting.

He immediately transmitted the throne to his crown prince and went forth as a monk under the Patriarch. After seven days, he realized the fruit of Arhatship. The Patriarch comforted and instructed him deeply, saying, "While you remain in this kingdom, skillfully deliver others.
Now there is one of great capacity for the Dharma in a foreign land; I shall go there to transform them. Upon receiving this, [the King] said: "I have been delivered."
The Master said, "I manifest my traces throughout the ten directions; when you move your thoughts, I shall arrive. Why trouble yourself by coming here? The Patriarch replied, "So be it.

Thereupon, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the Bhikṣu Hralena of the country of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna), saying, "While you are in that country, teaching the flock of cranes, you are about to realize the fruit of the Way;
you should know this for yourself. At that time, Hralena was expounding the Sūtras for King Ratramudrā.
In the *Luo-ge* (Verses on the Stone), it is recorded that suddenly a strange fragrance appeared, forming into clusters. The King asked, "What omen is this?
Ratnamati replied, "This is the fragrant precursor sent by the patriarch Mañjuśrī from Western India, who is about to arrive to transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. The King said:
"What is the spiritual power of this master like? Le-na replied, "This master has received a distant prediction from the Buddha that he shall widely proclaim the profound transformation in this land.
At that time, the King and He-le-na both paid homage from afar.

The Patriarch, knowing this, immediately took leave of the bhikṣu De-du and went to the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna), where he accepted the offerings of the King and He-le-na. Later, He-le-na questioned the Patriarch.
He said: "I have resided in the forest for nine *śatakas* (India reckons one year as one *śataka*). I have a disciple named Nāgaputra, who was intelligent from childhood;
though I have investigated his origins throughout the three periods of time, I could find no root of his past. My master said:
'This boy was born into a Brahmin family in the Land of Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*) during the fifth *kalpa*. He once offered sandalwood to a Buddhist temple to serve as a mallet.'"

When the bell was struck, he received the retribution of keen intelligence and was revered by the assembly. Again, [the Emperor] asked, "By what karmic conditions did I cause this flock of cranes to appear?
The Patriarch said, "In the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu. You were about to attend a gathering at the Dragon Palace, and all your disciples wished to follow you.
You observed that among the five hundred members of the assembly, there was not a single person capable of managing the exquisite offerings. At that time, the various..."
The disciple said, "Master, you often preached the Dharma that those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma. Now, since this is not so, what 'saintliness' can there be?
You then immediately ordered him to attend the assembly. From the time you abandoned this life to take up another, you traveled through various kingdoms transforming beings.
As for your five hundred disciples, because their merit was slight and their virtue thin, they were born among the feathered tribes. Now, moved by your kindness, they have become cranes.
The assembly followed him. Helana asked, "By what skillful means can you cause them to attain liberation? The Patriarch replied, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure;
you should listen and receive it, so that you may transform beings until the end of time. He then spoke this verse: "The mind turns following the myriad objects;
where it turns, the reality is profound. If, while following the flow, one recognizes one's own nature, there will be neither joy nor sorrow."
The Twenty-third Patriarch, Venerable Holena, was a native of the country of Mo-zhi (Yuezhi). His clan was Brahmin; his father was named Qiansheng, and his mother was Jinguang.
Because they had no son, she prayed before the golden pillar of the Seven Buddhas, whereupon she dreamed of the summit of Mount Sumeru.
There was a divine child who, holding a golden ring, said, "I have come. Upon waking, [the mother] found she was pregnant.

When the child was seven years old, he wandered through the villages and saw the vulgar sacrifices of the common people. He entered the temple and rebuked them, saying, "You recklessly invoke calamity and fortune to delude the people.
You waste livestock and grain every year, causing immense harm. Having finished speaking, the temple structure suddenly collapsed. Because of this, the village...
The community called him the Holy Son. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life. At thirty, he met the Venerable Maṇḍara, who transmitted to him the treasury of the Dharma-eye.
He traveled to Central India to propagate the teachings; there, the king was named Abhayasāgara, who held profound faith in the Buddha-way.

As the Patriarch was in the midst of expounding the True Dharma, the King suddenly saw two individuals dressed in vermilion and plain white robes bowing before him. The King asked, "Who are these people?
The Patriarch replied, "These are the Sun and Moon Devas. Because I previously preached the Dharma for them, they have come to pay their respects.
After a long while, they vanished, and only a wondrous fragrance remained. The King asked, "How many realms do the lands of the sun and moon comprise? The Patriarch—
He said, "The worlds transformed by the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas each contain ten billion Mount Merus, suns, and moons; if I were to explain this in detail, I could not finish.
When the King heard this, he was filled with joy. At that time, the Patriarch propagated the Unsurpassed Way and delivered those with whom he had a karmic connection.

Because his senior disciple, the Dragon Prince, had died young, there was an elder brother named Siṃha who was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory; he served a Brahmin teacher. His teacher—
After he had passed away, [the monk] took refuge in the Venerable One and asked, "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind?
The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, there is no place for the mind to be applied. [The monk] asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the Buddha-work?
The Patriarch said, "If you have any application, it is not merit. If you have no action, that itself is Buddha-work. As the Sūtra says: "That which I have performed..."
"...merit. Because there is no 'mine' (mama-kāra). Having heard these words, Shizi immediately entered the Buddha-wisdom.

At that time, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of atmospheric phenomenon is this? Shizi replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth;
furthermore, there are five paths of black vapor stretching horizontally across its midst. The Patriarch asked, "What is the omen of this? [Shizi] said, "Do not..."
"This can be known," [Nanyue] said. The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India.
It shall cling to your person; I am about to pass away. I now entrust the Dharma-eye to you; guard and uphold it well. He then spoke a verse:
"When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable. When it is clearly understood that nothing is to be attained, Then at the moment of attainment..."
It is not said that he attained realization.
Regarding the twenty-fourth patriarch, Bhikṣu Siṃha:
he was a native of Central India, a Brahmin by caste, who attained the Dharma.
While traveling, he arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was a man named Parika who had originally practiced dhyāna-vipaśyanā;
thus, there were five groups of followers who clung to signs, abandoned signs, or maintained silence through their meditative concentration and insight.

The Patriarch interrogated and transformed them, and while the four groups all remained silent and submitted in their hearts, only the meditation master Dharmadatta, having heard that the four groups had been rebuked, came forward in a state of indignant resentment. The Patriarch—
[The Master] said, "Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Why have you come here? Now that you have arrived here, why do you say you are practicing concentration?
He replied, "Although I have come here, my mind remains undisturbed. Concentration follows the person who practices it; how could it reside in a particular location?

The Master said, "Since you, Virtuous One, have come, your practice has also arrived. Since there is no fixed location, how can it depend on the person who practices it? He replied, "Because concentration is practiced by the person, it is not..."

The man said, "I practice meditation; I shall come here. I have practiced that meditation constantly. The Patriarch said, "It is not that the person practices meditation; rather, it is that meditation practices the person.
Therefore, when you come here of your own accord, who will be practicing the meditation? He replied, "It is like a pure, bright pearl, with no obscurations inside or out.
If meditation is thoroughly mastered, it must necessarily be like this. The Patriarch said, "If meditation were thoroughly mastered, it would indeed resemble a bright pearl. But now, I see that you—"

[The Master] said: "This is not the nature of a pearl. The other replied: "That pearl is transparent and clear; both inside and out it is perfectly still. My mind is undisturbed, just as this [pearl] is pure.
The Patriarch said: "That pearl has no interior or exterior. How can you, O worthy one, claim it is 'still'? Impure things do not waver."
This samādhi is not the pure [state]. Damodara received the patriarch’s awakening; his mind-ground became brilliantly clear.

Once the patriarch had gathered the fivefold assembly and his fame spread far and wide, he began to seek a Dharma heir. He encountered an elder who led forth his son and asked the patriarch, "This boy is named Sthavira.
From birth his left hand has been clenched into a fist, and though he is now grown, he has never been able to open it. We pray that Your Reverence..."
This was to reveal his past causes. When the Patriarch saw him, he immediately reached out his hand and said, "Give me back my pearl.
The boy quickly opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In a previous life, I was a monk named Vatsa.
Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea, I received this pearl as an offering and entrusted it to him. That he now returns my pearl is but natural."

The elder then renounced his son for the monastic life. The Patriarch immediately conferred upon him full ordination; because of these prior conditions, he was named Vasiṣṭha. The Patriarch then said to him:
"My teacher had a secret prophecy that you would encounter hardship before long. The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma is now transmitted to you.
You must protect it so that it may universally moisten all future generations. He spoke in verse: "The true teaching is known..."
At the moment of seeing, both knowing and seeing are the mind; when the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing, and this knowing and seeing is right here and now.
Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Suta, instructing him to go to another land and transform beings according to their capacities.

Having received these instructions, Suta traveled directly to South India. The Patriarch, however, felt that he could not evade the inevitable and remained alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, in his own country...
There were two non-Buddhist practitioners, one named Māmuta and the other named Durlabha. Having studied various magical arts, they plotted together to incite a rebellion;
they then stole the appearance of Śākya disciples and secretly entered the royal palace. They said, "If we do not succeed, the guilt shall fall upon the sons of the Buddha.
Since the sorcery was committed by themselves, the calamity would surely follow immediately. The King indeed became enraged and said, "I have long placed my heart's devotion in the Three [Jewels]..."
"O Treasure, why have you brought about such harm as this? He immediately ordered the destruction of the monastery and the expulsion of the Śākya community.

Furthermore, he personally took up a sword and went to the Venerable One’s quarters, asking, "Master, have you realized the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied, "I have already realized the emptiness of the aggregates."

The king asked, "Have you transcended birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I have already transcended birth and death. The king said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head.
The Patriarch replied, "This body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head? The king then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable One's head.

White milk surged upward several feet high. The King’s right arm also spun off and fell to the ground. He passed away after seven days. Xuansha Shibei said: "Whether great or small, Master Śāriputra did not even know how to act as the master.
Xuanjue then challenged him: "Tell me, was the blow struck or not? Fenyang Wude Zhenzao provided a different response: "I knew the Master would not be stingy.

Xuedou Chongxian said: "A masterful sovereign; he naturally possesses his own ground. Huanglong Huinan said: "I, Huanglong, wish to ask Xuedou: Since he is a masterful sovereign, why did his arm fall off? Jingshan Daowu Congyue said: "The fellow Meng Babang goes about it in this way again."

Tiantong Hua said: "Xuansha said, 'Great or small, this Venerable One does not even know how to take charge. The Master said: 'A fellow who follows along with the coarse woolen rug. Xuange asked: "Tell me, did he strike home or not?

The Master said: "Using shrimp to catch turtles. Fenyang said differently: "I know you do not begrudge [the truth]. The Master said: "Taking a mistake for a mistake. Xuedou said: "The master ruler has his natural place. The Master said: "Drawing water and setting fire. Cuiyan said: "At that time, the Patriarch extended his neck, and the King raised his sword. The Master said: "..."

"At that time, was there anyone who could have counseled him to stop? To this day, no one has been able to resolve this public case (kung-an). How would you monks of today resolve it? The Master said, "Do not try to talk in your sleep. Bajiao said, "Selling jewels and bumping into a blind Persian. The Master said, "This is the crime of slandering another.

Langye said, "Jibin had a fine sword, but alas, the sword had no eye. "The Venerable One had a fine lion, yet he did not know how to turn it back against itself. The Master said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled. He then continued, "This one..."

"You fellows have been utterly exterminated by this mountain monk. Do you still see Venerable Siṃha? He suddenly picked up his staff, struck once, and said: "Cultivate yourself and be careful in your conduct; fear bringing disgrace upon your ancestors. The *Gufeng Shensong* (Deep Verses from Solitary Peak) says: "Originally a man of the mountains, I love to speak of mountain talk.
In the fifth month, I sell pine-wind; In the human world, it would likely be priceless."
The Twenty-fifth Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (Póshè斯多) Bodhisattva:
He was a native of Kaśmīra. His clan was Brahmin; his father was named Śāntacaryā (Jìxíng), and his mother was Nityasukhā (Cháng ānlè).
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently became pregnant. When he was born, his left hand was in a fist.

Handu met the Venerable Siṃha, who revealed his past causes and secretly transmitted the Heart-Seal (cittamudrā) to him. Later, he traveled to South India and reached Central India, where the king was named Kaniṣka;
the king paid him homage and provided offerings. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist teacher known as Nirātma-guru.
Previously, the King had held him in high esteem. Envious of Bodhidharma’s arrival, he wished to debate with him, hoping that by winning, he might consolidate his own position.
Thus, before the King, he said to Bodhidharma, "I understand silent debate; it does not rely on verbal expression. Bodhidharma asked, "Who shall determine victory and defeat?
He replied, "We do not contend for victory or defeat; we seek only the meaning. Bodhidharma asked, "What do you take to be 'meaning'? He—
He said, "I take 'no-mind' (wúxīn) to be the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can you grasp the meaning?

He replied, "When I speak of 'no-mind,' it is a designation, not the meaning. The Patriarch said, "When you speak of 'no-mind,' it is a designation, not the meaning; when I speak of 'non-mind' (fēixīn), it is the meaning, not the designation.
He asked, "If it is the meaning and not the designation, who is able to discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "As for your 'designation is not the meaning,' this..."

"What is the name of that which is called 'name'? He replied, "It is for the sake of discerning what is not meaning; therefore, it is called 'the nameless name. The Patriarch said, "If the name is already not a name, then the meaning is also not meaning. Who is it that discerns? What is there to be discerned?
Thus they exchanged questions and answers fifty-nine times, until the outsider was silenced and submitted in faith.

(Bazhao Qing said: "It is like an elephant or a horse that is unruly and difficult to tame; one must apply various forms of pain and suffering until they reach the very marrow of the bone before it is finally subdued. Dayang Xuan said: "Like a clam...")

The two mandarin ducks held each other fast; both died in the hands of the fisherman. It is said: "What use is there for elaborate words? Jingshan Daowu said: "Bodhidharma, what use is there for such distress? At that time, had he seen him say, 'I ask the Master to discuss this in silence, without resorting to speech,'" [the outcome would have been different].

He then said, "The meaning has fallen. Is there anyone here now who can engage in a silent debate with Miaoxi? Perhaps some monk might come forward and say, "The meaning has fallen," to which I would reply, "I know you are making your living inside a ghost cave.

Chushi Qi said: "If I were the twenty-fifth patriarch, as soon as I saw a non-Buddhist enter the gate, I would strike him out with a staff. Would that not make me a true man? Why wait for him to say, 'Please, Master, let us debate in silence,' and then go back and forth fifty-nine times? That would be far, far removed from the truth.
At that time, the Patriarch suddenly turned his face north, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying: "My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, today..."
Encountering these hardships, he took his leave of the king and traveled south, reaching the Southern Heavens (Dakṣiṇāpatha). There he lived in seclusion within the mountain valleys.

At that time, the king of that land was named Devaśrī (Heavenly Virtue), who welcomed him and offered him sustenance. The king had two sons: the first was named Guṇottara (Superior Virtue), who was fierce and violent yet possessed of great physical vigor;
the second was named Ratnamati (Jewel Mind), who was gentle and mild but had suffered from chronic illness since childhood. The patriarch then explained the law of cause and effect to them.
The King immediately resolved his doubts. Furthermore, there was a master of incantations who harbored resentment toward the Patriarch’s Way;

he secretly placed poison in food and drink. The Patriarch knew of this yet ate it, causing the practitioner to suffer misfortune instead. He then went forth to join the Patriarch as a renunciant, who immediately conferred the full ordination upon him.
Sixty years later, Emperor De-sheng ascended the throne; he again placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths and brought trouble upon the Patriarch. However—
As with Mita, who was imprisoned for offering remonstrance, the King suddenly questioned Nanyue Huizhao, saying, "In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive teachings have long been absent.
As for what you have transmitted, Master, to which school does it belong? Nanyue replied, "In Your Majesty's kingdom, there has indeed been no false dharma since ancient times.
That which I have obtained is precisely the Buddha-dharma. The King asked, "It has been twelve hundred years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. From whom did you receive it, Master? Nanyue—
[The Master] said: "The Great Being Dīpaṃkara personally received the Buddha’s seal; it was transmitted successively down to the twenty-fourth generation, the Venerable Siṃha.
I received it from him. The King asked: "I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha could not escape execution;
how then could he transmit the Dharma to later generations? The Patriarch replied: "When my teacher’s danger had not yet arisen, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the dharma-verses."
To manifest the lineage of his teacher, the King asked, "Where is that robe? The Patriarch immediately took the robe out from his bag and showed it to the King. The King ordered it to be burned;
though the five colors remained vividly distinct, the robe was as it was when the firewood was consumed. The King then felt remorse and paid homage to the Lion (Śrī).

Once the true successor was clearly established, he pardoned Guṇamati. Guṇamati then requested to leave the household life. The Patriarch asked him, "If you wish to leave the household life, you ought—"
"For what purpose? Maitreya replied, "If I were to leave the household life, I would not do that. The Patriarch asked, "What is it you would not do?

Prajñātāra replied, "As for my ordination, it was at Sālavana Monastery under the Tripiṭaka Master Upasena, who served as my preceptor for receiving the precepts. As for my spiritual teacher, he is the Great King’s paternal uncle, Bodhidharma.
When the King heard the Patriarch’s name, he was struck with awe for a long time and said, "I am a base and unworthy person..."
Upon succeeding to the throne, the king inclined toward heterodoxy and turned his back on the orthodox; forgetting his own honored uncle, he hastily commanded his attendants to specially invite him.
Daomu followed the envoys and arrived, whereupon he performed repentance for the king’s past transgressions. Hearing these admonitions, the king wept and apologized to Daomu.
The king further issued an edict for Sōng-seong to return to his own country. The great ministers reported, "Sōng-seong was exiled and cast down a cliff; he has now perished.
The king said to his ancestors, "The death of Sōng-seong is entirely my own doing. How may your great compassion cause me to be exempt from this sin?"
The Patriarch said, "Zongsheng is currently resting in seclusion among the crags; simply dispatch a messenger to summon him, and he will arrive immediately.

The King then sent a messenger into the mountains and indeed found Zongsheng sitting upright in meditative stillness. Upon receiving the summons, Zongsheng said, "I am deeply ashamed of Your Majesty's intent.
This poor monk has vowed to dwell among the crags and springs. Furthermore, Your Kingdom possesses a forest of virtuous sages, and Bodhidharma is Your Majesty’s—"

"Shu was the teacher of the Six Groups [of monks] and a dragon-elephant among those versed in the *Prātimokṣa*. I pray that Your Majesty will revere these two sages and thereby bring blessings to the imperial foundation.
Before the messenger had returned with his report, the Patriarch asked the King, "Do you know whether you have obtained the victory?

The King replied, "I do not yet know. The Patriarch said, "The first invitation has not yet arrived; upon the second command, he will surely come. After a long while, the messenger returned, and it was indeed just as the Patriarch had said.

The Master reflected that the conditions in China were now ripe and the time for his mission had arrived. He first took leave of the Patriarch’s stupa, then bid farewell to his fellow students, and finally went before the King.
He comforted and exhorted him, saying, "You should diligently cultivate pure deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem. My departure is not untimely;
within nine years, I shall surely return. Upon hearing the Master’s words, the King’s tears fell in profusion, and he said, "What sin has this country committed that [you must go]?"
"What auspiciousness does the land hold? Since you, my younger brother, have already formed a karmic connection there, it is not where I shall remain.

I only pray that you will not forget your fatherland and return early once your mission is complete. The King then prepared a great ship, filled it with various treasures, and personally led his ministers and officials to escort him to the seashore.

The Master voyaged across the vast deep for three full cycles of winter and summer before reaching the South Sea on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the gengzi year.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, received him with full state honors.
The memorial reached Emperor Wu. Upon reading the petition, the Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to invite him. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling.
The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond count.
What merit do these acts possess? The Master replied, "They possess no merit whatsoever. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit? The Master said, "These are merely matters of human..."
The causes for the minor fruits of the heavens are tainted (*sāsrava*); they follow form like a shadow. Though they exist, they are not real.
The Emperor asked, "What are true merits? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not sought through worldly means.
The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch replied, "Vast and open—there is no 'holy' one. The Emperor said:

"Who is it facing me? The Patriarch said, "I do not know. The Emperor did not understand. (Fenyang Shanzhao spoke on his behalf: "My disciple’s wisdom is shallow. Wuzu Ji spoke on his behalf: "Selling jewels, one encounters a blind Persian.

Baoning Yong spoke on behalf of the Emperor by sticking out his tongue to indicate it. Xuedou Xian composed a verse: "The Noble Truths are vast and open; how can one discern the mark? 'Who is it facing me?'—he replied, 'I do not know. From this, he crossed the river in secret."

"How can one avoid the thorns that grow? It would be better for the people of the land to pursue [the Way] before it is too late; for a thousand ages and ten thousand ages, they will only remain empty of remembrance. Do not merely remember! When the pure wind pervades the earth, what limit can there be? The Master looked around his attendants and said, "Is there still a Patriarch here?"
"Summon him here to wash the old monk's feet. The Patriarch, sensing that his timing was not yet ripe for conversion, secretly returned north of the Yangtze River on the nineteenth day of that month.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Luoyang; this was the first year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty.
He took up residence at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song. He sat facing a wall, remaining silent throughout the day; no one could fathom his intent, and thus he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin.
At that time, there was a monk named Shen Guang, a man of vast erudition who had long resided in the region of Yi and Luo.

Having extensively studied a multitude of books, he was skilled in discussing the profound principles of the Way. He often sighed, saying: "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi consist of ritual arts and worldly customs..."
The books of the *Zhuangzi* and the *Yijing* do not exhaust the wondrous principle. Recently I have heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma resides at Shaolin.
Since this sage is not far away, I shall surely go to reach the profound realm. Thus, I went there to attend upon him morning and evening. The Patriarch constantly sat upright, facing a wall.

Hearing no words of encouragement, Huiguang reflected to himself: "In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their veins to relieve the hunger of others, spread their hair to cover mud, and throw themselves off cliffs to feed tigers. If the ancients were such as this, what person am I?

On the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, it rained and snowed heavily. Huiguang stood firm and did not move. By dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees. The Master [Bodhidharma]...

Feeling pity, he asked, "You have been standing in the snow for a long time; what do you seek? Dharma-śāna wept with sorrow and said, "I only pray that the Master, out of compassion, will open the gate of ambrosia (*amṛta*) and extensively deliver all classes of beings.
The Patriarch said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast eons.
One must perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How could it be attained with small virtue, small wisdom, or a frivolous and arrogant mind?"

With his heart aspiring to the True Vehicle, he labored in vain through diligent toil. Upon hearing the Patriarch’s exhortation, he secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Patriarch.
The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma.
Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking is permissible. Thereupon, the Patriarch changed his name to [Huìnéng].
Huike said, "May I hear of the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Patriarch replied, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
Huike said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will grant you peace.
After a long silence, Huike said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unattainable. The Patriarch said, "I have granted you peace of mind."

Jing (Bazhao Che said: "The Vajra strikes the back of the clay man. Wuzu Jie said: "If it were truly so, what need would there have been for the coming from the West? Yunju Yuan said: "He had no wound himself; do not inflict injury upon him.

Nevertheless, though this be so, a single word is easy to utter, yet a team of four horses cannot overtake it once spoken. Baizhang Yuan’s verse says: "From beginning to end, seeking the mind, nothing can be found. In vast stillness, not a trace of the Shaolin man is seen. The old snow fills the courtyard, known once more for its cold; The nostrils remain, as ever, tucked above the upper lip.

Wuzu Yan, citing the passage where the Patriarch was asked to settle his mind, said: "Had Baizhang seen him at that time, he would have given him thirty blows. Why? Because others seeing this would have thought he was preaching the Dharma of settling the mind. But in the final analysis, what is it?"

The Bodhisattva Dragon King moves through the rain-soaked air, obstructing his body amidst upward-stretching layers of clouds. Zhaojue Qin asked: "At this very moment, where is the *dharmakāya*? Jingshan Gao composed a verse: "Seeking the mind, there is nowhere it can rest; I chew to pieces a glowing mass of iron.

Even if one opens their eyes with haughty pride, How can they compare to not being deceived by the Old Barbarian? Wanfeng Wei said: "Nine years facing the wall—concealing a blade in the dark. Standing in the snow waist-deep—thorns in the mud.

Shen Guang stepped on a poisoned arrow and was struck by doubt regarding the ox; yet he said, 'I sought the mind and could not find it. This is like being caught red-handed with the stolen goods. Bodhidharma said, 'I have finished settling your mind. Blood splatters against the Brahma Heaven. Now tell me: did he find the mind or not?"
"It can be attained. How would you explain it? Nine years passed. As he was about to return to India, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"The time has come. You should each speak of what you have attained. At that time, Dao Fu replied: "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters;
this constitutes the application of the Way. The Patriarch said: "You have attained my skin. Nizi Tongzhi said: "I..."
The Master said, "What you have now understood is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha: having seen it once, he never saw it again.
Dao Yu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist. In my place of vision, there is not a single dharma to be obtained.
The Master said, "You have attained my flesh. Finally, Huikě prostrated himself and stood in his place. The Master said:
He said, "You have obtained my marrow. Then, turning toward Huike, he told him: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa;
it was passed down through successive transmission until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it.

I also grant you this robe as a token of the Dharma. (Zhanfu Huai remarked: "When the Patriarch speaks thus, within a state devoid of calculation, he instead creates calculation. Within a state devoid of... )

Within the ruts of the tracks, they instead create further tracks. If one were to cause them to step upon the threshold of Deshan or Linji, they would have avoided being called "the wall-gazing barbarian monk" for nine years of cold sitting.

Even if it were so, one still could not avoid the calamity falling upon their descendants. Dayang Xuan said: "Tell me, if another person were to come forth, what would they obtain? He himself said: "Not obtained, not obtained. He also said: "The underlying meaning has not reached him. Cuiyan Zhi said: "The Second Patriarch was smeared right in his face by him."

"Do not speak of the marrow; you have not even touched the skin. Why, then, did he succeed to the Patriarchal seat? Wuzu Yan said: "At that time, had I seen those four men acting like this, I would have given each of them thirty blows of the staff. As for Baiyun himself, he too deserved twenty-nine blows, leaving one blow for all of you.

If among you there were anyone who could discern the sensation of pain, not only would you not have brought shame upon the former sages, but you would also have seen Baiyun. If, however, this is not yet the case, then when eating porridge or rice in the hall, you must chew it thoroughly.

I see many who swallow it whole. Jian’an Qing’s verse says: "Pressing on the eyes to create flowers, they establish the basis of their question; Having obtained its skin and marrow, they are deceived by it. Such blind fellows can only cause trouble; In the sixth month there is no frost, yet they say it is cold."

Gao Feng’s wondrous verse says: "The entire confession of death is offered in a single mouth; When sentiment is exhausted and principle reaches its limit, it is ultimately difficult to accommodate. If one were to debate the superiority or inferiority of skin and marrow, How could one see the five petals of the flower blooming red?

Wan Feng Wei says: "The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Yet Master Bodhidharma distinguished between skin and marrow—his making of distinctions was no small matter. Now tell me: did he have a Dharma to transmit to Shen Guang, or did he have no Dharma to transmit? If you say there was none, why did he entrust [the Dharma] at Shaoshi? If you say there was, [how can this be reconciled with the teaching that the Way is free from discrimination?]

Furthermore, tell me: what is it that you bestow? Huike said, "I pray the Master will point it out to me. The Patriarch said, "Internally, I transmit the Dharma-seal to accord with and realize the mind;
externally, I bestow the *kāṣāya* robe to establish the fundamental tenet. In future generations, when times grow thin and corrupt, doubts will compete to arise, saying:
'He is a man from the Western Heaven, while you are a son of this land. On what basis did he receive the Dharma, and by what do you prove it? You must now receive this..."
Regarding the Dharma of the robe: in the future, when difficulties arise, simply produce this robe along with my dharma verses to manifest its clarity; thus, your transformation will be unimpeded.

Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the transmission of the robe shall cease, yet the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra. There will be more than ten million who secretly correspond with it and achieve secret realization.
You must propagate it; do not disparage those who have not yet awakened. With a single thought, they may turn their faculties back toward the source and become identical to the Original [Nature].
"Very well. Listen to my verse: 'I have come to this land / To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. / One flower opens into five petals;
/ The fruiting of the result is accomplished naturally. The Patriarch further said: 'I have these four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which I also entrust to you.
This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter it. Since I arrived here, whenever..."
Five times I was poisoned. I have often tested this myself: when I placed a stone upon it, the stone would shatter.

Because I had not yet departed from South India, I came to this Eastern Land and beheld the Great Vehicle’s majestic presence within the Red County and Divine Land (China). Thereupon, I crossed the seas and traversed the deserts.
