I have sought a person for the sake of the Dharma, but our meeting was not yet harmonious; I appeared as if ignorant and dull-witted. Now that I have obtained your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled. (The Separate Record states:

When the Patriarch first resided at Shaolin Temple for nine years, he preached the Dharma for the Second Patriarch, teaching only: "Externally, cease all conditions; internally, let the mind be without breath. Let the mind be like a wall or a screen, and you may enter the Way.

Huike spoke variously about the nature and mind, but never once accorded with the principle. The Patriarch merely refuted his errors and did not explain the essence of the non-conceptual mind. Suddenly Huike said, "I have already ceased all conditions. The Patriarch asked, "Have you not fallen into annihilationism? Huike replied, "I have not.")
"Mie," the Patriarch said, "this is the essence of mind transmitted by all Buddhas; do not harbor further doubt. Having spoken thus, he went with his disciples to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen.
He stayed for three days. There was Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng, who had long admired the Buddha Vehicle.

He asked the Patriarch, "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the lineage is considered the ancestral source; what is the nature of that Way? The Patriarch replied, "It clarifies the mind-source of the Buddha, such that practice and understanding correspond."
He was named "The Patriarch" (Zu). He then spoke this verse: "One does not see evil and give rise to aversion; One does not observe good and strive to practice it.
One does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly; One does not cast off delusion to pursue enlightenment. Reaching the Great Way, one transcends all measure;
Penetrating the Buddha-mind, one goes beyond all degrees. Not sharing the same path as the ordinary or the sage— Transcendently, he is named 'The Patriarch'."

At that time, the Wei clan honored the teachings of Śākyamuni, and eminent practitioners of dhyāna were as numerous as a forest. Master Daoguang (Guangtong), the Vinaya Master, and Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master, were truly the phoenixes among the monastic community.
Upon witnessing the Master expounding the Way—rejecting external forms and pointing directly to the mind—they would frequently debate with him, their arguments rising like swarms of bees.
Yet, while the Patriarch [Bodhidharma] loftily propagated the profound breeze and universally bestowed the rain of Dharma, their limited perspectives proved unable to bear his greatness.

They vied with one another in giving rise to harmful intentions and repeatedly administered poison. By the sixth time, as his work of transformation was complete and he had found those to whom he could transmit the Dharma, he finally ceased to save them.
He passed away while sitting upright on the fifth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Yong’an era of Emperor Zhuang of the Wei dynasty, which was the year Wushen.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that same year, he was buried at Xiong’er Mountain, and a stupa was erected.
Three years later, while at Dinglin Monastery, Wei Songyun, returning from a mission to the Western Regions, encountered Sengzhu on the Pamir Mountains.
He saw the Master carrying a single shoe in his hand, striding alone and gracefully away. Songyun asked, "Where is the Master going? Sengzhu replied, "I am going to the West."
When Song Yun returned, he recounted the matter in full. When the disciples opened the tomb, there was only an empty coffin, with nothing but a pair of leather sandals remaining. (Heshan Fang said:

"Every time my late teacher, Xixin, brought up the story of the 'Single Sandal Returning to the West' to question his monks, it was truly difficult to clarify. Various quarters have some saying it refers to hidden and manifest forms; others saying one cannot have two; still others saying 'this alone is the reality.

If you think in such ways, you do not yet understand the Patriarch’s intent. Do you wish to see it? The verse says: 'Turbidity within purity, purity within turbidity— Do not say the qilin has grown a single horn. The road westward leads toward the east. )
It is so. In every great function, it is like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a chick; do not hesitate. (The subtle and essential spiritual mechanism is beyond calculation.
As for the Second Patriarch, Great Master Huìkě:
he was a native of Wúláo. His surname was Jī, and his father was Jí. Before there was a son, [the father]...

He once reflected to himself, "My family has honored the good; how could it be that we have no son? After he had prayed for a long time, one night he was moved by a supernatural light that illuminated his chamber.
His mother consequently became pregnant. When the child grew up, they named him Guang (Light) in commemoration of the auspicious sign of the light illuminating the room.

From childhood, his aspirations were extraordinary; he studied the *Shi* and *Shu* classics extensively and was particularly proficient in the profound principles of the Way (*xuanli*), yet he did not concern himself with managing family estates.
He delighted in wandering through mountains and waters. Later, upon reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a state of transcendent self-realization.

He then proceeded to Mount Xiangshan at Longmen in Luoyang, where he took ordination under the Chan Master Baojing. He received full precepts at Yongmu Temple and traveled among lecture halls, studying the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
At the age of thirty-three, he returned once more to Mount Xiangshan, where he remained in meditative seclusion throughout the day for another eight years. At that time—
In the midst of his silent meditation, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him, "You are about to receive the fruit of your practice;
why do you linger here? The Great Way is not far off; you should go south. Knowing that this was divine assistance, the Master changed his name to Shenguang (Divine Light).

The following day, he felt a pain in his head as if it were being pierced with needles. His teacher wished to treat it, but a voice from the air said, "This is the transformation of the bones; it is no ordinary pain."
The Patriarch then reported the matter of his vision of the deity to his master. The master examined the Patriarch’s cranial bone and saw that it rose up like five peaks.
He said, "Your marks are auspicious; you shall surely attain realization. As for the deity who directed you southward, this must be the Great Being Bodhidharma of Shaolin;
he will certainly be your teacher. Following these instructions, the Patriarch traveled to Shaoshi Mountain. There, he received the Dharma and transmitted it.

Regarding the history of his vestments, it is fully recorded in the chapter on Bodhidharma. After the Master entrusted his transformation at Shaolin and returned to the West, he succeeded in propagating the profound wind of the Dharma and extensively sought a dharma heir.
In the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, there came a layman over forty years of age who did not disclose his name or lineage;
he approached with formal salutations and asked the Patriarch: "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind ailment. I request—"

The Master was performing a rite of repentance for his transgressions. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgression so that I may repent it for you. After a long silence, the layman said, "I have searched for my transgression, but it cannot be found.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for your transgressions. You should dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

The layman said, "Now that I see the Master, I already know what the Sangha is; I only wonder, what are called the Buddha and the Dharma? The Patriarch said, "This very mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the..."
"This Dharma and the Buddha-Dharma are non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so.
The layman said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-Dharma—they are non-dual.

The Patriarch held him in high esteem. (Langye Huijiao said: "He still lacks the ability to say, 'What is this Brahma? Liangshan Guan, at the point where the search for sin can find nothing at all, asked: "Where has the nature of sin gone? He further said: "Not only...")

As for the nature of sin, even when sought, it is not found to exist. Yunju Qi said: "The Second Patriarch [Huike] held him in high esteem. Did he approve of his understanding of the Buddha-dharma? Or did he approve of his exposition of principles?
He then shaved his head and said, "He is my treasure; he should be named Sengcan. On the eighteenth day of the third month of that year, he received full ordination at Guangfu Temple.
From then on, his illness gradually improved. After serving him for two years, the Patriarch said: "Bodhidharma..."
From afar, from Zhugan (India), the treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma, together with the robe of faith, was secretly entrusted to me.
I now transmit it to you; you must guard and protect it so that it does not come to an end. Listen to my verse: "The ground of conditions exists inherently;
From this ground, flowers grow. Inherently, there is no seed; The flower has likewise never been born. After the Patriarch had transmitted the robe and the Dharma, he spoke again: "You..."
"Follow my instruction: you should dwell in the deep mountains; you must not yet go forth to transform others. There will surely be national turmoil.

Sengcan said, "Since the Master already knows this in advance, I pray that you will grant me further instruction. The Patriarch said, "It is not that I know it. This is what was recorded as a prophecy by Prajñātāra, which Bodhidharma transmitted:
'Though auspicious within, there is misfortune without. This refers to it. I have calculated the years, and it falls precisely upon this time."
"You, you must carefully reflect upon my previous words; do not fall into the calamities of this world. However, I too have karmic debts from past lives which I must now repay.

Go well and act with virtue; wait for the time to transmit [the Dharma] to the Patriarch. Having finished these instructions, he immediately departed for the capital of Ye. There, he preached the Dharma as appropriate to the occasion.
With a single voice, he expounded the teachings, and the fourfold assembly took refuge in him. In this manner, thirty-four years passed, after which he finally concealed his radiance.

He mingled with the common crowd, altering his appearance and demeanor. Sometimes he entered wine shops; sometimes he passed by butcher stalls; sometimes he engaged in street chatter; and sometimes he followed after menial laborers.
When people asked him, "Master, you are a man of the Way; why do you act in this way? the Patriarch replied, "I am merely training my own mind; what business is it of yours?
Furthermore, beneath the triple gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guan City County, he discoursed on the Unsurpassed [Dharma].
At that time, while the assembly was listening to the Dharma, there was a Dharma Master named Bianhe who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the monastery.

When his disciples heard that the Master [Sengzhu] was expounding the Dharma, they gradually drifted away. Bianhe could not contain his indignation and instigated a slander against Master Sengzhu with the local magistrate, Zhai Zhongkan.
Zhongkan was deluded by these perverse arguments and subjected Sengzhu to unlawful treatment. Sengzhu remained serene and submitted to his fate with equanimity; those who recognized him...
"Truth" refers to what is called "repaying a debt. At that time, his age was one hundred and seven years.

This was precisely the sixteenth day of the third month in the guichu year, the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty. (The attendant Haoyue asked Master Cen of Changsha: "An ancient worthy said, 'When one realizes it, karmic obstacles are originally empty.'"")

"Those who have not yet realized [the truth] must repay their karmic debts from the past. As for Venerable Siṃha and the Great Master the Second Patriarch, how did they manage to repay their debts? Changsha said, "Virtuous One, you do not recognize that all is originally empty. Haoyue asked, "What is meant by 'originally empty'?

Changsha said, "Karmic obstructions are it. Haoyue asked, "What are karmic obstructions? Changsha said, "'Originally empty' is it. Haoyue was speechless. Changsha then showed him the meaning with this verse: "Provisionally existent, yet fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, yet fundamentally not non-existent.
The principle of repaying karmic debts through nirvāṇa— In its single nature, there is no further distinction."
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan.
As for the Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, it is unknown where he was from. Initially, while still a layman, he went to visit the Second Patriarch.
Having received ordination and transmitted the Dharma, he lived in seclusion on Mount Wangong in Shuzhou.

Coinciding with the suppression of the Buddha-dharma by Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou, the Patriarch traveled between Taikou County and Sikong Mountain, dwelling in no fixed location for over ten years;
at that time, no one was able to recognize him. It was until the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the Renzi year (602 CE), when there was a novice monk named Daoxin.
At the age of fourteen, Xinxing came to pay his respects to the Patriarch, saying, "I pray that the Venerable One will, out of compassion, grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Xinxing attained great enlightenment. (Tianqi said:

"He knew only to ask for liberation, unaware that he was thrusting his head into a vat of glue. Had he not encountered a master at that time, how could the wedge have been used to extract the wedge? Only upon suddenly waking from a dream does one see that there is nothing at all.")

[The Master] said, "End. [He] struck him across the face and said, "Cat! Having served with labor for nine years, he later received the precepts at Jizhou, serving his master with even greater diligence. The Patriarch repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle mysteries;
knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma. The verse says: "The seed of the flower, though it depends on the earth, From the earth the flower grows.
If no one sows the seed, Neither flower nor earth will ever arise. The Master’s *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) says: "To the utmost..."
The Way is without difficulty; it is only that one dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or love, and all will be transparently clear.

A difference of even a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth. If you wish for it to manifest before you, do not maintain notions of favorability or adversity. To contend with favorability and adversity is the disease of the mind.

Failing to recognize the profound essence, you labor in vain by seeking stillness. It is perfectly identical to the great void—neither deficient nor superfluous. This is entirely due to grasping and rejecting.
Do not follow that which is inferior; do not pursue what has conditions, nor dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single kind of equanimity, all things are extinguished of their own accord.

Ceasing movement returns to stillness, yet stillness itself further stirs movement. To linger only on these two extremes, how could one know the single kind? If this one kind is not penetrated, both sides fail in their function.
To dispel existence and non-existence is to turn one's back on emptiness from within emptiness. Excessive words and excessive thoughts only lead further away from correspondence. Cut it off!

When words cease and thought is stilled, there is nowhere that does not penetrate. Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning; following after illumination, one loses the fundamental source.

If you reflect back for even a moment, this surpasses the previous emptiness. That previous emptiness underwent transformation entirely due to deluded vision. Do not seek the truth; simply require the cessation of views. When dualistic views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as right and wrong arise, confusion causes the mind to be lost. The duality exists because of the one; the one...
Do not cling to them either. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. Where there is no fault, there are no dharmas; where there is no arising, there is no mind.

The capacity [of the mind] is extinguished by objects, and objects sink along with the capacity. Objects exist because of the capacity, and the capacity exists because of objects. If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one emptiness.
This one emptiness is identical to the two, equally encompassing the myriad phenomena. Seeing neither the refined nor the coarse, how could there be partiality? Great!
The essence of the Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and increasingly slow.

To grasp it is to lose its measure and inevitably enter a deviant path. To let it be natural, its substance has no coming or staying. To follow one’s nature is to accord with the Way; to roam at ease is to be free from affliction.

To bind one's thoughts is to deviate from the truth; to be muddled and heavy is not good. Do not weary your spirit; what use is there for intimacy or estrangement? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not—
The six sense objects are not inherently evil; they return to the same state as perfect enlightenment. The wise person acts without artifice, while the fool binds himself.
There is no dharma apart from the Dharma, yet he delusively clings to it with self-love. To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error?

Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes. All dualistic extremes arise from one’s own deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—why labor to grasp them? Attainment...
Abandoning the distinction between right and wrong all at once—when the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; when the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are as one.
This oneness is profound in its essence; in a state of stillness, one forgets all conditions. Viewing the myriad dharmas as equal, one returns to spontaneity.
When the "why" is obliterated, it can no longer be compared to anything. In stillness there is no movement; in movement there is no stillness. Since both are unestablished, so too is the one.
How could there be such a thing? Reaching the ultimate limit, it does not abide by rules or regulations. The mind accords with equality; all that is done ceases. Doubt is completely purified;
right faith becomes straightened and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. Empty clarity illuminates itself spontaneously, without taxing the power of the mind.
It is not a place for discursive thought; consciousness and emotion find it difficult to fathom. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. This is essential.
It corresponds with urgency; it is simply called non-duality. Non-duality is universal sameness; there is nothing it does not encompass.

All wise ones of the ten directions enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor expansive; in a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. It is neither present nor absent; it is before one’s eyes throughout the ten directions.

The extremely small is identical to the great, as all boundaries and realms are forgotten and severed. The extremely great is identical to the small, as no limits or surfaces are seen. Existence is itself non-existence; non-existence...
This is precisely "existence. If it were not thus, one would certainly have no need for guarding. One is all; all is one.
If you can simply act in this way, why worry that you will not reach completion? Faith is non-dual; non-duality is faith. The path of words is cut off;

it is neither past, future, nor present. (Yuánwù Qín said: Many people misunderstand when they say, "The Ultimate Way is fundamentally not difficult, yet there is nothing that is not difficult," simply because they detest discrimination. If you understand it in such a way, even ten thousand years will not be enough—you will not have even dreamed of it.)
[Present]. As for the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin:
his secular surname was Sima; his family had resided in Henei for generations and later moved to Qizhou.
Guangji County. From birth he was extraordinary; in his youth he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The various gates of liberation were as if already familiar through past habituation.

Having inherited the tradition of his ancestors, he restrained his mind without sleep; for sixty years his side never touched his mat. In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Ji Prefecture.
There they encountered a band of rebels who besieged the city for seventy days without lifting the siege, leaving the multitude in a state of terror.
The Patriarch took pity on him and instructed him to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the bandits, looking toward the battlements, saw what appeared to be divine soldiers;
they said to one another, "There must be extraordinary people within this city," and they gradually withdrew.
In the year Jiashen of the Tang Wude era, the Master returned to Qichun and resided at Mount Poutou, where disciples gathered like clouds. One day, he went to Huangmei County.
On the road, he encountered a young boy whose physical features were extraordinary and refined. The Patriarch asked him, "What is your surname?
The boy replied, "I do have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one. The Patriarch asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch said, "Do you then have no surname?"

He replied, "They do not exist because their nature is empty. The Patriarch silently recognized her as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately dispatched an attendant to her mother’s residence to request that she be allowed to renounce the world.
Because of past karmic conditions, the mother showed no sign of reluctance; she thus relinquished her daughter to become a disciple. This led to the transmission of the Dharma and the robe.
The verse says: "The seed of the flower has the nature of arising; Depending on the ground, the flower arises. The Great Condition and the Nature..."

Combined. It should be born, yet it is not born (as the Song of Tiantong Juo says: "The fruit ripens at Huangmei; the white lotus blooms. When asked, it is only Buddha-nature; its essence differs from that of the common womb. The robe was passed on as the man of Nanling took it away").
Pine trees grow old on the western mountains; I have come again. Twice I borrowed this skin-sack—what has been accomplished? A single jar of wind and moon, profound and free from dust.
As for the Great Master Hongren of the Fifth Patriarch:
he was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. Previously, he had served as a laborer planting trees at Mount Poutu.
The man known as Songdao once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "You are already old;
even if you were to hear it, would you be able to transform others extensively? If you were to come again, I might still be able to wait for you.
Thereupon, he went to the edge of the water and saw a woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman said, "I have a father and brothers."
"You may go and seek him. She replied, "Yes; I shall dare to do so. The girl nodded her head in agreement and, turning her horse's reins, departed.
This girl was the youngest daughter of the Zhou clan. Upon returning home, she immediately became pregnant. Her parents detested her greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere else to turn, she spent her days spinning for hire within the village and stayed at night beneath a public inn. After some time, she gave birth to a son. Considering this an ill omen, [she...]
He was cast into a turbid stream. When he was seen the next day, floating upstream with his physical form appearing fresh and radiant, everyone was greatly astonished and subsequently picked him up.
He had become a young boy; following his mother, he went about begging for food, and the villagers called him "The Child Without Surname.
Later, he met Master Xinxing and received the Dharma, succeeding him in the propagation of the teachings at Mount Pòtóu. During the Xiánhéng era, there was a lay practitioner named Lú Huínéng.
He came from Xinzhou to pay his respects. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Lu said, "From Lingnan. The Patriarch asked, "What do you seek?
Lu said, "I only seek to become a Buddha. The Patriarch said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha?
Lu said, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could it be so with Buddha-nature? The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary man and rebuked him, saying:

"Go and work in the grain-pounding shed. Lu prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the mortar-house to perform labor between the pestle and the mortar, working without ceasing day or night for eight months.
The Patriarch, knowing that the time for the transmission had arrived, addressed the assembly, saying:

"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be merely memorized as my words. You must take this as your own responsibility. Each of you, according to your own inclination, compose a verse."

If his words and intentions were in perfect accord with [the Master’s], then both the robes and the Dharma would be entrusted to him. At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly.

Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular classics, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to. They all commended him, saying, "Were it not for the Venerable Xiuxiu, who else would dare to receive this?

Hearing the public acclaim, Shenxiu did not reflect further; he then wrote a verse upon a wall in the corridor, saying: The body is like a Bodhi tree, The mind is like a clear mirror stand. At all times we must diligently wipe them, And never let any dust collect.
"The body is the Bodhi tree; the mind is like a bright mirror stand. At all times, diligently wipe it clean; do not let it gather dust.
When the Patriarch was walking about, he suddenly saw this verse and knew it was composed by Shenxiu.

He then praised it, saying, "If future generations practice according to this, they too shall attain the supreme fruit. The wall was originally intended for the scholar Lu Zhen to paint the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* upon.
When he saw the painted images and the inscribed verse on the wall, he stopped painting and instead had everyone recite it.
While Lu was at the millhouse, he suddenly heard the recitation of the verse and asked his fellow students, "What chapter or phrase is this? His companions replied, "You do not know.

The Master is seeking a Dharma heir and has ordered each of us to compose a verse expressing our realization. This is the one composed by Venerable Xiu; the Master has praised it with deep admiration."
"The reward must be the transmission of the Dharma and the robe. Lu asked, "What was that verse? His fellow student recited it for him.
After a long while, Lu said, "It is beautiful, yet it is not yet fully realized. The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could an ordinary person like you know this?
Do not utter such mad words. Lu replied, "Do you not believe me? I wish to add a verse to harmonize with yours. The fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at him.
He laughed. That night, Lu secretly told a young boy to lead him to the corridor.
Lu himself held a candle and requested Zhang Riyong, the Regional Inspector, to write a verse beside Xiu’s verse, which read: "Bodhi originally has no tree; / A bright mirror is likewise not a stand.
/ Originally there is not a single thing; / Where could dust and grime gather? Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he said: "This..."
"Who is it that does this? You have not yet seen your nature. When the assembly heard the Master’s words, they paid him no further heed.

That night, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet? Lu said, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the mortar three times with his staff;
Lu immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room. The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose..."

According to the circumstances, he guided beings according to their varying capacities; thus, there arose the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the teachings of sudden and gradual enlightenment as pedagogical gateways.
Nevertheless, [he possessed] the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmaparyāya*—the treasury of the true eye of the Dharma (*dharmānayanidhāna*).
I entrust this to the foremost elder, Mahākāśyapa. It was transmitted successively through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived in this land.
There he met the Great Master Huike, from whom it has been inherited down to the present day.
I now entrust the Dharma-treasure and the robe I have transmitted to you. Guard them well yourself; do not allow them to be severed. Listen to my verse: Sentient beings...
"When one comes to sow the seed, the fruit arises from the ground. Since that which is insentient has no seed, that which lacks nature likewise has no birth.
The Practitioner Lu knelt to receive the dharma of the robe and asked, "Now that I have received the dharma, to whom shall the robe be entrusted?

The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him; therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest his attainment of the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe..."
"The source of contention shall end with your person; it shall not be transmitted further. For now, you must remain in seclusion, waiting for the time to manifest your transformation.

As for those who receive this robe, their lives are like a thread hanging from a string. Lu asked, "Where should I go into hiding? The Patriarch said, "When you encounter Huai, stop there; when you meet Hui, hide away.
After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed. That night he traveled southward, while the great assembly remained unaware.
He knew. From that time on, the Fifth Patriarch no longer ascended the hall. The assembly, filled with doubt and wonder, questioned him.
The Patriarch said, "My Way shall now proceed; why inquire further? They asked again, "Who has obtained the robe and the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "He who is capable obtains it.

Thereupon, the assembly deliberated that the name of Lu Xingzhe was Neng. Having searched for him and lost his trace, they secretly learned that he had obtained it, and they immediately set out together to pursue him.
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng:
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was by secular surname Lu. His ancestors were from Fanyang.
His father, Xingtao, was demoted to an official post in Xinzhou, Nanhai, during the Wude era, and thereupon registered his household there. He lost his father at the age of three; his mother...
He guarded his resolve and raised [his younger brother] with care. When they reached adulthood, their family was especially impoverished; the elder brother provided for them by gathering firewood.

One day, while carrying wood into the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until it reached the passage: "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere.
He experienced a profound realization and asked the guest, "What dharma is this? From whom did you receive it? The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
Upon reaching Master Ren at Huangmei, the Patriarch suddenly informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the sake of the Dharma.
He proceeded directly to Shaoyang Prefecture, where he met the man of noble conduct Liu Zhilue and formed a friendship with him. A nun named Wujinzang was Zhilue’s paternal aunt;
she regularly recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When the Master briefly listened to her, he immediately explained its meaning to her.

The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I ask for instruction regarding their meaning. The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters, how can you comprehend the meaning?
The Patriarch replied, "The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has nothing to do with written words. The nun was struck with wonder and marvel at this.

He addressed the elders of the village, saying, "This man is one who possesses the Way; you should invite him to receive our offerings. Thereupon, the local residents vied with one another to come and pay their respects.
Nearby was the site of an old temple, Bao Lin, which had long been abandoned. The community deliberated and decided to restore it so that he might reside there as his ancestral dwelling.

The fourfold assembly gathered like a mist, and in an instant, a jeweled monastery was formed. One day, the Patriarch suddenly thought to himself, "I have sought the Great Dharma; how could I stop midway?
The next day he set out and reached a stone grotto in the Western Mountains of Changle County, where he met Chan Master Zhiyuan.
The Patriarch then requested instruction; Zhiyuan said, "Observing your spiritual bearing, you are exceptionally outstanding; you are surely no ordinary man. My...
Hearing that Bodhidharma of the Western Regions had transmitted the Mind-Seal at Huangmei, you should go there to seek his judgment and resolve your doubts.
The Patriarch took his leave and proceeded directly to Mount Dongshan in Huangmei; this was the second year of the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty.
Upon seeing him, Master Ren recognized him in silence. Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma, instructing him to remain hidden between Huaiji and Sihui. (Ode)
On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Fengyuan era (the *bingzi* year), he arrived at Nanhai.

There he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong, who was preaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Faxing Temple. The Patriarch took up residence in the corridors. One evening, as the wind blew the temple banner atop the pagoda, he heard two monks debating:
one said it was the banner that moved; the other said it was the wind that moved. They exchanged arguments back and forth, yet neither had grasped the underlying principle. The Patriarch said:
"Is it appropriate for those of the secular world to rashly participate in such lofty discourse? It is simply that the wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind alone.
When Imprint Master (Yinzong) overheard these words, he stood upright in awe and marveled at them. Xuefeng Cun said: "The Great and Small Patriarchs have a dragon’s head but a snake’s tail.

They deserve twenty blows of the staff. When Upādhyāya Fu was in attendance, he gnashed his teeth. Xuefeng said: 'I speak thus; they also deserve twenty blows. Baofu Zhan said: "A thief’s heart is naturally fearful. This is like Xiao He establishing the laws. Wuzu Jie said: "For what reason? Baba said: [Silence].

Lingjian said: "The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. Since it is neither wind nor banner, where can one apply [the mind]? If there is anyone who can act as the Patriarch’s advocate, let them come forth and meet with Baling. He then offered this verse: "Not wind, not banner—nowhere to apply it;

Wind, banner—it has no place to rest. Even the swift falcon soaring in the vast heavens loses its track; The golden-haired lion crouching on the ground is likewise disoriented. A-he-he! Whether you realize it or not, It makes one longingly recall Xie Sanlang, Fishing alone on the cold river rain with a single line.

Xuedou Xian said: "The wind moves, the banner moves. Since it is both wind and banner, where can one apply it? If there is anyone who can act as Baling’s advocate, let them come forth and meet with Xuedou. Fachang Yu offered this verse: "It is not..."

The wind is not the banner; the black cat’s face is dappled with spots. The traveler at night covets only the bright moon, unaware that he is crossing waters in his clothes against the cold. Lektan Qing said: "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. If one were a person of keen intelligence, they would let go completely from a precipice and be able to take it up directly.

To look back and ahead only gives rise to further confusion. O benevolent ones, your own minds are moving. Is there anyone now who can act as the Master of the Patriarch? If there is, come forth and meet the Old Monk. Jingshan Gao said: "Do you wish to recognize Elder Fu?

A rhinoceros gazes at the moon, patterns forming on its horns. Do you wish to recognize Xuefeng? An elephant is startled by thunder, flowers enter its tusks. Tiantong Hua said: "One blind man leads a crowd of blind men, pulling each other along."

"Entering the Fire Pit. Xiaran Bao said: "It is indeed excellent; it is very good. Yet, it is not yet perfect. At that time, seeing the two monks disputing without end, he simply stepped forward and said, 'Virtuous ones, it is neither the banner moving, nor is it the wind moving,' and then he simply ceased speaking.

This did not merely cause the two monks to know where gratitude is due; it ensured that the descendants of the patriarchs throughout the world would feel a sense of indebtedness to the Master, never ceasing for a day. Do you understand? Though the myriad functions may not be consciously thought of, the power of spring ensures that when the time comes, the flowers must bloom of their own accord.
The next day, he invited Huizhu into his room to inquire about the meaning of the wind and the banner. Huizhu explained the principle in full detail, and Yinzong was [convinced].
Huineng rose and said, "This practitioner is certainly no ordinary person. Who is his master? The Patriarch had nothing further to conceal;
he directly recounted the circumstances of how he had attained the Dharma. Thereupon, Yinzong performed the rites of a disciple and requested instruction on the essentials of Chan.
He then addressed the fourfold assembly, saying, "Yinzong was once a full-fledged ordinary man, but now I have encountered a Buddha in flesh and bone. He then pointed to Lu... [seated] beneath him.
The layman said, "This is indeed it," and requested that the robe of transmission be brought forth so that everyone might gaze upon and worship it.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, Yinzong gathered various eminent virtuous monks to shave his head.

On the eighth day of the second month, he received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zhiguang at Faxing Temple; the ordination platform was that very one used by Guṇavarman during the Song dynasty.

This was established by the Tripitaka Master. The *Record of the Three Baskets* (*Sanzang ji*) states: "In the future, there shall be an incarnate Bodhisattva who will receive the precepts upon this altar.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha personally planted two Bodhi trees beside the altar and said to the assembly:
"One hundred and twenty years hence, there will be a Great Mahāsattva who, beneath these trees, shall expound the Unsurpassed [Dharma]."

He mounted [the vehicle] and delivered immeasurable multitudes. After the Patriarch had fully received the precepts, he opened the Dharma-gate of Dongshan beneath this tree, as if fulfilling a long-standing covenant.
On the eighth day of the second month of the following year, he suddenly said to the assembly, "I do not wish to remain here; I desire to return to my former retreat.
Thereupon, Master Yin-zong and more than a thousand monastics and laypeople escorted the Patriarch back to Bao-lin Temple. The Governor of Shaozhou—
The historian Wei Ju requested that [the Master] turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma at Dafan Temple and receive the Formless Mind-Ground Precepts (*amūrti-citta-bhūmi-śīla*).

His disciples recorded these events, titling the work the *Platform Sutra* (*Tánjīng*), which became widely circulated throughout the world. Later, he returned to Caoqi and rained down the great rain of the Dharma;
his students numbered no fewer than several thousand. In the first year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng, an imperial edict was issued stating: "I have invited the two masters Ān and Xiù..."
The Master was provided with offerings within the imperial palace. In the leisure between his myriad state affairs, the Emperor constantly investigated the One Vehicle.
Both masters [Huineng and Shenxiu] declined the honor, saying, "In the south there is Chan Master Neng, who secretly received the robe and Dharma from the Great Master Huineng;

you may go to him for questions. Now, the Inner Attendant Xue Jian has been dispatched to carry this imperial decree to invite him. We pray that the Master will look upon us with compassion and hasten to the Capital. The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, expressing his wish—

At the edge of the forest, Jian said, "The virtuous practitioners of meditation in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It has never been the case that liberation can be attained without relying on meditation and concentration. I do not know how the Dharma you teach, Master, compares to this.
The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; why should it depend on sitting? The Sūtra says: 'If one sees the Tathāgata...'"
"Sitting as if lying down—this is practicing a deviant path. Why? Because there is nowhere from which one comes, nor anywhere to which one goes;
if there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna. All dharmas are empty and quiescent; this is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting.

Ultimately, there is nothing to be realized, so how much less can there be 'sitting' in the conventional sense? Jian replied, "When your disciple returns, the Sovereign will surely question me. I pray that you, Venerable Master, will out of compassion provide instruction."
He showed him the essential point of the mind. The Patriarch said: "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of alternation.

'Ever-bright' is inexhaustible, yet it is also a name established in dependence upon its opposite, 'exhaustibility. Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Dharmas have no peer, for they do not depend on one another. Jian said:
"Light is a metaphor for wisdom, and darkness illustrates affliction. If a person who cultivates the Way does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter [affliction]..."

[The questioner asked: "Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) and the beginningless cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), by what means can one attain liberation? The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi;
they are non-dual and without distinction. To use wisdom to illuminate afflictions is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those such as the sheep and the deer."
Those of great wisdom and superior faculties are not like this at all. Jian asked, "What is the insight and understanding of the Mahāyāna?

The Patriarch said, "Luminosity and ignorance—these two natures are non-dual. This non-dual nature is the true nature. As for the true nature: it does not decrease when dwelling among the ignorant and foolish;
it does not increase when among the worthy and the sages; it is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions; and it remains as it is while residing in meditative concentration."
It is not quiescent; it is neither interrupted nor eternal; it does not come nor go; it does not abide in between, nor within or without;
it is neither born nor extinguished. Its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); it is eternally abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way.

Jian asked: "The Master speaks of 'neither born nor extinguished. How does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch said: "What the non-Buddhists call 'neither born nor extinguished' is merely using extinction to bring things to a halt."
Arising. By means of arising, extinction is revealed; yet extinction is not truly extinguished, for arising is said to be non-arising.

When I speak of that which is neither born nor extinguished, it is because it was originally unborn and is now likewise unextinguished. This is why it differs from the heterodox paths. If you wish to know the essential point of the mind:

Simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever; you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Having received this instruction, he attained sudden and great enlightenment. He paid his respects and took leave to return to the capital, where he submitted a memorial reporting the Master’s words.
An imperial edict was issued to express gratitude to the Master, and he was further granted a *mò-nà* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, five hundred bolts of silk, and a precious alms bowl.
The Patriarch was asked by a monk, "Who can attain the essential meaning of Huangmei? The Patriarch replied, "One who understands the Dharma of the Buddha can attain it.
The monk said, "Does the Master attain it? The Patriarch said, "I do not attain it. The monk asked, "Why does the Master not attain it?"

The Patriarch said, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. (Fenyang Zhao [Zhaozhuo] said in his place: "Only then do we know that the secret intent is difficult to transmit. Cuiyan Zhi said: "To understand it is two heads; not to understand it is three heads.

How then can there be a path for one to emerge? Yuanwu Keqin’s verse says: "Chopping nails and cutting iron—great skill appears as clumsiness. Holding up a single phrase: 'I do not understand the Buddha-dharma.

Let the leaves fall and the flowers bloom as they may; let us ask no more of spring's chill or autumn's heat. Peculiar! Ten thousand ages, the cold pond and the moon in the empty realm. Jingshan Rujing said: "Do you see the Patriarch? If you do not see him, I shall point him out for you: *Jiabo*! *Jiabo*! It has leaves but no sprouts. Suddenly—"

A violent wind arises. It is just like the tattered *kāṣāya* of Master Wang in the corner of the wall under the eastern corridor of the thirty-six courtyards of Daixiangguosi Temple in Dongjing. After all, what is it? Return to the hall for tea. Chushi Qi said:
"Striking the head of a stone man—*bò bò*, discussing the reality. One day, the Patriarch said to the assembly:
"Good friends, each of you should purify your minds and listen to my teaching of the Dharma. All of you, your own mind is the Buddha; do not harbor further doubt.
There is not a single thing outside that can be established; everything is the fundamental mind that gives rise to the myriad dharmas. Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'The mind gives rise to the seeds.'"
When various dharmas arise, the mind arises; when various dharmas cease, the mind ceases.

If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one must attain the samādhi of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi*) and the samādhi of a single practice (*ekavyūha-samādhi*).

If, in all places, one does not dwell upon characteristics, and within those characteristics neither produces hatred nor attachment, and is likewise without grasping or rejecting, and does not think of matters such as benefit, success, or failure, then one will be peaceful, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene.

This is called the Samādhi of One Mark. If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind without wavering, that very site becomes a true Pure Land;
this is called the Samādhi of One Practice. If a person possesses these two samādhis, it is like the earth having seeds:
it can contain and nurture them until their fruit is brought to fruition. The Samādhi of One Mark and the Samādhi of One Practice are likewise so.
I now preach the Dharma, just as the seasonal rain universally moistens the great earth. Your Buddha-nature is like various seeds;
encountering this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi; those who follow my practice...
Certifying the Sublime Fruit. In the first year of the Xuantian era, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "I have humbly received the robe and the Dharma from the Great Master.
Now I preach the Dharma for you, yet I do not transmit the robe. This is because your roots of faith are pure and mature;
you are resolute and free from doubt, and are thus capable of undertaking the great task. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; the universal rain falls upon them all.'"
"Once birth has occurred, once the delusions of the mind have been suddenly awakened to, the fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously realized. Having spoken this verse, he further said:
"That Dharma is non-dual; the mind is likewise so. That Way is pure and devoid of all marks. You must be careful not to contemplate purity, nor to empty the mind.
This mind is fundamentally pure; there is nothing to be grasped or rejected. Each of you must exert yourselves and go forth happily according to conditions. [End of] Excerpt.
There was a monk who recited the verse of Chan Master Wo-lun: "Wo-lun has skill; He can cut off a hundred thoughts.
When facing objects, his mind does not arise; Thus, Bodhi grows day by day. Upon hearing this, the Patriarch said, "This verse does not clarify the ground of the mind.
If you follow it and practice accordingly, it will only add further fetters. He then showed him a verse, saying: "Hui-neng has no skill; I do not cut off thoughts."
A hundred thoughts arise as the mind encounters objects. How can Bodhi be made to grow? On the first day of the seventh month in the second year of the Xiantian era, he said to his disciples:
"I wish to return to Xinzhou; you must quickly prepare the boats. At that time, the great assembly was filled with grief and longing, entreating the Master to remain.
The Patriarch said: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest *nirvāṇa*. Since there is coming, there must be going; this is the principle."

"It is always thus. This physical frame of mine must return to its source. The assembly asked, "When you depart from here, Master, when will you return? The Patriarch said, "Leaves fall and return to the root;
when one comes, there are no lips. Fayun Xiu said: "It is not only that there are no lips when coming;

there are also no nostrils when going. Baizhang Yuanwu said: "The Patriarch may truly be called one who understands how to borrow a hand to perform a fist-punch. There are certain fellows who often say, 'The words are still ringing in our ears. Have they not heard it said: 'Ziqi has gone and does not return; how deeply lamentable this vast expanse! One does not know within heaven and earth who truly knows.'"
"Who, then, is this sound? Wuzu Yan said, "The Patriarch spoke thus, yet he still lacked awakening. He asked again, "Whom did your Dharma-eye transmit to and receive from?
The Patriarch replied, "Those with the Way attain it; those without a mind penetrate it."
The Special Transmission Outside the Teachings, Volume Three;
The Special Transmission Outside the Teachings, Volume Four:
Dharma Heirs Branching Out from the Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Dayi.
Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou (the first generation after the Fourth Patriarch).
Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou was a native of Yanling in Runzhou. His surname was Wei. At the age of nineteen, he...

Having read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and attained a clear understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he suddenly sighed and said: "The classics of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma;
the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he entered the monastic order under a master and shaved his head.

Later, he entered Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou and dwelt in a stone chamber on the northern cliff, where there was a marvel of hundreds of birds offering flowers. This occurred during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.
The Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric signs from afar and knew that there was an extraordinary person on that mountain.

He went in person to seek him out and asked the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way here? They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, who is not a practitioner of the Way? The Patriarch said:
"Who is this person who is a man of the Way? The monk had no reply. Another monk said, "About ten li from here in the mountains there is one named Lanrong;
he does not rise when seeing people, nor does he join his palms. Might he not be a man of the Way? The Master then entered the mountains.
Seeing that his teacher sat upright and composed, looking back at nothing, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here?
The teacher replied, "I am contemplating the mind. The Patriarch said, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this mind? The teacher was speechless; he then rose, prostrated himself, and said:
"Virtuous One, where do you dwell in seclusion? The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk has no fixed abode; I go either east or west. The Master asked, "Do you know Chan Master Daoxin?
The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him? The Master said, "I have long admired his virtue and hope to pay my respects to him.
The Patriarch said, "Chan Master Daoxin is I myself. The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here? The Patriarch...
The Master said, "I have come specifically to visit you. Is there no other place for rest? The Master pointed behind him and said, "There is another small hermitage.
He then led the Patriarch to the hermitage; looking around the hermitage, they saw only tigers, wolves, and the like.
The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this [fear] remaining. The Patriarch asked, "What is this? The Master was speechless.

[The Master] spoke. (Xuedou Xian, acting on his behalf, said: "But he also made a gesture of fear. He further acted on his behalf, saying: "He should have let him go. After a short while, the Patriarch [Huineng] was sitting in meditation upon the stone where the Master was seated.
The Master wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛). Upon seeing it, the Patriarch stood up in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this [character] remaining.

The Master did not yet understand, so he bowed his head and requested an explanation of the essential truth. The Patriarch said, "Indeed, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates all return to the single square inch of the mind.

The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all rooted in the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, gates of concentration, and gates of wisdom, as well as spiritual powers and transformations, are entirely inherent within it."
It is sufficient. It does not depart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are, from the very beginning, empty and quiescent.
All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans are equal in their nature and characteristics.
The Great Way is vast and open, transcending thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma as this you have now attained; there is nothing further to seek.
“Dharma, you need only let your mind be free and at ease. Do not perform contemplative practices; do not clarify the mind; do not give rise to greed or anger;
do not harbor anxiety or worry. Vast and unobstructed, move freely in all directions. Do not perform any good deeds; do not commit any evil deeds.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever meets your eyes or encounters your conditions is entirely the wondrous function of the Buddha. The Master said, “Since the mind is already complete, why [is there still delusion]?”

“What is this Buddha? What is this mind? The Patriarch said: “It is not the mind that does not inquire about the Buddha; it is not the case that inquiring about the Buddha is not the mind. The Master asked:
“Since you do not permit the practice of contemplative visualization (*vipaśyanā*), when objects arise, how does the mind counteract them?

The Patriarch said: “The conditions of objects have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind. If the mind does not insist on assigning names, from where would deluded sentiments arise? Deluded sentiments...
Since it does not arise, the true mind is naturally all-pervasive and knowing. You need only follow the mind with freedom; there is no longer any need for antidotes.

This is precisely what is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, which is without change or variation. I have received the Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching from Master Can; I now transmit it to you.
You must now receive my words with earnest attention and remain on this very mountain. Hereafter, there shall be five who attain realization and will carry on the lineage.

“You have a profound transformation. (A monk asked Nanquan: “When Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds bring flowers to offer him? Nanquan said, ‘It was simply because he was treading the steps of the Buddha at every step. The monk asked, ‘After he saw him, why did they no longer come?

Nanquan said, ‘Even if they did not come, they would still fall short of Old Wang by a hair’s breadth. Yunmen cited this, saying, ‘Nanquan only knew how to climb higher step by step; he did not know how to let go from the void. A monk asked, ‘What is climbing higher step by step?

Yunmen said, ‘The World of Fragrant Accumulation. The monk asked, ‘What is letting go from the void? Yunmen said, ‘Filling the ditches and blocking the ravines. A monk asked Zhaozhou: “How was it before Niutou had seen the Fourth Patriarch? Zhaozhou said...)

Zhaozhou said, "Sufficient firewood, sufficient water. The monk asked, "What is it like after seeing this? Zhaozhou said, "Sufficient firewood, sufficient water. Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng to spend the remainder of his life there.

From that time on, the Master’s Dharma seat flourished greatly. During the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, Xiao Yuanshan, the local magistrate, invited the Master to the Jianchu Monastery to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The listeners gathered like clouds; when they reached the "Chapter on Cessation and Stillness" (*nirodha-vyupaśama-parivarta*), the earth shook.
Prince Boling asked the Master, "When one applies the mind with such precision (*jiǎjiǎ*), how can it be peaceful and secure? The Master replied, "Precisely..."
Just when the mind is functioning, it is precisely without a mind to function. To discourse on names and forms is wearisome; to speak directly is free from complexity.
Without a mind, there is precisely the functioning; in constant use, there is precisely no [mind]. Now, where I speak of the state of no-mind, it is not different from having a mind.
Chan Master Xuanting of Anguo Temple (Sixth generation under the Fourth Patriarch; successor to Niutou Wei).
Chan Master Xuanting of Anguo Temple in Xuanzhou initially went to attend upon Chan Master Wei.

While standing in attendance, a monk who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asked, "What is the meaning of the principle of true nature and dependent origination? After Wei remained silent for a long while, Xuanting suddenly called out, "Virtuous One!"
At the very moment one gives rise to the single thought of inquiry, this is the dependent origination within the true nature.

Upon these words, that monk attained great enlightenment. (Jingshan Daokai said: "Before the single thought of inquiry has arisen, it cannot be that there is no dependent origination. At that time, a monk asked: "Before the single thought of inquiry has arisen, what do you call dependent origination?

Miaoxi said: "I also want you to speak in such a way. Chushu Qi said: "The Kunlun slave wears iron trousers; with every strike of the staff, he takes a step forward. Wanfeng Wei said: "This monk knows how to open his mouth to question others, but he does not know the dependent origination of the true nature. It brings trouble upon Master Ting when he says: 'Virtuous One, at the very moment...'"

The moment one gives rise to the thought of questioning, this is dependent origination within the true nature. Although that monk lost his nostrils, he attained a point of awakening; yet, in the end, he expended no small amount of effort. But tell me: before he had even asked, where did the conditions reside?
Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing (the seventh generation under the Fourth Patriarch, a successor of Master Su of Helin):
Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a native of Kunshan in Suzhou.

At the age of twenty-eight, he encountered Master Su, who said to him, "Observing your spirit and temperament, you are truly a treasure of the Dharma. The Master was moved to realization by this. Thereupon—
He requested to become a disciple. [The Master] personally shaved his head and then instructed him, saying: "As you travel along the current, stop whenever you encounter a path.
The Master then journeyed south and reached Lin’an. Seeing a mountain to the northeast, he questioned a woodcutter, who said:
This is Mount Jing; it was here that [Zhaozhou] halted his staff. A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "There are carp on the mountain;

there is dust and chaff at the bottom of the sea. (Jingshan Xinyun said: "This public case is because National Teacher No. 1 answered with such novelty that from ancient times to the present, no one has caught even a whiff of its verbal fragrance.

Today, he pushes the sun and moon aside, turns the mountains and rivers upside down, sucks dry the springs, and overturns the five peaks. He ensures that there is no dust at the bottom of the well so that for a hundred kalpas it remains eternally clear; the carp sprout wings and soar high into the clouds. Now tell me, does this monk understand or not?")
Mazu sent someone to deliver a letter. In the letter, he had drawn a circle. When the Master (Dongshan) opened the seal, he placed a dot within the circle and then sealed it back and returned it.
Upon hearing this, National Teacher Zhong said, "Master Qin is still being deluded by Master Ma. Baofu Zhan asked, "Where is the point of delusion? How can one avoid being deluded?

Xuedou Xian said, "Setting aside for a moment that Jingshan was deluded, if he had presented it to the National Teacher, what other skillful means could he have employed to avoid being deluded? An old master said, "At that time, he should have sat upon it and left it at that. There were also others who held this view.

The Way. It is merely a matter of drawing a line. If it were like this, one would simply be shameless. How dare you claim that the teachers of the world all possess the diamond eye and can perform vast supernatural transformations—would that still allow you to escape?

Where Xuedou sees it, he wishes for everyone to know together: at the very moment Mazu drew that line, he was already deluded himself. Wuzu Ji said, "Two colors, one match. He also said, "Three people point the way; what is intended to be done? Weishan Zhe said, "Do you all recognize Mazu of Jing Mountain? A single drop of ink forms two dragons.

National Teacher Huizhong said, "Master Qin was still deluded by Master Mazu. This can truly be called "sharing the same breeze across a thousand miles. Have you not heard it said: "Holding a night-bright talisman in hand, how many know the heavens?"

Xiao Fushan Yuan said: "Let us set aside Master Qin being deluded by Master Ma for a moment; how many people has National Teacher [Zhongyi] deluded? Xuedou said: "At that very moment, when Master Ma drew his picture, he had already deluded himself.

He has pierced the nostrils of everyone in the world. Jingshan Daowei Gao said: "For Master Ma it was the bitter cold of mid-winter; for National Teacher No. 1 it was the gradual heat of early summer. Although the cold and heat differ, both have not missed their proper season.

Why then did National Teacher Zhongyi say, 'Master Qin is still being deluded by Master Ma'? Do you understand? When the lotus leaf moves without a breeze, there is certainly a fish swimming beneath. Chushi Zhiyuan Qi said: "A drop of ink placed within the circle (the *yuanxiang*) renders the sun and moon lusterless and the heavens and earth dark. At first, he did not delude Master Qin; it was Master Ma who..."

The Master was first deluded himself; this has repeatedly brought calamity upon Old Nanyang. What a total mess! After a long silence, he said: "Throughout my life, I have laid open my liver and gall toward others; yet those who know me are as if they do not. Mazu sent Zhizang to ask him:
"In the twelve periods of the day, what do you take as the objective realm? The Master replied: "Wait until you have returned, and then there will be news for you."
Zhizang said, "I shall return right now. The Master said, "When you deliver my message, you must ask about Caoxi.
Lord Cui Zhao asked, "I, your disciple, wish to leave the household life now; may I do so? The Master said, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man."
"This is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. At this, the Master had an awakening.

In the third year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong summoned him to the imperial court, where he personally paid him homage. One day, while sitting in the inner courtyard together with National Teacher Zhong, the Master said:
Seeing the Emperor’s carriage approaching, the Master rose to his feet. The Emperor asked, "Master, why do you rise?

The Master replied, "How can you, O Patron, perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment (*catur-īryāpatha*)? The Emperor was pleased and said to the State Preceptor, "I wish to bestow a title upon the Venerable Master.

The State Preceptor joyfully accepted the decree, and he was thus granted the title Guoyi (National One). (Jingshan Gaofeng said: "If not within the four modes of deportment, how else could one see National One?")
Chan Master Daolin of Niaoke (the eighth generation descendant of the Fourth Patriarch and dharma heir of Qian of Mount Jing):
Chan Master Daolin of Niaoke in Hangzhou was a native of Fuyang in that same prefecture. During the reign of Emperor Daizong, when he learned that National Teacher No.
1 had been summoned to the imperial court, the Master went to pay his respects and subsequently received the True Dharma. Upon returning south, he saw Mount Qinwang, where there was a tall...
A pine tree grew there, its branches curling like a canopy. He subsequently took up residence upon it; thus, people of the time called him Chan Master Niaoke (The Bird’s Nest).
He had an attendant named Huìtōng, who one day suddenly wished to take his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going now? He replied, "Huìtōng has left home for the sake of the Dharma.
Since the Master does not deign to grant me compassionate instruction, I am now going to various places to study the Buddha-dharma. The Master said:
He said, "If this is the Buddha-dharma, we have a little of it here as well.

Huigong asked, "What is the Master’s Buddha-dharma? The Master picked up a wisp of cloth from his body and blew upon it. Huigong thereupon attained realization of the profound principle. (Daguishou said:

"It is a pity that this monk took the sounds and colors of his mouth for his entire life; he did not realize that his own radiance covers heaven and earth. Shending Yin, having raised this case, then picked up a wisp of cloth from his body and showed it to Da.

[The Master] blew [on the feather] once more and said, "Do you understand? In the future, do not let me down. Zhenjing Wen’s verse says: "The bird's nest blows the cloth hair; The red sun is high at noon. Because the King of Zhao loved swords, The people of the whole state all wear blades. Jingshan Daoyuan said:

"Even if Guishan were to pass such a judgment, he has not yet seen Bird Nest in his dreams. Chushi Qi said: "If one could shout upon the moment the cloth hair was picked up, one would avoid being scrutinized by those in all quarters.
My saying this is also for the sake of increasing delusion through idle matters. During the Yuanhe era, Minister Bai Juyi was sent to govern this prefecture. Consequently, he entered...
The Prefect went to visit the Master and asked, "The place where the Chan Master resides is extremely dangerous.
The Master replied, "Your Excellency’s position is even more dangerous. The Minister said, "I hold office that stabilizes the mountains and rivers; what danger could there be?

The Master said, "When fuel and fire intersect, the nature of consciousness does not rest—is this not dangerous? He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "All evils..."
"Do not do evil; practice all that is good. The Court Gentleman said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say this.
The Master replied, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it. The Court Gentleman bowed and withdrew.
The Dharma Heir of the Fifth Patriarch, Chan Master Dàman, who branched out from his lineage:
Chan Master Dàomíng of Mǒngshān (the first generation after the Fifth Patriarch).
Chan Master Dàomíng of Mǒngshān in Yuánzhōu was a native of Póyáng and a descendant of Emperor Xuāndì of the Chen dynasty. His country had fallen.
He settled among the common people. Because his royal ancestor had once held an official appointment, he was consequently granted the title of General.
He went to rely upon the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch, where he applied himself with all his heart to investigation and study, yet initially attained no realization or awakening.

Upon hearing that the Fifth Patriarch had secretly entrusted the robe and the Dharma to Lu the Layman (Huineng), he immediately led several dozen like-minded companions to track him down. They pursued him until they reached Mount Dayu, where Lu saw them.
The Master ran up to him and immediately cast his robe and bowl onto a flat rock, saying, "This robe represents the seal of faith; can it be contested by force? You may take it as you please.
The Master then tried to lift it, but it remained unmoved like a mountain. Hesitating and trembling with fear, he said, "I have come to seek the Dharma, not for the sake of this robe.
I pray that the Practitioner will grant me instruction. Lu said, "Do not think of good; do not think of evil."
"At this very moment, which one is the original face of Master Ming? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment;
his entire body broke into a sweat, and he prostrated himself in weeping obeisance. He asked, "Beyond these secret words and secret meanings you have transmitted, is there any further intent?
Lu said, "What I am telling you now is not secret. If you turn your light back upon yourself..."
"The true face of oneself—this mystery lies precisely within you. The Master said, "Although I have been among the assembly at Huangmei, I have not yet realized my own true face.
Now that I have received your instruction on the point of entry, it is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves."
"The practitioner here is now Master So-and-so. Lu said, "If that is so, then you and I share the same teacher at Huangmei.
Guard and uphold [the Dharma] well yourself. The Master asked again, "Where should So-and-so go in the future? Lu replied:
He encountered Yuan Kezhi at Mount Meng, where he took up residence. The Master paid his respects and thanked him, then hurried back down to the foot of the pass.
He said to the crowd, "Just now I climbed the high peaks and looked far out; there was no trace of him at all. We should seek him by another path. Everyone agreed with this.
Once the Master had returned, he went alone to Panshui Terrace on Mount Lu. After three years had passed, he finally went to Mount Meng in Yanzhou.
He loudly proclaimed the profound transformation. Originally named Huiming, he changed his name to Daoming to avoid the first character of the Sixth Patriarch’s name.
His disciples were all sent across the mountain pass to the south to pay their respects to the Sixth Patriarch.
Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou (the second generation under the Fifth Patriarch, successor to Chan Master Xiu of the Northern School).
Chan Master Daoshu was a native of Tangzhou. Having met Chan Master Xiu, he realized the subtle truth upon hearing his words.
He then selected Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou to build a thatched hut and dwell there. There was often a rustic man who wore simple, plain clothing and spoke in strange, unconventional ways.
It was extraordinary. Beyond his speech and laughter, he manifested the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, celestial immortals, and others;
sometimes he emitted divine light, and sometimes he produced sounds. When the master’s disciples beheld these things, none could fathom them.

This continued for ten years, after which he suddenly vanished without a trace or shadow. The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The rustic has displayed many-colored conjurations to dazzle and delude [you]."
People think that as long as this old monk neither sees nor hears them, their tricks will come to an end; yet my not seeing and not hearing is inexhaustible.
This was said by the Venerable Puzhao Duo of Mount Song (a successor of An Fa).
The Monk Puzhao Duō (Broken Hearth Fall) of Mount Song did not disclose his name or lineage, and his words and deeds were unfathomable.

He lived in seclusion on Mount Song, where there was a shrine in a mountain valley that was considered highly efficacious. Within its hall stood only a single hearth, upon which sacrifices were offered by people from near and far without ceasing;
many living beings were slaughtered for these offerings. One day, the Master led an attendant monk into the shrine and struck the hearth three times with his staff, saying: "Tsk! This—"
The hearth is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the sacred come? From where does the numinous arise? Yet you thus slaughter living beings.
[He] struck it three more times, and the hearth collapsed and fell apart. In a moment, there appeared a man in green robes and a tall cap.
He prostrated himself before the Master. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am the hearth god of this temple.

Having long endured the retribution of my karma, today I have been fortunate enough to hear the Master preach the Dharma of non-arising; thus I have attained liberation from this place and shall be reborn among the devas. I have come specifically to express my gratitude.
The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature; it was not my words that forced it upon you. The spirit bowed once more and vanished. A short while later—
An attendant monk asked, "We have served the Master for a long time, yet we have not received any instruction.

What essential principle did the hearth-god obtain that he was able to be reborn in heaven? The Master said, "I simply told him that he was composed of clay and tiles; I had no other principle to impart to him.
The attendant monk remained silent. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It is originally present."

[The Master asked: "What is the nature of this? Why does it not function? The attendant monks then prostrated themselves. The Master said, "A fall! A fall! A break! A break! Later, Zen Master Yifeng recounted this to National Teacher An.

The National Teacher sighed and said, "This man has realized that things and self are one and the same. He may be compared to the bright moon in the sky—there is nowhere it is not seen. It is difficult to grasp the thread of his discourse.

Yifeng asked, "I wonder, what kind of person can grasp the thread of his discourse? The National Teacher replied, "One who does not know. Longmen Yuan composed a verse on this: "Calamity and fortune, majesty and severity do not reside in the numinous; The remnants of cups and cold roast meat are met with laughter."
"Who is this person? Since he departed, there has been no news; the old man of the wilds still beats the sacrificial drum. A monk came from the assembly of Niutou.
The Master asked, "From whose Dharma assembly have you come? The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, circumambulated the Master once, and departed.
The Master said, "In Niutou’s assembly, such a person should not exist. The monk then returned to the Master’s shoulder, joined his palms, and stood there. The Master said, "Indeed..."
However, it is indeed so. A monk asked, "What is a person of great icchantika? The Master said, "To pay respect and prostrate.
[The monk] asked, "What is a person of great diligence? The Master said, "To suffer insult and harbor anger. Thereafter, nothing was known of his final end.
Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan (Third generation under the Fifth Patriarch; successor to Jiji of Mount Song).
Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain was a native of Pingyuan. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song.
He immediately entered Mount Taiyi, and his disciples filled the hall. During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Wenzong was fond of eating clams;

the officials along the coast had previously presented them in succession, causing the people great exhaustion. One day, among the imperial delicacies, there was one that would not open even when split.

The Emperor, marveling at this anomaly, immediately burned incense and prayed for it to open. When it was opened, he beheld the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the marks of a Brahma-like appearance.

The Emperor then placed it within a casket of gold-encrusted sandalwood, covered it with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Temple, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and prostrate before it.
He then questioned his ministers: "What auspicious omen is this? Some reported that Chan Master Weizheng of Taishan Mountain had long...
