He was well-versed in the Buddha-dharma. [The Emperor] requested an imperial edict to question him. The Emperor immediately issued the edict. When the Master arrived, the Emperor questioned him about the matter.
The Master said, "Your servant has heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause; this is merely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. Therefore, a sūtra says:
'Those who are to be saved by this body shall see this body appear and the Dharma shall be preached for them. " The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has already appeared."
Furthermore, he had not yet heard a Dharma teaching. The Master said, "Your Majesty, observing this, do you consider it permanent or impermanent? Do you believe it or not?
The Emperor replied, "This is a rare and extraordinary matter; I believe it deeply. The Master said, "Your Majesty has already heard the Dharma teaching.
The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy, and he issued an edict to all monasteries throughout the realm that each must establish an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Chan Master Junji of Mount Song (Dharma heir of Pozhau Duo).
A monk asked, "What is one who practices good? The Master said, "Carrying a cangue and wearing shackles.
The monk asked, "What is one who commits evil? The Master said, "Cultivating dhyāna and entering samādhi. The monk said, "I am of shallow capacity."
"Please, Master, point directly. The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good; if you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil.
After the monk had been silent for a long time, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "An evil person has no thoughts of goodness."
"A good person has no evil mind. Thus it is said: "Good and evil are like floating clouds; both have no place of arising or ceasing.
Under these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Later, when Pòzhuò Duò heard this case cited, he said: "This man has realized that all dharmas are unborn. (Jiànfú Huái said:

"In front, the official seal does not admit even a needle; behind, private carriages and horses pass through. If you can discern this, I grant you the eye of dharma-discrimination. [Zhāojié Qín said: 'If you exhaustively investigate goodness, from where does goodness come? If you thoroughly examine evil, from where does evil...']")

From what does this arise? Someone asked Chongning, "What is one who practices great cultivation? He replied, "Practicing Chan and entering meditative concentration. [The questioner] asked, "What is one who performs great work? He replied, "Carrying a cangue and bearing shackles. Now tell me, are these the same or different?
Jingshan Gao said, "Alas, how can one avoid forming deluded thoughts before the skull?"
The Chan Master Zhicheng of Jizhou, a collateral successor of the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Mirror Chan Master (the first generation after the Sixth Patriarch).
As for the Chan Master Zhicheng of Jizhou, he was originally from Tahe in that same prefecture. He first studied under Chan Master Xiu, and later, because...
As the two schools flourished, the disciples of Xiu frequently derided the Southern School, saying: "Master Neng cannot recognize a single character; what excellence does he possess? Xiu replied:
"He has attained teacherless wisdom and deeply realized the Supreme Vehicle; in this, I am not his equal.

Furthermore, our own master, the Fifth Patriarch, personally entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma—how could that have been for nothing? What I regret is that I am unable to travel far [to see him]."
"Go and draw near. You have received the bounty of the state in vain. All of you, do not remain here; you may go to Caoxi to resolve your doubts. When you return one day, you must speak of it for me.
Upon hearing these words, the Master paid his respects and took his leave, traveling to Shaoyang. There he joined the assembly for formal inquiries, yet did not mention where he had come from.
At that time, the Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "There is now a thief of the Dharma who is secretly staying among us."
Huike went out to pay his respects and related the matter in detail. The Patriarch said, "How did your teacher instruct the assembly?

Huike replied, "He used to exhort the great assembly, telling them to settle the mind and contemplate stillness, sitting for long periods without lying down. The Patriarch said, "To settle the mind and contemplate stillness is a sickness, not dhyāna;
to sit for long periods and constrain the body—what benefit is there in this from the perspective of principle? Listen to my verse: 'Since birth, sitting without lying down.'"
"Dead and lying down, not sitting; a single set of stinking bones. Why establish merit or fault? The Master asked, "I do not yet understand by what Dharma you instruct people, Reverend.
The Patriarch said, "If I were to say that I have a Dharma to give to others, I would be deceiving you.
I simply follow the occasion to untie the bonds; it is provisionally called samādhi. Listen to my verse: "The ground of the mind free from transgression is the precept of self-nature."
"The mind-ground free from delusion is the wisdom of self-nature; the mind-ground free from distraction is the concentration of self-nature.

Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the original vajra; the body’s going and coming is fundamentally samādhi. Upon hearing this verse, the Master repented and apologized, immediately vowing to take refuge.
He then presented his own verse, saying: "The illusory body of the five aggregates—how can illusion reach its ultimate end? Turning toward True Suchness, the dharmas still do not become pure."
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou:
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou was a native of Fengcheng in Hongzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and had already recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times.
The Patriarch asked him, "In reciting this sūtra, what do you take as its fundamental principle? The Master replied, "I study it..."
The man was dull-witted; from the beginning, he had merely recited the text according to the letter, for how could he have known its essential tenets?

The Patriarch said, "Try reciting it for me once, and I shall explain it for you. The Master then recited the sutra aloud. When they reached the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the Patriarch said, "Stop.
This sutra fundamentally takes the appearance of the World-Honored One through causes and conditions as its central theme. Even though it employs many kinds of parables, it is still..."
There is nothing that transcends this. What is the reason? It is solely for one great matter. This one great matter is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra; do not think that the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong to the Buddha's knowledge and vision alone.
"We have no share in this. If you interpret it in such a way, you are slandering the sutras and defaming the Buddha. Since he is already a Buddha, he has already perfected knowledge and vision;
why would he need to open them further? You must now believe that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are nothing other than your own mind;

they have no separate essence. The Master said, "If that is so, then one need only understand the meaning; there is no need for the trouble of reciting the sutras, is there? The Patriarch said, "The sutras..."
What fault is there? How could it obstruct your mindfulness? It is simply that delusion and awakening depend on the person; loss and gain depend on you. Listen to my verse:

"When the mind is deluded, the *Lotus Sūtra* revolves [around it]; When the mind is awakened, it revolves the *Lotus Sūtra*. If one recites for a long time without clarifying oneself, One becomes an enemy to the meaning of the text.
Without thoughts, every thought is correct; With thoughts, every thought becomes deviant. When neither existence nor non-existence is reckoned, One forever drives the white ox."

Upon hearing the verse, the Master [Zhizhe] spoke again, saying: "The sutras state that even the great śrāvakas and even the bodhisattvas, though they exhaust their thoughts and measure with their intellects, cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Now, you claim that an ordinary person merely by awakening to their own mind attains what is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Unless one possesses superior faculties, such a teaching will inevitably invite doubt and slander. Furthermore, the sutras speak of three vehicles, including the Great Ox-Cart."
"How do you distinguish [this] from the white ox cart? The Patriarch said, "The intent of the sutra is clear, yet you yourself are deluded and turn your back on it.

That the followers of the three vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom lies in their habit of measuring it with their own intellects. Even if they exhaust all their thoughts to investigate it together, it only becomes more remote.
The Buddha originally spoke for the sake of ordinary people; he did not speak for the sake of Buddhas. If you are unwilling to believe this principle," [he continued].
You have withdrawn from him, yet you do not realize that you have already mounted the white ox cart and are still searching for the three carts outside the gate.
Furthermore, the sutra clearly tells you that there are neither two nor three; why do you fail to understand? The three carts are provisional, intended for the past;
the One Vehicle is real, intended for the present. It is simply to teach you to leave the provisional and return to the real—to return to the real.
Thereafter, in truth, there will be no name [for me]. You should know that all precious wealth belongs entirely to you;
as you enjoy it, do not form the thought of a father, nor the thought of a son, nor even the thought of ownership. This is called upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
From kalpa to kalpa, his hands did not let go of the scroll; from day to night, there was no moment he did not contemplate it.
Having received this inspiration, the Master leaped for joy and praised him in verse: "I have recited three thousand sections of the sutras, yet a single phrase of Caoxi has been lost."

"Without clarifying the intent of the supramundane, how could one ever cease the madness of successive lifetimes? The provisional teachings of the sheep, deer, and ox were established; the excellence of the beginning, middle, and end was proclaimed.
Who would have known that within the burning house there originally dwells the King of Dharma? The Patriarch said, "From this day forward, you may truly be considered a monk who recites the sutras.
From then on, the Master understood the essential meaning and never ceased his recitation and upholding of the scriptures.
Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu:
Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu was a native of Ānfēng. Initially, he studied the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* approximately one thousand times.
Yet he did not understand the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms, so he paid obeisance to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the Three Bodies:
the Pure Dharma Body is your nature; the Complete Reward Body is your wisdom; and the thousands of billions of Transformation Bodies are your practice.
If one departs from the original nature and speaks of the Three Bodies separately, this is called having a body but lacking wisdom. If...
To realize that the three bodies (trikāya) have no inherent nature is precisely what is called the enlightenment of the four wisdoms (caturjñāna).

Listen to my verse: “Inherent nature possesses the three bodies; Their manifestation and illumination form the four wisdoms. Without departing from the conditions of seeing and hearing, One transcends and ascends to the stage of Buddhahood.

I now speak this for you; Believe it with clarity and you shall never again be deluded. Do not emulate those who run about in pursuit, Who spend their whole days merely talking of bodhi. The Master said: “Four...”
"May I hear the meaning of wisdom? The Patriarch said, "Since you have already realized the three bodies, you have naturally clarified the four wisdoms; why ask further?
If one were to speak of the four wisdoms apart from the three bodies, this would be called having wisdom without a body. It is precisely this having wisdom—"
This results in a state of ignorance. Again, he spoke in verse: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; The Wisdom of Equality has a mind free from ailment.

The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. The five, eight, six, and seven [consciousnesses] transform as fruit and cause;

They exist only as conventional designations and lack intrinsic nature. If one leaves no attachment where transformation occurs, then amidst the profuse arising [of phenomena], they are forever still."

He entered the *nāga-samādhi*. (Regarding the transformation of consciousness into wisdom, the teachings state: the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks; the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality;

and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Although the sixth and seventh are transformed during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are transformed upon the fruition, this is merely a transformation of their names, not a transformation of their essence. The Master paid his respects and expressed his gratitude.

He praised him with these verses: "The three bodies are originally my own essence; the four wisdoms are fundamentally the clarity of the mind. Body and wisdom are fused without obstruction, responding to things by assuming forms as required.
To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; to cling to a state of preservation is not true refinement. Through the teacher, the wondrous principle has been understood;
at last, the name of defilement is extinguished."
Chan Master Zhiche of Jiangxi was surnamed Zhang and named Xingchang.
In his youth, he was a man of chivalrous spirit. Following the division of the Buddhist community into Northern and Southern schools...
Although the two patriarchs had transcended self and other, their disciples vied with one another in love and hatred.

At that time, the followers of the Northern School established Master Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch, yet they harbored jealousy toward the transmission of the robe by Dajian, which became known throughout the world.
However, the Patriarch had foreseen this matter in advance and placed ten taels of gold in his quarters. At that time, Xingchang received [the teachings of] the Northern School.

A man who had been commissioned by others entered the Patriarch’s chamber with a blade, intending to do him harm. The Patriarch extended his neck toward him; Xingchang swung the blade three times, yet it caused no injury at all.
The Patriarch said, "The upright sword is not crooked; the crooked sword is not upright. I owe you only the gold, not your life.
Startled, Xingchang collapsed, and only after a long time did he regain consciousness. He begged for mercy and repented his transgression, immediately vowing to leave.

At the residence, the Patriarch then said to Jin: "You should leave for now; I fear that the assembly might instead bring harm upon you. You may come another day in a different guise, and I shall receive you.
Xingchang followed these instructions and fled under the cover of night. He joined the monastic order to become a monk, where he observed the precepts with diligence.
One day, remembering the Patriarch’s words, he traveled a great distance to pay his respects and asked: "I, your disciple, have previously read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*..."
"Venerable Sir, I do not yet understand the meaning of 'permanent' and 'impermanent. I beg the Master’s compassion to explain this briefly for me.
The Patriarch said, "That which is impermanent is the Buddha-nature. That which is permanent is the discriminating mind regarding all phenomena, both good and evil.
Xingchang said, "What the Master has said greatly contradicts the scriptural texts. The Patriarch said, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how would I dare to contradict it?"
Regarding the Buddhist sutras, Xingchang said, "The sutras state that the Buddha-nature is permanent, yet you, Master, say it is impermanent.
You say that all dharmas, both good and evil, and even the bodhicitta, are all impermanent, yet you say they are permanent.
This is contradictory and causes students to become increasingly confused. The Patriarch replied, "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, I once heard the nun Wujin..."
[Zang] read it through once and then began to expound it. There was not a single word or meaning that did not accord with the scriptural text;
even for your sake, I have never had two different teachings. Xingchang said, "The student’s capacity for understanding is shallow and dull.
I pray that the Master will explain this in detail. The Patriarch said, "Do you know? If Buddha-nature were permanent, what further need would there be to speak of good and evil dharmas? Then...
Even until the end of kalpas, not a single person would have given rise to the Bodhicitta;
therefore, my teaching of impermanence is precisely the Buddha’s teaching of the Way of True Permanence.

Furthermore, if all dharmas were impermanent, then every individual thing would possess its own self-nature that undergoes birth and death, and there would be places where the nature of true permanence does not pervade; therefore, I speak of permanence.
This is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.
Because ordinary beings and non-Buddhists cling to false permanence, while those of the two vehicles conceive of the permanent as impermanent, they together constitute the eight inversions.

Therefore, within the definitive teachings on Nirvana, he refutes those biased views and explicitly proclaims true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity. You should now rely upon these words.

This betrays the true meaning. By misinterpreting the Buddha’s final, subtle, and perfect words—mistaking impermanence for annihilation and death for permanence—what benefit is there even in reading them a thousand times?
Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor and spoke this verse:
"Because they cling to a mind of impermanence, The Buddha taught the nature of permanence. Those who do not understand these skillful means Are like those picking lotuses in a spring pond."
[Daowu said: "Gravel! Now that I have exerted no effort, the Buddha-nature appears before me; it was not bestowed by my teacher, nor is there anything I have attained myself.
The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration. You should be named Zhiche (Thorough Penetration). The Master bowed in thanks and departed.
Chan Master Zhichang of Xinzhou.
Chan Master Zhichang of Xinzhou was originally from Guixi in that province. He entered the monastic life in his childhood with the resolve to seek the realization of one's nature.
One day he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? What do you seek? The Master replied, "I, this student..."
He recently visited Master Da Tong. Da Tong asked, "Do you see empty space? He replied, "I see it. Da Tong asked, "When you see empty space, does it have any form or characteristics?
He replied, "Empty space has no shape; how could it have any characteristics? Da Tong said, "Your own fundamental nature is like empty space.
When you turn back to observe your own nature, you find that not a single thing can be seen; this is called right view. There was nothing more.
When one thing can be known, this is called true knowledge. There is no blue, yellow, long, or short; one simply perceives the source, the pure and luminous essence of awakening.
This is what is meant by "seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha," and it is also called the "Land of Ultimate Bliss" and the "Wisdom and Vision of the Tathāgata.
Although practitioners have heard these explanations, they are still not yet fully resolved. I beg the Venerable Master for further instruction so that there may be no more lingering doubts.
[Zhi] said, "The teacher's explanation still retains views and knowledge; that is why you have not yet understood. I shall now show you a verse, which says:
'Not seeing a single dharma, yet maintaining the view of non-existence, Is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.

Not knowing a single dharma, yet clinging to the knowledge of emptiness, Is just like lightning flashing within the great void. When such views and knowledge arise in an instant, One mistakenly recognizes them [as the truth].'"
"When have you ever understood the skillful means? You should, in a single thought-moment, know your own error; your own spiritual radiance is constantly manifest.

Upon hearing this verse, the Master’s mind was suddenly enlightened. He then composed a verse of his own, saying: "Groundlessly giving rise to conceptual understanding, Seeking Bodhi by clinging to forms.

If the mind harbors even a single thought of awakening, How can it transcend its former delusion? The source-body of self-nature is inherently awakened; To follow after reflections is a waste of effort."
Wandering through the cycles of transmigration, they fail to enter the chamber of the Patriarchs and remain bewildered, pursuing both extremes.
Regarding Chan Master Zhidao of Guangzhou:
Chan Master Zhidao of Guangzhou was a native of Nanhai. Initially, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch and asked: "I, a student..."

Having left the household life and studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for barely more than ten years, he had not yet clarified its essential meaning. He requested, "I pray that the Venerable Master will grant me instruction.

The Patriarch asked, "What is it that you have not understood? He replied, "'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased...'"
"Quiescent extinction is bliss. [The student] expressed doubt regarding this. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt it?
He replied, "All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The form-body is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing.
The dharma-body is permanent, lacking cognition and awareness. The Sūtra says: 'When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. I do not yet understand this."
What kind of body attains quiescence? What kind of body experiences bliss? If it were the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then at the time of its extinction, the four great elements would disperse;

being entirely of the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*), it could not be called blissful. If it were the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that attains quiescence, it would then be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones.

Who, then, would experience pleasure? Furthermore, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the essence of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the function of arising and ceasing.

Thus, there is one essence and five functions; arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the essence; when there is cessation, the function is withdrawn back into the essence.

If one allows for further rebirth, then the class of sentient beings is neither interrupted nor extinguished. If one does not allow for further rebirth, then they would forever return [to extinction].
"Quiescent extinction is identical to insentient things. If this were so, then all dharmas would be suppressed and subdued by nirvana;
they would not even be able to arise—what joy could there be in that? The Patriarch said: "You are a son of the Śākya clan.

Why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism to discuss the Supreme Vehicle? According to your understanding, apart from the physical body, there exists something else..."

The Dharma-body is free from arising and ceasing; one seeks it in quiescence. Furthermore, when one infers the permanence and bliss of Nirvana and yet claims there is a body that experiences [suffering], this is merely clinging to birth and death and being addicted to worldly pleasures. You should now know that the Buddha [speaks thus] for the sake of all who are deluded.
They recognize the aggregation of the five skandhas as their own self-nature and discriminate all dharmas as external objects.

They take birth as good and death as evil, flowing and shifting from moment to moment; unaware that all is like a dream or an illusion, they suffer in vain through saṃsāra, perceiving the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa as a state of suffering.
Seeking and striving throughout the day, the Buddha, out of compassion for them, reveals the true bliss of nirvāṇa. Kṣetra...
That which has no characteristic of arising possesses, in each moment, no characteristic of cessation; furthermore, there is nothing further to be extinguished through arising and cessation.
This is the quiescent extinction manifest before one. At the time it is manifest before one, there is also no measure of its being manifest before one.

This is called "constant bliss. This bliss has no experiencer, nor is there anyone who does not experience it. How could there be such designations as "one substance" or "five functions," let alone anything else?
To say that *nirvāṇa* suppresses all phenomena so that they never arise again is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse:
The unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa* is perfectly luminous, eternally quiescent, and illuminating. The ignorant and foolish call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation.
Those who seek the two vehicles regard it as non-action (*akṛtya*). All these belong to the conceptualizations of the mind—the sixty-two views.
Fundamentally, one falsely establishes empty and provisional names; what, then, constitutes the meaning of reality? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate this without grasping or rejecting.

By knowing that the phenomena of the five aggregates, as well as the "self" within the aggregates, and all external manifestations of forms and individual sounds and appearances, are equal to dreams and illusions, they do not give rise to views of ordinary beings or sages, nor do they form a conceptual understanding of nirvana. This applies to both extremes and the three periods of time.

Severance. One should constantly employ the functions of the sense faculties without giving rise to the notion of "functioning. One analyzes all phenomena without giving rise to the notion of "analysis.
Even when the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and winds strike the mountains together, the bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—the mark of nirvāṇa—is thus.
I now speak these words by force to cause you to abandon false views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you only a slight understanding.
[The Master] heard the verse and, leaping for joy, prostrated himself and withdrew.
Chan Master Zhenjue of Yongjia—Chan Master Zhenjue of Yongjia was named Xuánjué.
A native of the Dai clan from his home prefecture, he entered the monastic order at the age of seven and extensively explored [the scriptures].
The Tripitaka Master was refined in the perfect and subtle Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Amidst the four modes of deportment, he constantly remained in silent meditative contemplation.
Later, together with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang, he traveled to Caoxi. Upon first arriving, he shook his staff, circumambulated the Patriarch three times, and stood there upright.
The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand majestic demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. Great Virtue..."
“From what direction have you come? he asked. “To give rise to such great arrogance. The Master said, “The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift.

The Patriarch said, “Why do you not realize that there is no birth? Once realized, how could there be any swiftness? The Master said, “If one realizes it, there is no birth; once realized, there is fundamentally no swiftness. The Patriarch said, “So it is, so it is.
At that time, the entire assembly was without exception struck with astonishment. Only then did the Master assume his full dignified demeanor.

He paid his respects. After a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Is your departure too soon? The Master replied, "Since it is fundamentally not moving, how could there be such a thing as 'soon'?
The Patriarch asked, "Who knows that it is not moving? The Master replied, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to discrimination.

The Patriarch said, "You have truly grasped the meaning of non-arising. The Master replied, "If there is no arising, how can there be a 'meaning'? The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who is it that distinguishes?"
[The monk] said, "It is separate. The Master said, "Even discrimination is not the mind. The Patriarch sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one night.

At that time, he was called Yixiu Jue (One-Night Enlightenment). [Xuedou Xian cites this up to the point of "I am superior," then shouts: "If he had let out this shout at that moment, he would have avoided the appearance of a dragon's head and a snake's tail. Furthermore, regarding the place where [the monk] stood upright—" ]

Dai Zu said: "Before you have even reached Caoxi, I shall give you thirty blows! Fushan Yuan said: "The beginning was not reached; the end was excessive. Shuzhong Yun said: "Yongjia received echoes in the void; the Patriarch took the wrong for right. Xuedou shaves hair from a tortoise’s back; Fushan fits horns onto a horse’s head.

To circumambulate the meditation seat three times with eyes like copper bells—to urge him to stay for one night with a head like a wooden ladle. The pine wind and river moon are known by few; the Persian merchant of the South Sea gives birth to the Baize. The *Zhengdao Ge* says:
"Have you not seen the idle man of the Way, who has severed study and is non-active? He does not remove..."
Deluded thoughts do not seek the Truth; the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature. The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.

When the Dharma-body is fully awakened, there is not a single thing; it is the original, self-originated, natural, and true Buddha. The five aggregates are like floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness.
The bubbles of the three poisons arise and subside in vain; realizing the true mark, there is neither person nor dharma. In a single instant, the karma of Avīci hell is extinguished.

If one uses false speech to deceive sentient beings, one will bring upon oneself the punishment of having one’s tongue pulled out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Sudden awakening brings about the realization of Tathāgata-dhyāna.

The essence of the myriad practices of the six perfections is perfectly complete. Within the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly clear; upon awakening, all is empty, and not even a "great chiliocosm" exists.
There is no sin or merit, no loss or gain. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire. For some time now, the mirror of the dust has never been polished;
today, you must clearly analyze it. Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If there truly is no birth, there is nothing that does not exist.
Born! Summon the wooden man of the mechanism and ask him: "Seeking the Buddha through exertion, when will it be accomplished? Let go of the four elements; do not grasp at them.
Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with eating and drinking. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all is empty. This is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment.

This is the definitive teaching that manifests the True Vehicle. If there are those who are unwilling to accept this and instead investigate according to their own whims, they must directly cut off the root to reach the Buddha.
This is what is sealed. I am unable to pluck the leaves and seek out the branches. People do not recognize the mani jewel; it is personally recovered within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Its six kinds of divine functions are both empty and not empty; its single perfect radiance is both color and not color. By purifying the five eyes, one attains the five powers;
only through realization can it be known, for it is difficult to fathom. It is no difficulty to see one's form in a mirror, yet to grasp the moon in water—[this is how it is].

Who can grasp this? He always walks alone and always strides forth by himself. Those who have attained enlightenment travel together upon the path to Nirvana. His style is archaic and his spirit is pure; the wind of his character rises naturally high.

His appearance is haggard and his bones are firm, yet people pay him no heed. This impoverished monk claims in speech that he is poor; in truth, it is his body that is poor, while his Way is not poor.
As for being poor, his body is often clad in coarse, tattered rags; as for the Way, his mind harbors a priceless treasure. That priceless treasure—

Its use is inexhaustible; benefiting beings in accordance with their capacities, it is never withheld. The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within its essence; the eight liberations and six supernatural powers are the seal of the mind-ground.
Those of superior capacity, with a single resolution, understand everything; those of middling and inferior capacity, despite much hearing, remain largely in disbelief.
Simply untie the soiled garment from within your own breast—who could boast of diligence toward the external? Let others slander you, let others be wrong; hold the torch...
To burn incense for the heavens is but to weary oneself in vain. Hearing this, it was as if I had drunk nectar; it melted away my delusions and suddenly entered the inconceivable.
To view malicious words as merit—this makes them my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Without resentment toward slanderers, how could one manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience?
My fundamental realization is thorough, and my explanations are thorough; with concentration and wisdom perfectly clear, I do not stagnate in emptiness. It is not...
But I alone have now attained full realization; the bodies of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are identical.

I roar the lion’s roar with fearlessness; when the hundred beasts hear it, their brains split apart. The fragrant elephants flee in haste, losing their majesty; the devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy.
Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and streams, I sought teachers and inquired after the Way to practice Zen.

Since I recognized the path of Caoxi, I have known that birth and death are not mutually involved. Walking is Zen; sitting is Zen. Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, my essence remains at peace.
Even if one encounters a sharp blade, one remains ever serene; even if one is given deadly poison, one remains at ease.
My Master met the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and, through many kalpas, served as the Immortal of Forbearance. Time and again he was born, time and again he died; birth and death drifted on, without end.
Since attaining sudden enlightenment to non-arising, what anxiety or joy can there be regarding honor or disgrace? He entered the deep mountains to dwell among the orchids.
If one dwells amidst towering peaks and deep seclusion beneath long pines, leisurely sitting in stillness within the home of a wild monk, such quiet abiding is truly serene and elegant.
Awakening is immediate and requires no effort; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are not like this.

Giving with a mind fixed on appearances produces the merit of rebirth in heaven, yet it is like an arrow shot upward into the void: when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about only further rebirth in the future.
How can such "as one wishes" compare to the gate of the unconditioned reality-mark (dharmatā), which transcends all in a single leap and enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata?

If you only obtain the root, do not worry about the branches; it is like a pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon. Once you are able to understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting yourself and others will never be exhausted.
The river moon shines and the pine wind blows; throughout the eternal night, what need is there to do anything? The Buddha-nature is the jewel of the precepts.

The Seal of the Mind-Ground: Mist, dew, clouds, and rosy mists are the robes upon his body; The dragon-subduing bowl and the tiger-releasing staff; The two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly and distinctly.
This is not a matter of displaying forms or grasping at empty things; It is the personal trace of the Tathāgata’s precious staff. Seeking no truth, he does not sever delusion;
He understands that these two dharmas are empty and signless. Without signs, without emptiness, and without non-emptiness— This is precisely the Tathāgata.
Come to the true mark of reality: the mirror of the mind reflects clearly and without obstruction. Vastly lucid and transparent, it pervades the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātu*.

Within it, the myriad phenomena are reflected like a dense forest; this single, perfect luminosity is neither internal nor external. To recklessly reject cause and effect out of a sense of empty openness is to invite calamity and misfortune.
To abandon attachment while clinging to emptiness is likewise a sickness—it is like fleeing from drowning only to leap into a fire. Abandoning delusion...

The mind grasps at ultimate truth; the mind of grasping and rejecting becomes crafty and hypocritical. When practitioners do not understand this and yet apply themselves to cultivation, they truly become like those who mistake a thief for their own son.
The depletion of the wealth of Dharma and the destruction of merit—none of these arise except from this mind-consciousness.
Therefore, the Gate of Chan brings the mind to an end, entering suddenly into the power of non-arising insight. A great man wields the sword of wisdom; Prajñā...
Sharp as a vajra flame, it not only shatters the minds of externalists, but long ago it struck terror into the hearts of celestial Māras.

It rolls the thunder of the Dharma and beats the drum of the Dharma; it spreads the clouds of compassion and sprinkles sweet nectar. As dragons and elephants trample upon them, the moisture is boundless;
those of the three vehicles and five natures are all awakened. Upon the Snowy Mountains, there is no fat or grease mixed in; pure ghee alone emerges, which I have always received.
The single nature perfectly penetrates all natures; the one dharma universally contains all dharmas.

As the single moon universally appears in all waters, all moon-reflections in the waters are subsumed within that one moon. The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature, and my nature likewise merges with that of the Tathāgata.
The single stage is fully endowed with all stages; it is neither form nor mind, neither karma nor practice. In the snap of a finger, it is perfectly accomplished.

Eighty thousand gates vanish in a single instant; three great kalpas are extinguished in a flash. Whether they be all numerical categories or non-numerical categories, what connection do they have with my numinous awakening?
It cannot be disparaged and cannot be praised; its essence is like empty space, without boundaries or shores.
Without leaving this very place, it is eternally profound and still. Seek it and you will know that it cannot be seen. It cannot be grasped and cannot be relinquished; it is unobtainable.
How could it be otherwise? To speak in silence and to remain silent while speaking—the Great Gate of Giving stands open without obstruction.
When someone asks me what school I understand, I reply: "It is the power of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Whether this is right or wrong, people do not know;
whether one acts contrary to the flow or with it, even the heavens cannot fathom it. I have already practiced through many kalpas in the past; this is no idle deception. I establish it thus.
The Dharma-banner establishes the fundamental tenets; clearly, Caoxi is the Buddha’s mandate. Kāśyapa was the first to transmit the lamp;
twenty-eight generations are recorded in the West. When the Dharma flowed east into this land, Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch.

The transmission of the robe through six generations became renowned throughout the world; as for those who attained the Way thereafter, their number is beyond reckoning. Truth does not stand, for delusion is fundamentally empty. Existence...

There is neither the simultaneous negation nor the emptiness of emptiness; the twenty gates of emptiness are fundamentally unattached. The single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently identical.
The mind is the root and dharmas are the dust; these two are like stains upon a mirror. When the stains and grime are completely removed, the light finally appears.
When mind and phenomena both vanish, their nature is the Truth. Alas, in this degenerate age and evil time, sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline.
We are far removed from the Sages and false teachings run deep; demons are strong while the Dharma is weak, resulting in much resentment and harm.

Upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the sudden gate, they resent it and seek to destroy it, wishing to smash it to pieces like tiles. What is done in the mind brings calamity upon the body; there is no need for grievance or complaint, nor should one lay blame on others.
If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma-Wheel of the Tathāgata.

In a sandalwood forest there are no other trees; dense, lush, and profound, it is the dwelling place of the lion. In this tranquil realm and secluded grove, he wanders alone; wild beasts and flying birds all flee far away.
When the lion cubs follow after him, at three years of age they are already able to let out great roars. If a jackal were to pursue them...
O Dharma King! For a hundred years, demons have opened their mouths in vain. The Perfect and Sudden Teaching does not accommodate human sentiment;

if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must struggle for it directly. It is not that this mountain monk seeks to display egoism; I fear that if one practices otherwise, one will fall into the pit of annihilationism or eternalism.

"Not non-being, not being"—to err by a hair's breadth is to lose a thousand li. To affirm "it is" is for the Dragon Girl to suddenly attain Buddhahood; to deny "it is not" is the path of the evil Śāriputra.

Born into this state of entrapment and downfall, since my youth I have accumulated learning; I have also investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and śāstras. Distinguishing names and characteristics, I knew no rest;
I was like one entering the sea to count its sands, merely exhausting myself in vain. Yet the Tathāgata sternly rebuked me: "What benefit is there in enumerating the treasures of others?
From the beginning, I have been frustrated, realizing my travels were empty; for many years I have needlessly been a guest of the wind and dust. To plant...

Their natures are perverse and their understanding erroneous; they do not comprehend the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching. Those of the Two Vehicles exert themselves in diligence yet lack the Bodhi-mind; those of external paths possess cleverness yet lack true wisdom.
They are both ignorant and foolishly deluded, giving rise to real understanding from an empty fist or a pointing finger.

Clinging to the finger as the moon, they labor in vain; within the phenomena of sense organs and objects, they falsely concoct strange fabrications. Failing to see that even a single dharma is the Tathāgata, they remain lost.
Only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara. When fully realized, karmic obstacles are inherently empty;
yet if not realized, one must still repay past debts. Starving, one cannot eat the king’s banquet; sick, how could one be cured by meeting the King of Physicians?

Practicing dhyāna amidst desire through the power of wisdom and insight, a lotus born from fire is never destroyed. Even those who have committed grave offenses through reckless giving, upon awakening to non-arising, attain Buddhahood early.
He is present now, delivering the fearless Lion’s Roar. He deeply laments those who are ignorant, stubborn, and callous;
they know only that committing grave offenses obstructs Bodhi, yet they do not see the Tathāgata’s opening of the secret instructions. There were two bhikṣus who committed acts of lust and killing;

while Upāli saw their transgressions as increasing their karmic fetters like a firefly’s glow, the Great Being Vimalakīrti instantly dispelled their doubts, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow. Do not think...

Discussing the power of liberation, its wondrous function is as infinite as the sands of the Ganges (the *Chuanteng* edition reads: "This is precisely my good spiritual friend"). I dare not decline the toil of the fourfold offerings;
even ten thousand taels of gold could be spent upon them. To grind one's bones and crush one's body would not suffice to repay this debt;

a single phrase, clearly understood, transcends billions. The King of Dharmas is most supreme; the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all together realized it. I now understand...
This wish-fulfilling jewel: those who believe and accept it will all be in accord with it. Clearly seeing that not a single thing exists, there is neither person nor Buddha.
The great trichiliocosm and its myriad worlds are like bubbles on the sea; all sages and worthies are like lightning flashes.

Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head, one’s perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom shall never be lost. The sun may grow cold and the moon may grow hot, but the various māras cannot [overcome]—
It can destroy false teachings. When the majestic elephant carriage advances with imposing power upon the road, who could see a cicada-killer (shrimp) able to block its tracks?
A great elephant does not travel on the narrow paths of a hare; great enlightenment is not constrained by petty details. Do not slander the vast expanse of heaven with your limited, narrow views.
Since you have not yet understood, I shall now resolve it for you.
As for Chan Master Zhihuang of Hebei:
when he first visited the Fifth Patriarch, although he had consulted him on matters of resolution, he followed the gradual path of practice.
He then traveled north of the Yellow River, where he built a hermitage and sat in long-term meditation. For more than twenty years, he never showed a trace of indolence.
Later, encountering the encouragement of Master Ce, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. Moved by his journey from afar, the Patriarch granted him instruction and resolution.
At these words, the Master attained sudden and profound enlightenment; the state of mind he had cultivated during the preceding twenty years left no trace whatsoever.
National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang:
National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang was a native of Zhuji in Yuezhou. His secular surname was Ran. Having received the seal of the mind...
He resided at Dangzigu on Mount Baita in Nanyang for over forty years, never descending from the mountain. His practice of the Way became renowned throughout the capital.

In the second year of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty, an imperial messenger was dispatched with an edict to summon him to the capital, where he was accorded the honors due to a teacher.

When Emperor Daizong ascended the throne, he again invited him to reside at Guangzhai Monastery, where he remained for sixteen years, preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of his listeners.
At that time, the Tripitaka Master of Great Ears from Western Heaven arrived at the capital, claiming to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds.
Emperor Suzong ordered the National Teacher to test him. As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the Teacher, he prostrated and stood to his right.
The Teacher asked, "Have you attained the power of knowing others' minds? Tell me, where am I right now? The Tripitaka Master replied, "The Master is..."

[The Master] said, "As the teacher of an entire nation, how could you go off to West River to watch the boat races? After a long silence, he asked again, "Tell me, where am I right now? The Tripitaka Master replied, "As the teacher of an entire nation, how could you be on Tianjin Bridge watching monkeys perform? The Master remained silent for a long while, then asked once more, "Tell me, where am I right now? The Tripitaka Master replied, "You are in the Dharma Hall. The Master said, "I am not there. The Tripitaka Master said, "Then where are you? The Master said, "I am right here. The Tripitaka Master said, "Where is 'here'? The Master struck him three times with his staff and said, "You have been traveling back and forth between India and China for thirty years; why did you not bring back even a single Buddha-dharma? The Tripitaka Master bowed and withdrew. The Master then said to the assembly, "Do you see this foreigner? He has traveled back and forth between India and China for thirty years, yet he does not know where the Buddha-dharma is. If you wish to seek the Buddha-dharma, you must look within your own minds. Do not seek it outside yourselves. The Tripitaka Master then composed a verse and presented it to the Master: "I traveled from India to the East, Seeking the Buddha-dharma in the world. For thirty years I have wandered, Yet I have found nothing at all. Today I meet the Great Teacher, Who strikes me three times with his staff. Now I know the Buddha-dharma, It is simply this very mind. The Master said, "If you have truly realized this, you may leave. The Tripitaka Master then departed. Later, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "That foreign monk was a man of great capacity. Had he not encountered me, he would have spent his life in vain. If you do not encounter a true teacher, you will surely fall into the common crowd. The assembly was deeply moved. This is recorded as the "Beating of the Foreign Monk" case. It is said that the Tripitaka Master was a man of great wisdom and virtue who had traveled extensively throughout the five regions of India. He had heard of the fame of the Master and thus came specifically to seek him out. Although he had studied the scriptures and treatises for many years, he had never encountered a true teacher. Upon meeting the Master, he immediately wished to test him, yet he was unable to withstand the Master’s spiritual power. Thus, he was defeated and withdrew. This is why it is said that if one does not encounter a true teacher, one will surely fall into the common crowd. One must know that the Buddha-dharma is not something to be sought through intellectual understanding or verbal debate; it must be realized through the direct transmission of the mind-seal. Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha-dharma is not in books; it is in the mind. If you can understand this, you will realize that the Buddha-dharma is not far away—it is right here before you. If you do not understand, you will continue to wander in birth and death, seeking it elsewhere. Be careful! Be careful! Do not let your efforts go to waste. This is the essential point. Study it well! Study it well! This is the "Beating of the Foreign Monk" case. "Where is he? The Tripitaka Master could not fathom this. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit!

Where is your *abhijñā* (supernatural power) of knowing others' minds? The Tripitaka Master was speechless. (A monk asked Zhaozhou: "The Great-Eared Tripitaka Master failed to see the National Teacher for the third time. I wonder, where was the National Teacher? Zhaozhou said, 'He is on top of the Tripitaka Master's nostrils.

Later, the monk asked Xuansha: 'Since he is on the nostrils, why did he not see him? Xuansha said, 'It is precisely because he was too close. (A monk asked Yangshan: "Regarding the Great-Eared Tripitaka Master, why did he [fail] on the third occasion?")

He did not see the National Teacher. Yangshan said, "The first two times were the mind encountering objects; the latter was the person’s own enjoyment of samādhi, which is why he did not see him. Furthermore, a monk asked Xuansha, and Xuansha said, "Tell me, did you see him during those first two times?

Baizhang Yuan said, "If the National Teacher were inside the nostrils of Tripitaka, what would be difficult about seeing him? Yet you do not realize that the National Teacher is in Tripitaka’s very eyes. Cuiyan Zhi said, "As for Tripitaka himself, did he see the National Teacher’s nostrils?

Gaofeng Miao said, "How great the National Teacher’s lifelong skill! It has all been exposed by this barbarian monk. Nevertheless, it is fortunate to have met a sagely sovereign who can testify to it. Jinshu Wuzhun said, "If there were anyone here now..."
"The Way is within the eyes of the Tripitaka; why then do you not see it? Guanghui said to him, "It is not within your realm. One day he called his attendant; the attendant responded.
Thus there were three calls and three responses. The Master said, "I thought it was I who had failed you;

it turns out it was you who failed me. Jingshan Gaofeng said: "In the monastic communities, this is called 'The National Teacher’s Three Calls to the Attendant. From this point on, there has been much fuss and complication. Only Xuedou saw through the very marrow of the ancients when he said: 'When the National Teacher called the attendant three times, pointing [at him] was not reaching him.

Miaoxi said: 'Truly so. When the attendant responded three times, reaching him was not pointing [at him]. Miaoxi said: 'But it is not like that. I thought it was I who had failed you; who knew it was you who failed me? He could not deceive Xuedou. Miaoxi asked: 'Who?"'

The Master said, "Furthermore, I summon the great assembly: 'It is well; Xuedou cannot deceive me. Nevertheless, Xuedou also cannot deceive Miaoxi; Miaoxi also cannot deceive you all; and you all also cannot deceive the pillar. Xuansha said, 'The attendant, however, understands.

Xuedou said, 'Imprisoning prisoners increases their cleverness. Miaoxi said, 'Two prizes, one tally. Yunmen asked, 'What is the point where the National Teacher betrayed the attendant? To understand this is also groundless," said Xuedou.

Yun said, "I originally did not understand. Miaoxi said, "This is what Xuefeng meant. Yunmen also said, "What is it? This is where the attendant betrayed the National Teacher; even grinding one's bones to powder would not repay him. Xuedou said, "Pointless, pointless. Miaoxi said, "He drew the arrow by himself. Chan Master Nanyue Huairang, Dharma successor of the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Dajian: His secular surname was Du;
he was a native of Jinzhou. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty, [he was born].
On the day of his birth, at the age of fifteen, he went to Yuquan Temple in Jingzhou and left the household life under the guidance of Vinaya Master Hongjing.

In the second year of the Tianshou era, he received full ordination. Thereafter, he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka. One day, he sighed to himself, saying: "Now, as for one who has left the household life..."
Regarding conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, there is nothing superior to this in the heavens or among humans. He then went to Caoxi to visit the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch said, "What thing comes in such a manner? The Master was speechless.
After eight years had passed, he suddenly attained a realization. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding.
The Patriarch asked, "How so? The Master replied, "To describe it as a thing is not correct. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still need for cultivation and realization?
The Master replied, "Cultivation and realization are not absent; however, one must not be defiled by them. The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is [the state of] all Buddhas."
"You are thus protected and mindful by me; as you are thus, so am I. The Indian master Prajñātāra had prophesied:
"From beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. The Master attended him at his side for fifteen years.
In the second year of the Xiāntián era, he went to Mount Heng and resided at Pánniē Temple. During the Kāiyuán era, there was a śramaṇa named Dàoyī (who was the aforementioned [Huineng]).

The Patriarch was at Mount Heng, where he constantly practiced seated meditation. Master [Nanyue Huairang] knew he was a vessel for the Dharma and went to ask him, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation?
Daoyi replied, "I hope to become a Buddha. The Master then took a brick and began polishing it on a stone in front of the hermitage.
Daoyi asked, "What are you polishing that for? The Master said, "I am polishing it to make a mirror. Daoyi said, "How can you polish a brick [to make a mirror]?"
"Can it become a mirror? The Master said, "Since polishing a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation make one a Buddha?
Daoyi asked, "How then is it so? The Master said, "It is like an ox pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, would you strike the cart or would you strike the ox? Daoyi had no reply.
The Master spoke again, "Do you study sitting meditation, or do you study sitting as a Buddha? If you study..."
"Regarding sitting meditation: meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study by imitating the Buddha’s posture, the Buddha is not a fixed form.
Within the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as the Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha; if you cling to the form of sitting, you do not penetrate its principle.
Upon hearing this instruction once, he was like one drinking clarified butter (amṛta). He prostrated and asked: "How should I apply my mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?"
The Master said: "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like sowing seeds below; my exposition of the essential Dharma is like the moisture from heaven.
Because your conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way. He asked again: "The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be perceived? The Master said:
The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground is able to perceive the Way; the same is true for the signless samādhi. Daoyi asked, "Is there arising and ceasing?
The Master said, "If one perceives the Way through arising and ceasing, gathering and dispersing, that is not perceiving the Way.
