The Layman said, "Exactly so. The Master was speechless. The Layman said, "I told you it was merely coincidental.
On another day, he asked the Layman, "I have a question to ask; do not be sparing with your words. The Layman said, "Please go ahead."
[The Master] came forward. The Master said, "So you do cherish your words. The Layman said, "This very greeting has unconsciously fallen into his trap.
The Master then covered his ears. The Layman said, "A true master! A true master!"
Master Liang of Xishan was a native of Shu.
He was quite proficient in lecturing on the sutras and śāstras. Having gone to visit Mazu, Mazu asked him, "I have heard it said that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras;
is this true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so. Mazu asked, "With what do you lecture? The Master replied, "With..."
The Master was lecturing on the Heart Sūtra. The Patriarch said, "The mind is like a skilled performer; the intellect is like the assistant. How can you hope to understand it through lecturing?
The Master raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot be lectured upon, can empty space be lectured upon? The Patriarch replied, "Indeed, empty space can be lectured upon.
The Master, dissatisfied, was about to leave when the Patriarch called out, "Lecturer! The Master turned his head, and the Patriarch said, "It is."
"What is it? The Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment, and immediately prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "Why do you, dull-witted master, prostrate yourself?
The Master replied, "I believed that no one could surpass me in the exegesis of the sutras and śāstras.

Today, having been questioned by the Great Master, the lifelong achievements of my life have all at once melted away like ice. Having offered his thanks, he withdrew and went into seclusion in the west of Hongzhou."
"Mountains. No further news. (Fayan Yi said: "Look at this ancient; he was so compassionate in teaching people. How do you understand him now? Do not huddle together here in deluded thoughts.)"
When Layman Pang came to Master Qifeng, the Master said, "A layperson enters the monastery so frequently; what are you looking for?
The Layman looked back at both sides and asked, "Who says such a thing? The Master then gave him a shout (*du*). The Layman said, "It is here."
"Right here," the Master said. The layman asked, "Is this the Way of Dangyang? The Master said, "What about the one behind you? The layman turned his head and said, "Look, look!
The layman then said, "The grass-thief has been utterly defeated. The layman then asked, "How many *li* is it from here to the Peak?
The Master said, "Where have you come from? The layman said, "Truly steep and firm; one cannot even question it. The Master [nodded].
The Master said, "How many are there? The layman said, "One, two, three. The Master said, "Four, five, six. The layman said, "Why do you not say seven?
The Master said, "As soon as you say seven, there is already eight. The layman said, "It is so; it is so. The Master said, "Add as much as you wish.
The layman said, "I cannot speak with such barefacedness. The Master said, "Give me back my 'Pang-er' at such a time!"

The protagonist arrived. The layman said, "What a young spirit you are! The Master said, "A fine greeting; yet your question does not hit the mark. The layman said, "I thought so, I thought so. (Tiantong Hua says:
To manifest great capacity and display great function is not merely like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, nor is it like a swift flame passing through the wind.

One must look upon precipices on level ground and flatlands in the midst of sheer heights. Observe these two elders: they have entered the tiger’s den and penetrated the very source. Reaching the point where patterns intertwine and the blade moves with mastery, attaining great freedom—why then has he never reached the Flower Peak?)

It is just as Qifeng said: "Return to me the master of this moment—Master Pang! The layman replied, "What need is there for such spirit? Guizong placed his eye right here, wishing for everyone to have a sudden flash of realization.
After a long silence, he said: "The bamboo shadows sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir; the moon pierces the depths of the waves, yet the water leaves no trace."
Daiyō Oshō, Daiyō Oshō. Because he met Zen Master I, he asked him:

"Recently, there have been a certain kind of teachers who instruct people regarding the matter before their eyes, taking this as a means of guiding others. Do you understand this? "I do," [replied I].
[The student] said, "Before the colors have even appeared, there is nothing. I wish to pose a question here; I do not know if it is permissible.

The Master said, "I have already answered you; do not speak of 'permissible' or 'impermissible. [The student] asked, "Do you recognize what is right before your eyes? The Master said, "If it is right before your eyes, how would you go about recognizing it?
[The student] said, "In any case, it will be subject to scrutiny. The Master said, "By whom? [The student] said, "By me. The Master said, "... (The Master remained silent).
The Master then shouted. Yicán stepped back and stood there. The Master said, "You only know how to look forward; you do not know how to look behind.
Yicán replied, "Adding frost upon snow. The Master said, "In this, neither of us gains any advantage."
One day, while traveling along a road, Master Bailin encountered Layman Pang. The Master asked, "Have you ever shared the phrase by which you attained realization at Mount Nanyue with anyone?
The Layman replied, "I have. The Master asked, "To whom did you share it?"
The man—the Layman—pointed to himself with his hand and said, "Pang Gong. The Master said, "Even if it were Miao-de or Kong-sheng themselves, they would not have been able to praise him sufficiently.
The Layman then asked, "Master, who knows the phrase by which you have attained power?
The Master put on his bamboo hat and walked away. The Layman said, "Be careful on your way. The Master did not look back. (Jingshan Daoyuan said: "If this matter had not been [handled] by Pang... )

Master Gōng: "Bailing was nearly mistaken in his comparison to a human being. Even so, all the hundred spirits must yield one move to Old Páng. Why? At that time, had he not obtained that broken straw hat to cover his skull, what face would he have had to see Old Páng?

Chūshí Qǐ said: "When Bailing donned the hat and departed, clearly state the phrase by which he gained power. For what reason did the Elder Miaoxi say, 'What face does Bailing have to see Old Páng'? This too is a case of supporting the strong rather than the weak. If someone were to act as the host for Miaoxi, I would ask:

What is the phrase by which he gained power? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! If you hesitate even for a moment, I shall strike you across the spine with my staff. Tìānqǐrèi said: "When masters meet, it ultimately does not depend on..."

To make a living by means of words and phrases is not to abide within those words and phrases. One must ensure that the eight seas flow unimpeded; when questioned, one must ride the wind, and in responding, remain sovereign. Who would not praise such a one? Why, then, at the very end, did he instead pursue [the truth] without uttering a single word?
"The bird flies high because the sky is vast; the fish leaps because the deep pool is profound."
The Monk Niu-tou of Jinzhou:
This monk would regularly prepare his own meals to offer to the assembly of monks.

When it was time for the midday meal, he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the hall, perform a dance, and laugh heartily, saying, "O sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat! (Changqing Ling said, "This is very much like using the meal as a cause...")

**Celebrating the Great Light’s Teaching** A monk asked, "What was the meaning of Changqing saying, 'To celebrate and praise because of the meal'? Daguang then performed a dance. The monk bowed. Daguang said, "What principle did you see that you immediately bowed?

The monk then performed a dance. Daguang said, "This wild fox spirit! Dongchan Qi said, "The ancients personally took the initiative to prepare the meal; having finished the dance, they called others to eat. What was their intention? Do you understand yet? As for Changqing and Daguang, were they manifesting [the truth]?"

The meaning of the ancients is analyzed separately for others. Now I ask the Venerable: when you hold your bowl and grasp your alms-basin every day, or when you welcome and see someone off—do you act exactly as the ancients did, or is there a different principle?

If you say it is different, how do you make it so? If you say it is the same, you have just reached their dance, yet you are still called a wild fox spirit. Do you have a point of realization here? If you have not realized it, where is the eye of your travel-study? Xuedou Xian said: "Even so, Niu-nyou was not acting with a good heart.

He added this verse: "The first arrow was light, but the second arrow is deep; Who says that yellow leaves are gold? If the waves of Caoxi are like this, Countless ordinary people will sink into the mud. Zhaojue Qin said: "Now tell me, the Great..."

Guangyun said, "This wild fox spirit! 'Hiding his head white, at the edge of the sea black'—are they the same or different? This lacquer bucket! He also says, 'A fine monk. Tell me, are they the same or different?
The Master, because Linji had come, held his staff crosswise and sat before the abbot’s quarters. Linji then clapped his hands three times and went back to the hall.
The Master then went down, performed the formal greetings, and asked: "When host and guest meet, each has their proper etiquette. You, Senior Monk—"
"How can you be so discourteous? Linji said. "What did you say? As the Master prepared to open his mouth, Linji struck him with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*).
The Master made a gesture of falling over; Linji struck him again with his sitting cloth. The Master said, "Today I have not had my way," and then returned to the abbot’s quarters.

[Later,] Guishan asked Yangshan, "Between these two venerable elders, was there a winner and a loser? Yangshan said, "If there were a winner, they both won; if there were a loser, they both lost. Guishan remarked, "One used a scorched brick."
"Striking at the very bottom of the ice. One person gains an advantage is another's disadvantage. Let those with eyes discern this!
Master Luyuan of Shaozhou ascended the hall and said: "The direct meaning from the West—how could it be difficult to speak? Among you, do not..."
"There is one who has attained the Way; come forth and try to speak of it. When a monk came out and bowed, the Master struck him and said, "At what time have you come forth?

He then returned to his quarters. (The monk reported this to Changqing Huiheng. Changqing said, "Not bad, not bad. Baofu Zhan spoke on his behalf, saying, "It was for the sake of the Master that he did not spare his life.
Chengtian Zong said, "The Dharma-vehicle is not easy to uphold. These two old fellows could not support it. I say that if this monk had not come forth, the staff would have been the source of milk.")
When Yangshan was a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), he recited the sutras with a loud voice. The Master rebuked him, saying, "This novice monk recites the sutras as if he were weeping.
Yangshan replied, "Huiji [myself] am only like this; I do not know how you, the Master, would do it. The Master then looked at him.
Yangshan said, "If it were like that, how would it differ from weeping? Thereupon, the Master ceased.
Master Songshan and Layman Pang were drinking tea together. The Layman pointed to his tea caddy and said, "Everyone has their share;
why is it that no one can speak of it? The Master replied, "Precisely because everyone has their share, they cannot speak of it."
The layman said, "Elder brother, why is it that you can speak? The Master said, "One must not remain without words.
The layman said, "Truly so! Truly so! The Master then drank his tea. The layman said, "Elder brother, as you drink your tea, why do you not bow to your guests?
The Master said, "Who? The layman said, "Pang Gong. The Master said, "Why bother to bow further? Later, Danxia heard of this.
He then said, "Had it not been for Songshan, I would have been nearly deluded by this old fellow.
When the Layman heard this, he sent someone to deliver a message to Danxia, saying, "Why did you not realize it before the bag was even lifted?"
As for Master Ze-chuan:
he was a native of Shu. While he and Layman Pang were conversing, the Master asked, "Do you still remember the principle [you realized] when you saw Stonehead?
The Layman replied, "I am still fortunate enough to have the Master bring it up again. The Master said, "I knew this would happen after a long time."
The Master was acting with arrogance. The layman said, "Master, you are not only as decrepit as Master Pang.
The Master said, "Those two were contemporaries; how much difference is there between them? The layman said, "Master Pang was vigorous and healthy, and he surpassed you, Master.
The Master said, "It is not that he surpassed me; he simply lacked your head-wrap (fukuto). The layman took off his head-wrap and said, "Now he looks exactly like you, Master. The Master—
He simply laughed loudly. While the Master was picking tea, the layman said, "The Dharma-realm admits no body;

do you still see me, Master? The Master replied, "It is not the Old Teacher. When he finished answering the layman's question, the layman said, "To have a question and an answer is merely the ordinary way.
The Master then continued picking tea without listening. The layman said, "Do not take offense at my having questioned you so casually just now."
The Master also paid him no heed. The layman shouted, “This impolite old fellow! I shall take you before a man of clear eyes one by one.

The Master then cast aside his tea basket and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters. Xuedou Xian said: “Zhuoquan only knew how to hold fast to his borders; he could not live or die together with him.

Had he stripped off the layman’s headcloth at that moment, who would have dared call him Layman Pang? Jiangshan Qin said: “Twice he was ignored; he cast away the basket and went straight back. Tell me, where does the ultimate meaning lie? Do you understand? It is like a bitter gourd.”
"When the bitter is bitter to the root, the melon is sweet to the stem. Thus, the old man from Chuang has experienced much.
Regarding the Monk Dadi of Xinzhou:
having received the imperial mandate from Jiangxi, he constantly concealed his name. Whenever students came to question him...
He would simply strike the ground with his staff to indicate [the answer]. At that time, he was called "Master Striking the Ground" (Dadidi Heshang).
One day, a monk hid the staff away and then posed a question to him; the Master merely opened his mouth.

The monk asked his attendant, "If someone asks the Master every day and he simply strikes the ground, what is the meaning of this? The attendant immediately took a piece of firewood from inside the hearth.
[He] threw a piece [of wood] into the cauldron. (Jingshan Daokai said: "Raising a son who does not equal his father; the family lineage will decline for a generation.
Regarding Master Xiuxi of Xiuxi, Tanzhou: Guishan asked, "When sound and form are pure and true, what is the Way? The Master said, "Chaos."
"What is the Way? Guishan then walked from east to west and stood there. The Master said, "If it were not like this, it would be a disaster.
Guishan then walked from west to east and stood there. The Master then descended from his meditation seat;
as he had taken only two steps, Guishan seized him and asked, "What is the matter of sound and form being utterly true? The Master then gave him a slap. Guishan said:
"Thirty years from now, there will not even be anyone left to serve tea. The Master said, "What would you do with this fellow Gushan?
Gushan laughed heartily.
While Baizhang Huashang was lying down at Jiangxi Baizhu, Daowu approached and pulled the blanket over him. The Master asked, "What are you doing?
Daowu replied, "Covering you. The Master asked, "Is it for the one who is lying down, or for the one who is sitting? Daowu said, "It is neither of these two."
[Daowu] said, "What can be done about the covering? Dowu said, "Do not speak in confusion. While the Master was warming himself by the fire, Dowu asked, "What is this?
The Master said, "Harmony. Dowu said, "If that is so, you have escaped right at the head.
The Master said, "How long has it been since we were last apart? Dowu then shook his sleeves and departed. One day, Dowu...
Returning from outside, the Master asked, "Where have you been? Dao Wu replied, "I have come to pay my respects.
The Master said, "Why do you use these two pieces of skin? Dao Wu said, "I borrow them. The Master said, "If he has nothing to lend to you, what then?
Dao Wu said, "Precisely because he has it, I borrow it."
Caotang Heshang of Jingzhao.
After he finished his studies under Daji, he went to the place of Haichang Heshang.
Haichang asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Daochang. Haichang asked, "What place is this here? The Master said:
Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
Regarding the Monk of Xingping at Jingzhao Xingping Monastery: when Dongshan came to pay his respects, the Master said, "Do not bow to an old decrepit man. Dongshan replied:
"The ritual is not for the elderly. The Master said, "One who is not elderly does not receive ritual greetings. Dongshan said, "He also does not stop [the greeting].
Dongshan then asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? The Master said, "It is precisely your own mind.
Dongshan said, "Even so, this is still a point of doubt for me. The Master said, "If it is thus, then go ask the wooden man."
Dongshan said, "I have a single phrase that does not borrow from the mouths of the sages. The Master said, "Try to say it. Dongshan said, "It is not I.
As Dongshan was taking his leave, the Master asked, "Where will you go? Dongshan said, "Following the current, there is no fixed destination.
The Master said, "Is it the Dharma-body following the current, or the Reward-body following the current? Dongshan said, "Neither."
This is the explanation. The Master then clapped his hands (Baofu said, "Dongshan has his own style," and then added separately, "How many people have you found?").
Regarding the monk Xixiao, when Monk Lusi asked, "Every thought clings to objects; every mind is eternally tranquil," the Master said, "Yesterday..."
Later, there was also someone who spoke in this manner. Lushi asked, “What did you say? The Master said, “I do not know. Lushi said, “Please, Reverend, explain it.
The Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk. Lushi shook out his sleeves and departed.

The Master called to the assembly, saying, “Keep your eyes open at the crown of your heads” (Jiangshan Qin said: “Although this old monk has no eyes at the crown of his head, I can still discern that your bones have been exposed. Why? A venomous snake in an ancient tomb wears horns upon its head”).
Nanshan Menghu Weizhao. Master Shuilao of Hongzhou.
When he first visited Mazu, he asked: "What is the very meaning of the coming from the West?"
The Patriarch said, "Prostrate yourself. As soon as the Master prostrated, the Patriarch stepped on his chest and knocked him down.
The Master attained great enlightenment; rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary!

Hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings—only upon the tip of a single hair can one recognize the source. He bowed in gratitude and withdrew. (Langye Jue said: "O Assembly, what do you say?")

"Has Shuilao awakened yet? Tiantong Jue said: "Master Mazu should not have let him go. When he rose and spoke thus, he should have simply asked: 'From where did you get this single hair-tip? Waiting for him to hesitate—"

"Give him another kick! ○ After the Master had taken up residence [at the monastery], he would tell the assembly every day: "Ever since I took one bite from Mazu’s kick, I have laughed without ceasing until this very day."
Master Fubei. When Laywoman Lingxingpo came to pay her respects, the Master offered her a seat and tea.

The woman then asked, "To whom do you entrust the phrase that cannot be spoken even with one's full strength? The Master replied, "Fubei has no superfluous words. The woman said, "I have not yet arrived."
Fubei said, "It is not to be doubted. The Master said, "If you have another point of excellence, do not hesitate to bring it forth.
Fubei folded her hands and wept, saying, "Alas! To this sky of suffering, you add yet more grievance. The Master was speechless. Fubei said, "In words, you do not know the biased from the correct;
in principle, you do not recognize the inverted from the upright. To act as a teacher for others is to invite calamity. Later, a monk recounted this to Nanquan, who said, "How bitter!"
Fubei was once rebuked by this old woman. Later, when the woman heard of it, she laughed and said, "Master Wang still lacks a certain turn of phrase.
When the Chan traveler Chengyi encountered the old woman, he asked her, "In what way does Nanquan still lack a turn of phrase?
The woman then wept and said, "How tragic! How painful! Chengyi was at a loss for words. The woman asked, "Do you understand? Chengyi—
Chengyi stood with his palms joined. Ba said, "Dead Zen monks are as numerous as hemp and millet. Chengyi presented this to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, "If I had seen this stinking old woman, I would have asked her until her mouth was mute.
Chengyi asked, "I wonder, Master, how would you have questioned her? Zhaozhou then struck him. Chengyi said, "Why did you strike me instead?"
Zhaozhou said, "As for this fellow who has died while still clinging to life, if I do not beat him now, when shall I wait to do so? He then struck him several blows.
Upon hearing this, the old woman said, "Zhaozhou deserves to receive a blow from my hand. Later, a monk reported this to Zhaozhou, and Zhaozhou wept, saying:
"How tragic! How painful! When the old woman heard these words, she joined her palms and sighed, saying, "Zhaozhou’s eye pierces through the four worlds.
Zhaozhou instructed a monk to ask her, "What is Zhaozhou’s eye? The old woman then raised her fist.

The monk returned and reported this to Zhaozhou, who composed a verse, saying: "When the occasion arises, he presents it face-to-face; Face-to-face, he acts with the swiftness of the occasion. The report..."
"You, Laywoman Lingxing, why do you lose yourself in this sound of weeping? The laywoman replied with a verse: "The Master has already understood the sound of my weeping;
now that it is understood, who is there to know it? At that time in the kingdom of Magadha, how many would have lost the opportune moment before their eyes?"
Master Longshan of Tanzhou (also known as Master Yishan). When Dongshan and his senior master Mi were traveling by way of the mountain, they saw vegetable leaves floating down a stream.
Dongshan said, "This is a deep mountain with no people; why are there vegetables flowing along? Is there perhaps a practitioner of the Way living here?"

They then consulted together on how to clear the grass and proceed along the stream. After traveling five or seven li, they suddenly saw the Master, whose emaciated form and extraordinary appearance struck them.

Setting down their luggage, they paid their respects. The Master said, "There are no paths on this mountain; from where have you come, Ācārya? Dongsan said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of there being no path, from where did you enter, Reverend?
The Master said, "I do not come as a wandering monk. Dongsan said, [“Then where have you come from? The Master said, “I have not come from among the clouds and waters. Dongsan said, “...”.
"How long has the Master resided on this mountain? The Master said, "Neither spring nor autumn.
Dongshan asked, "Did the Master reside here first, or did this mountain reside here first? The Master said, "I do not know. Dongshan asked, "Why do you not know? The Master said:
"I have not come from among humans or devas. Dongshan asked, "Master, what principle have you realized that you dwell on this mountain?
The Master said, "I saw two clay oxen fighting and entering the sea; until this very day, there has been no further news.
Only then did Dongshan assume his full ceremonial demeanor and prostrate, asking, "What is the guest within the host? The Master replied, "Green mountains shroud white clouds."
[The monk] asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "A lifelong non-leaving of the door. [The monk] asked, "How far apart are guest and host?
The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the long river. [The monk] asked, "When guest and host meet, what words are spoken?

The Master said, "The clear breeze brushes the white moon. Dongshan took his leave. The Master then composed a verse, saying: "I have lived all along in a thatched cottage of three bays; I have never left the gate for even a single day."
A single ray of divine light; ten thousand phenomena are at rest. Do not bring right and wrong to judge me; the artificiality of this floating life is irrelevant.
Because he burned his hermitage and entered the deep mountains, he was no longer seen. Later generations called him Master Yinshan (Hidden Mountain).
The Layman Pangyun was a layman from Xiangzhou. When he first visited Shitou, he asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Shitou covered his mouth with his hand, whereupon Pangyun attained sudden enlightenment. Later, he became a friend to Danxia.
One day, Shitou asked, "Since you first met this old monk, how have you conducted yourself in your daily activities?
The layman replied, "If you ask about my daily activities, there is no place to open my mouth. He then presented a verse, saying: "In daily activities, there is nothing different."
Only I alone am in harmony with it. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting; in every place there is no tension or discord. Who would assign the titles "red" or "purple"?
Hills and mountains are utterly free of a speck of dust. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions—carrying water and hauling firewood.
Shitou said this, and later went to attend Mazu, asking: "Who is it that does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas? Mazu replied: "Wait until you..."
"To drink up the waters of the West River in a single gulp"—this is what I tell you. Under these words, the Layman suddenly grasped the profound essence (*xuanzhi*).
He remained to attend upon him for two years; from then on, his wit and eloquence became swift and sharp, and he was sought after by practitioners throughout all quarters.
Later, when he took his leave of Yaoshan, Yaoshan ordered ten Zen guests to escort him to the gate. Upon reaching the entrance, the Layman pointed to the snow in the air.
[Zhaozhou] said, "Fine snow, flake by flake, does not fall anywhere else. A Chan guest named Quan said, "Where does it fall?
The Layman [Zhaozhou] then gave him a slap. Quan said, "You must not be so hasty. The Layman said, "To call yourself a 'Chan guest' like this—you haven't escaped Yama, the King of Hell, yet!
Quan asked, "What about you, Layman? The Layman slapped him again and said, "Your eyes!"
Seeing [others] like the blind, speaking like the mute. (Xuedou Xian’s alternative to the first question says: "Just grasp the snowball and strike! ○ There was a daughter named Lingzhao.
He constantly sold bamboo water-strainers and fences to provide for his morning and evening needs. A lay practitioner composed a verse for him which said:

"The mind is as it is, and the environment is likewise. There is neither reality nor unreality; there is no concern for existence, nor any restriction regarding non-existence. He is neither a sage nor a holy one, but an ordinary person who has understood the matter."
Easy, how easy! Within these very five aggregates lies true wisdom. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the One Vehicle is the same.
How could there be two in the formless Dharmakāya? If one abandons afflictions to enter Bodhi, one does not know where the Buddha-ground might be found.
Furthermore, a verse says: To protect life, one must kill; Only when killing is exhausted does one dwell in peace. If you can grasp the meaning within this, An iron boat will float upon the water.

Shangfu (Zhaojue Qin said: "Tell me, what is it that you kill? Killing the lives of sentient beings is the view of ordinary people. Killing the six thieves and afflictions is the view of the masters of the seats. Killing Buddhas and Patriarchs is the view of the great icchantikas.

As for the portion belonging to the patch-robed monks, after all, what is it that you kill? Try to settle this and judge for yourself. Zhongfeng Ben said: "Is it not the equality of a single thought between killing living beings and protecting them?

To deliberate in such a manner is to blind the eyes of men. While sitting, a layman asked Lingzhao: "The ancients said, 'Clearly bright at the head of the hundred grasses; clearly bright is the Patriarch.'"
The Master asked, "How do you understand this? Lingzhao said, "Old and decrepit as you are, why do you speak such words?
The Layman asked, "What about you? Lingzhao said, "Clearly at the tips of the hundred grasses; clearly is the meaning of the Patriarchs. The Layman then smiled.
As the Layman was about to pass away, he said to Lingzhao, "Observe the sun for its timing; report to me when it reaches noon. Lingzhao...
Lingzhao suddenly announced, "The sun has already reached its zenith, yet there is an eclipse.

As the Layman went out the door to observe, Lingzhao immediately ascended her father’s seat, joined her palms, and passed away while sitting. The Layman smiled and said, "My daughter is sharp and quick-witted. Thereupon, they extended the period of mourning for another seven days.
When the Prefect, Lord Yu Gudi, came to inquire after his illness, the Layman said to him, "I only wish to empty all that is within."
"There is. Be careful not to take as real that which does not exist. Dwell well in the world; all things are like shadows and echoes.
Having spoken these words, he rested his head upon Master Gao’s knee and passed away. *Jiaowai biezhuan*, Volume Five.
*Chiao wai pieh chuan*, Scroll Six:
The Third Generation under Nanyue;
Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun (Dharma Heir of Baizhang Hai).
Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou was a native of Min. While traveling to Tiantai, he encountered a monk with whom he conversed and laughed as if they were old acquaintances.
Upon looking closely at him, he found the man’s gaze piercing others; thus, they traveled together. They happened upon a mountain stream whose waters had suddenly surged.
He cast aside his hat, leaned on his staff, and stopped. The monk led the Master across together. The Master said, "If you wish to cross, brother, cross by yourself.

The monk immediately lifted his robes and stepped upon the waves as if walking on level ground. Looking back, he called out, "Come across! Come across! The Master said, "Tsk! You self-satisfied fellow!
Had I known earlier, I would have cut off your shins. The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I—"
[He was] beyond reach. Having finished speaking, [the figure] vanished. Later, while traveling to the capital, the Master was inspired by another person and went to visit Baizhang.
Baizhang asked, "Majestic and imposing, from what direction have you come? The Master replied, "Majestic and imposing, I have come from Lingnan.
Baizhang said, "Being so majestic and imposing, for what purpose do you come? The Master replied, "Majestic and imposing, there is no [purpose]."
For another matter, he prostrated himself and asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the school, how do you instruct us? Baizhang remained silent for a long time.
The Master said, "I must not allow future generations to let this lineage be cut off. Baizhang said, "I thought you were a man of substance."
He then rose and entered the abbot’s quarters. The Master followed him in and said, "I have come specifically for this purpose.
Baizhang said, "If that is so, you must not fail me hereafter. One day, Baizhang asked the Master, "Where have you been?
The Master replied, "I went to Mount Daxiong to gather mushrooms. Baizhang asked, "Did you see a tiger? The Master then acted [as if he were crouching].
The sound of a tiger. Baizhang took up an axe and made a gesture as if to strike. The Master (Yunmen) immediately struck Baizhang with a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned.
He then ascended the hall and said, "At the foot of Mount Daxiong there is a great beast;

all of you must look out for it! Today, that old fellow Baizhang has been personally bitten by its fangs. (Later, Guishan Lingyou raised this question to Yangshan, to which Yangshan replied, "How would you handle it, Master?")

Tianping Shanzhao said, "At that time, Baizhang should have struck him down with a single blow of his axe. Why did it come to this? Yangshan said, "Not so. Tianping asked, "And what about you, my son? Yangshan said, "Baizhang only knew how to ride the head of the tiger."

Chan Master Changqing Da’an of Fuzhou (styled Lãn’ān) was the son of the Chen family of that commandery.

Carrying his solitary staff, he traveled to various regions and encountered an old man who said to him, “Master, if you go to Nanchang, you shall surely attain something. Thereupon, the Master proceeded to Baizhang and paid his respects.

The student asked, "A practitioner wishes to seek out the Buddha; what is it that is the Buddha? Baizhang said, "It is very much like riding a cow while searching for the cow. The Master asked, "What is it like after one has recognized him? Baizhang said, "It is like a person riding a cow until they arrive home. The Master asked, "And after arriving home? Baizhang said, "One dismounts from the cow and forgets both the cow and the rider. The Master said, "Afterward, how does one enter the house? Baizhang said, "One sits on the seat and eats the meal. The Master said, "After eating the meal, how does one rest? Baizhang said, "The body is at ease and the mind is at peace. The Master said, "How does one avoid falling into the ordinary? Baizhang said, "One must not despise the ordinary. The Master said, "How does one avoid falling into the holy? Baizhang said, "One must not cling to the holy. The Master said, "How does one avoid being stained by the holy and the ordinary? Baizhang said, "One must not have any thought of the holy or the ordinary. The Master said, "How does one avoid being stained by non-thought? Baizhang said, "One must not have any thought of non-thought. The Master said, "If there is no thought of non-thought, then what? Baizhang said, "At this point, even the Buddhas of the three times do not know. The Master said, "Excellent! Excellent! He then composed a verse for him: "Riding a cow, seeking the cow; Having found the cow, one returns home. Having arrived home, one dismounts the cow; Then one forgets both cow and rider. Once the cow and rider are forgotten, One enters the house and sits upon the seat. Sitting upon the seat, one eats the meal; Eating the meal, one rests in peace. Body and mind are both at ease; Yet one must not despise the ordinary. Not despising the ordinary, Nor clinging to the holy— Thus one is unstained by the holy or the ordinary. Without the thought of the holy or the ordinary, Even the Buddhas of the three times do not know. The Master said, "This is truly the Dharma of the Buddhas. He further instructed him: "You must maintain this state day and night, whether walking or sitting, without interruption. Do not let it be lost for even a single moment. If you can do this, you will surely attain liberation. The Master said, "I am now old and feeble; I shall transmit this Dharma to you. You must propagate it widely throughout the world so that it may benefit all sentient beings. Having spoken thus, he passed away. Zen Master Hōtan Fukan of Hōtai was a native of Hongzhou. Having attained the essential meaning under the guidance of Baizhang, he went to visit Master Mōgen.
As soon as Mōgen rose to greet him, the Master stepped forward, seized him, and said: "To open your mouth is to lose it; to close it..."

Chan Master Shenzan of Guling (Dharma Heir of Baizhang Hai).

Chan Master Shenzan of Guling in Fuzhou originally received his monastic training at Dazhong Temple in that same prefecture. Later, while traveling on pilgrimage, he encountered Baizhang and attained enlightenment.
Upon returning to his place of training, his original teacher asked him, "While you were away from me, what work or realization have you gained?"
He replied, "I have no business at all. He was then sent to perform manual labor. One day, while the Master was bathing, he ordered the attendant to remove the dirt from his back.
The attendant then patted his back and said, "A fine Buddha hall, yet the Buddha is not holy. The Master turned his head to look at him;
the attendant said, "Though the Buddha is not holy, he is at least able to emit light. On another day, while the Master was reading a sutra by the window, a bee flew in.
The master saw him trying to get out through the window paper and said, "The world is this vast and wide, yet you refuse to come out; instead, you bore into old paper.
When will that ever end? He then spoke a verse: Refusing to leave the Gate of Emptiness, You throw yourself at the window—how very foolish!
Boring into old paper for a hundred years, On what day will you finally emerge? His master set aside the sutra and asked, "Whom did you encounter while traveling on foot?"
"I have observed that your speech has been extraordinary from beginning to end. The Master said, "I, this humble one, received from Venerable Baizhang the pointing out of a place of rest;
I now wish to repay his compassionate virtue. Thereupon, the Abbot informed the assembly and prepared a vegetarian feast, requesting the Master to preach the Dharma.
The Master then ascended the seat and proclaimed the tradition of Baizhang, saying: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.

Its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters. The nature of mind is unstained and is fundamentally perfected; simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
At these words, the Founder attained realization, exclaiming: "I never expected that in my old age I would hear such ultimate matters!"

Chan Master Tong of He’an Temple in Guangzhou was ordained at Shuanglin Temple in Wuzhou. From his youth, he spoke little;
people of the time called him "Tong Who Does Not Speak. He went to visit Mazu, but by the time he reached Jiangxi, Mazu had already passed away. He then went to call upon Baizhang.
Sudden Dispelling of Doubts. One day, the Master summoned Yangshan and said, "Bring me a small bed.

"What is that object over there by the bed? Yangshan replied, "A pillow. The Master said, "What is this object here by the pillow?
Yangshan replied, "Nothing. The Master called out, "Huiji! Yangshan responded, "Yes? The Master asked, "What is it?
Yangshan had no reply. The Master said, "Go."

Chan Master Dao of Weiguo Monastery in Jingzhao received a newly arrived monk for an audience. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Henan."
The Master said, "Is the Yellow River clear yet? The monk had no reply. (Wuwei Shan You spoke on his behalf: "A little fox cub wants to cross; just cross. Why harbor doubts?")

Chan Master Hui of Dongshan in Hongzhou was once with Nan-yung in the tea hall. A monk approached and said, "I do not know you.
Nan-yung said, "Since I do not accept you, and you do not see me, whom do you not know? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "You must not ask him such a question so abruptly. Nan-yung said, "What about Da-yü himself?
Da-yü seized the monk and said, "It is you who act this way; it brings trouble upon me as well," and he gave him a slap.
Nan-yung laughed loudly and said, "The bright moon and the blue sky. Da-yü’s attendant arrived, and the Master asked, "The Vajra..."

The attendant said, "Who would dare to question me? The Master said, "Is that sufficient? The attendant said, "One still requires another to inspect it."

Regarding the name Chuo (Hong Juefan’s *Linjian Lu* states: "The second-generation Dharma-heir of Baizhang was Chan Master Fǎzhèng, a preeminent disciple of Dàzhì. His ancestors once recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* without disclosing their names; thus, he was commonly called 'Nirvāṇa Heshang. He presided over the Chengfa seat and performed the greatest service among the masters.

It was he who led the assembly in clearing the fields while others expounded the Great Meaning. Great adepts such as Huangbo and Guling all held him in the highest esteem. The Tang literatus Huang Wuyi composed a detailed stele inscription for him, calligraphed by Liu Gongquan, which remains unsurpassed in antiquity and modernity. However, the entry for Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*—placing him among the dharma heirs of Mazu—is an error. Upon examining the *Zengsheng Zhengzong Ji*, one finds both Weizheng and Fǎzhèng listed separately)."* **Note:** The term "Heshang" (和尙) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit *upādhyāya*, meaning "preceptor" or "teacher.

The text identifies two distinct figures: Fǎzhèng (法正), the second-generation heir of Baizhang, and Weizheng (惟政), who is erroneously conflated with him in the *Chuan Deng Lu*. The passage clarifies that Fǎzhèng was the true successor to Baizhang Huaihai and a highly revered figure in his own right. The mention of the *Zengsheng Zhengzong Ji* serves as a corrective to the earlier records. The final sentence indicates that the source text contains both names, Weizheng and Fǎzhèng, thereby resolving the confusion.

However, while the successive generations of Baizhang can be counted, Mingjiao has merely seen their names; he was unable to distinguish them and thus preserved them all together. Now, one should take the Liu stele as authoritative.

Zhaozhou Guanyin Monastery (also known as Dongyuan). Chan Master Congshen was a native of Haoxiang in Caozhou; his surname was Hao.

Nanquan then sat up and asked, "Are you a novice with a master, or a novice without a master?
The Master said, "A novice with a master. Nanquan asked, "Who is your master? The Master stepped forward, bowed, and said, "It is bitterly cold in the middle of winter."
I humbly wish that the Venerable Master enjoys ten thousand blessings. Nanquan held him in high regard and permitted him to enter his room.

Nanquan said, "To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate from it. The Master said, "If one does not intend to direct oneself toward it, how can one know it is the Way? Nanquan said:

Zhaojue Qin said: "Nanquan’s single instance of extending his hand was certainly characterized by gathering and releasing, seizing and letting go.

However, it has not yet revealed the matter that transcends [the ordinary]. For instance, if the entire earth is the Tathāgata-garbha, where would you place the jewel? If the entire earth is the *maṇi* jewel, where would you place the garbha? If you can clearly understand the point of turning the body, [you will see]."

"Allowing you to possess one eye," Jingyin Chengyun said. Nanquan’s responsive engagement and his methods of granting or revoking are indeed worth observing; yet, when scrutinized, he ultimately could not point out where the pearl was. [The Master] said: "You do not understand my words. This is precisely the treasury; where, after all, is the pearl? Is it that the sea god knows its worth but does not know its price? The monk bowed again, and the Master struck him once more and drove him away. Upon returning, the monk related this incident to others.
Jiashan said, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. Jiashan said, "It is fortunate that you do not understand;

The assembly was startled by this. The next day, when the assembly had gathered for the morning discourse, Guīzōng said: "Last night..."
"Let a monk who has attained great enlightenment come forward. Master [Zhaozhou] stepped out and said, "I, this humble one.
Guizong said, "What principle have you seen that you speak of 'great enlightenment'? Try to explain it to me. Master Zhaozhou said, "A nun was originally made by a woman. Guizong marveled at this.
The Master then took his leave and departed. Guizong followed him out to see him off and presented him with a bamboo hat.
The Master received the hat, placed it on his head, and walked away without looking back even once.
Master Puhua (Dharma Heir of Panshan Ji):
The Master Puhua of Zhenzhou was a man of unknown origins. He served as a disciple of Panshan, secretly receiving his true instructions, yet he feigned madness and spoke without restraint.
Following the passing of Panshan, he went to the northern regions to propagate the Dharma; at times...
In a city, or amidst burial mounds, he shook a single bell and said: "If it comes from the bright side, strike it on the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, strike it on the dark side;
if it comes from the four directions and eight quarters, strike it with a whirlwind; if it comes from empty space, strike it with a continuous barrage.
One day, Linji ordered a monk to seize him and asked, "What if it does not come in any of these ways? The Master pushed him away and said, "Come tomorrow, Great Compassionate One."
There was a meal in the monastery. When the monk returned, he reported this to Linji. Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow. (Wuzu Yan said: "If it were Wuzu, it would not be so.
If someone asked, 'What if they do not come in this way at all? I would strike him with a shout. He would surely say, 'Wuzu uses blind shackles and blind blows.

I want you to speak exactly like that. Why? You may report it to the various quarters as you please. Whenever he saw anyone, regardless of their status, he would ring his staff once. At that time, he was called "Puhua" (Universal Flower).

Once, when Master [Huai]tang entered the Linji Monastery at night to eat raw vegetables, Linji said, "This fellow looks exactly like a donkey.

and made a gesture of being struck. The Commander of Cavalry and Infantry ordered his men to strike the Master with five blows of the staff. The Master [received them].
He said, "It seems so, yet it is not. Once, while the Master was walking through the marketplace shaking a bell, he sang out:
"I seek a place to go, but it cannot be found. At that time, Daowu encountered him, seized him by the collar, and asked, "Where do you intend to go?

Suddenly, Linji entered and asked, "Are you an ordinary man or a sage? The Elder replied, "Now tell me, are you an ordinary man or a sage? Linji then—
"Ho! The Master pointed with his finger and said, "The bridegroom’s son from He-yang; the old woman’s Zen of the wooden pagoda;
Linji, that little fellow—he alone possesses a single eye. Linji said, "This thief! The Master said, "Thief! Thief! and then went out.
At the beginning of the Xian-tong era of the Tang dynasty, as he was about to pass away, he entered the marketplace and said to the people, "I beg of you for a *zhidu* (monk’s robe). Some people...
He was offered a padded jacket, and then a cloth robe, but he accepted neither; shaking his bell, he departed.

Linji had a coffin sent to him, and the Master laughed, saying, "That fellow Linji is too talkative," and then accepted it. He then took leave of the assembly, saying, "Puhua will die at the East Gate tomorrow.
The people of the district followed one another to escort him out of the city. The Master called out in a stern voice, "Today..."
The burial did not accord with the principles of the "Green Bird" (Qingwu) divination. He then said, "Tomorrow, the transformation [of death] shall take place at the South Gate;

people will follow after me. Again he said, "Tomorrow, departing through the West Gate would be auspicious. People began to depart more rarely, and once they had left, they returned. The people's resolve gradually slackened.
On the fourth day, he personally carried his coffin out through the North Gate; shaking a bell, he entered the coffin and passed away. The people of the commandery rushed out of the city.
They lifted the coffin to look inside, but he was already gone; they heard only the sound of a bell in the air gradually fading away, its origin unfathomable.
Chan Master Liangsui of Shouzhou (a successor of Magu Cheshan).
Chan Master Liangsui of Shouzhou went to visit Magu. When Magu saw him approaching, he took up a hoe and went to weed the grass.
The Master went to where Mazu was weeding, but Mazu paid him no heed and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters, closing the door behind him.
The next day the Master went again; Mazu closed the door once more. The Master then knocked on the door. Mazu asked, “Who is it? The Master replied, “Liangsui.”
As soon as his name was uttered, he suddenly attained realization and said, "Master, do not deceive Liangsui.
Had I not come to pay my respects to you, Master, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for the rest of my life. Magu then opened the door to meet him.
Upon returning to his lecture hall, he said to the assembly, "What all of you know, Liangsui knows entirely; what Liangsui knows, you do not."

Had he not prostrated to the Master, he would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for a lifetime. Thus, one also knows there are places where people are deceived. He also asked: "What is the place where Liangsu knows?

Donglin Yan said: "What all people know, Liangsu knows entirely; what Liangsu knows, all people do not know. What is the place where Liangsu knows? The Monk Zhilin of Hunan would frequently revile Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, calling them both malevolent spirits; he held a wooden sword in his hand.

Claiming for himself that he had subdued Māra, as soon as he saw a monk approach to visit him, he would say, "Māra has come! Māra has come! and brandish his sword wildly before returning to his quarters.
He continued in this manner for twelve years. Later, he set aside his sword and remained silent. A monk asked, "Regarding those twelve years ago..."

Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou (Dharma Heir of Huangbo Xiyun).
Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou, whose name was Daoming, was a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan. His eyes possessed the rare quality of double pupils (*chongtong*).
He aligned himself with the Seven Stars and reached the ultimate meaning of the Way under Huangbo.

Later, at the request of the fourfold assembly, he resided at Guanyin Monastery, where his community regularly numbered over a hundred. For several decades, students would challenge him with probing questions, to which he would respond immediately;

his words were steep and perilous, never following conventional paths. Consequently, those of shallow capacity often ridiculed him, while only those of profound learning and keen intellect marveled at and submitted to him.

Consequently, people from all directions looked toward him with devotion and all addressed him as "Venerable Elder. Later, he returned to Kaiyuan (now renamed Doushuai), where he lived in a room weaving *púxié* (rush shoes) to support his mother;

The rebels wished to discard it, yet they could not lift it despite exerting all their strength. They sighed and said, "Muzhou has a great sage."

"If you wish to support the Great Dharma and proclaim the School of the Patriarchs, this old fellow is quite capable of it. Do you all wish to see Muzhou? using a wedge to extract a wedge—it is only by returning to this old man Muzhou that one succeeds. If someone were to ask me such a question today, I too would answer in this way. Why? Because 'when the law is fully applied, there are no subjects. Ascending the hall, he said:
I once saw Baizhang; he did not distinguish between good and evil. As soon as the assembly had gathered, he struck them all at once with his staff.
He then called out to the assembly, and when they turned their heads, he said, "What is this? There is no place for conversation here. Master Huangbo was also like this;
he called to the assembly, and when they turned their heads, he said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind."

"Still there is a slight gap. (Xuedou Xian said: "What need is there to say 'still there is a slight gap'? It is simply not yet so. According to Xuedou, he would have struck everyone down at once as they assembled and let it rest. Or perhaps there is someone with an unperforated iron hammer.)

"The bandits have passed over the ladder. Xuedou wanted people to take this up and carry it; he was raising waves where there was no wind. Today, I will not do so at all.
