Chan Master Nengren Kumu Zuoyuan of Yanshan in Wenzhou was a native of the Lin clan of the Seven Fujians. Initially, he visited Xuefeng Yu;
subsequently, he relied upon Foxin Cai. With both, his spiritual faculties were in accord. Later, while relying on Dahui at Yunmen Hermitage, one night...
While sitting in the assembly hall, he saw a monk trim a lamp and attained sudden realization. He composed a verse, saying: "Trimming up the lamp is fire;
It shatters the ignorance of kalpas. Returning to the hall, I bump into the Holy Monk; I nearly let him slip past me face-to-face. What is it that does not slip away?
Fifteen years ago it was extraordinary; Now, as before, it is simply this. Dahui presented him with a verse in response.

It is said: At the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one releases the body; rising up, one remains as ever alert and clear. Eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty, there is nothing at all to do;
what need is there to discuss whether one is the person of old or not?
Chan Master Yian Shan-zhi of Jiangshan (Dharma heir of Jingshan Daokai).
Chan Master Yian Shan-zhi of Jiangshan in Jiankang Prefecture was a native of Yunmeng in De’an.
Initially, he studied under Miaoxi at Huiguan Peak. One day, Miaoxi asked him, “Where are you from, Upādhyāya? The Master replied, “De’an.”
A man from the province [of Anzhou] was present. Miaoxi said, "I have heard that you, a man from Anzhou, are skilled at wrestling. Is this true? The Master then assumed a wrestling stance.
Miaoxi said, "When people from Hunan eat fish, why do those from Hubei get a bone stuck in their throat? The Master performed a somersault and departed.
Miaoxi said, "Who would have known that within cold ashes, there is a single bean ready to burst? One day, while serving as the Palace Guard Commander...

When Minister Chen Shunjing was conversing on the meaning of tea with various mountain masters, he raised the kōan regarding "the phrase that has no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree" and asked the assembly to offer their critical evaluations.
All of them sought to please him with clever and ornate words. The Master was the last to speak, saying:
"Zhang beats oil, Li beats oil; they do not beat his whole body, but only his head. Minister Chen was greatly delighted.
Attendant Jinli (a successor of Dajian Huigao of Mount Jing).
A native of San Mountain, he had long served Dahui and once silently investigated the "Bamboo Stick" koan, yet found no entry point.
One day, having finished his period of seclusion, he requested instruction. Dahuì said, "You are a man from Fuzhou. Let me give you a metaphor:
it is like taking a fine grade of lychee and peeling away the skin and shell all at once, placing it in your mouth with your hand;
it is simply that you do not know how to swallow it. The Master could not help but laugh and said, "If the Monk swallows it, that will be trouble!"
Later, Dàhuì asked the Master, "Regarding the lychee you swallowed the other day, it was simply that you did not know its flavor.
The Master replied, "If one were to know its flavor, it would lead to even greater calamity."
Chan Master Miaozong of Zishou Nunnery (Dharma Heir of Jingshan Gaofeng).
Chan Master Miaozong Wuzhuo of Zishou Nunnery in Pingjiang Prefecture was the granddaughter of Chancellor Su Song.
At about thirty years of age, she grew weary of the world’s fleeting nature, cast off her worldly finery, and sought instruction from various veteran masters, having already entered the correct path.
Xin served as summer retreat head at Mount Jing. When Dahui ascended the hall, he cited the kōan concerning Yushan’s initial meeting with Shitou and his subsequent encounter with Mazu.

Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. After Dahui descended from the seat, the Layman Feng Jie, known as Budong, followed him to the abbot’s quarters and said, “I have understood the kōan the Master just cited. Dahui replied, “Reside...”
"What do you say, O Master? He replied: "To say 'it is so' is not permitted. *Suru svāhā*.
To say 'it is not so' is also not permitted. *Śiri svāhā*. To say both 'it is so' and 'it is not so' is altogether not permitted. *Suru-śiri svāhā*."

Dahui brought this up as an analogy for his teacher. The teacher said, "I once saw Guo Xiang’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi*. Those who understand it say, 'It is actually the *Zhuangzi* that is commenting on Guo Xiang.
Dahui, finding these words extraordinary, again raised the "Rockhead and the Old Woman" dialogue to question him.

The teacher replied with a verse: "A single-leaf skiff glides upon the vast and boundless; Oars displayed and paddles danced, departing from the notes of Gong and Shang. Clouds, mountains, and the sea..."

The moon has been cast away; he has won only the long dream of Zhuang Zhou’s butterfly. Daohui should stop. Feng Gong suspected that his realization was not rooted in truth. Later, when they passed through Wuxi, Feng invited Daohui onto his boat and asked: "A woman gave birth to seven sons; six did not meet with a true知音 (zhīyīn—'one who knows the sound'). This one alone was not even worth keeping, so she threw him into the water. Daohui, the Master, said: *The seven children are the seven consciousnesses;* *Six do not encounter the True Mind;* *This one alone is also not worth keeping;* *He too is cast into the great ocean.* Feng Gong was greatly moved and attained awakening. He then composed a verse: *The Great Matter is originally not difficult;* *Only because of deluded thoughts it becomes hard to see.* *If you can put down the mind that seeks the Way,* *Then the Way will naturally appear before you.* Feng Gong then took leave of Daohui and returned to his home village. Daohui later went to visit him there, where Feng Gong said: "I have already attained the Way. Daohui asked: "What is the meaning of 'The Great Matter is originally not difficult'? Feng Gong replied: "It is like a person who has lost their way and, upon finding it, says, 'How could this be difficult? Daohui said: "You have indeed attained the Way. Feng Gong then bowed. Daohui said: "Do not say that you have attained the Way. You have merely attained a state of non-attainment. Feng Gong then composed another verse: *The Great Matter is originally not difficult;* *Only because of deluded thoughts it becomes hard to see.* *If you can put down the mind that seeks the Way,* *Then the Way will naturally appear before you.* Daohui said: "You have attained the Way, but you have not yet attained the Way. "The man of the Way understands this principle. But how do you understand it? The Master replied, "All that has been submitted above is entirely the truth.
Mr. Feng was greatly astonished. Later, when Dahui hung up his plaque for the evening session, the Master entered the room. Dahui asked, "The ancients did not leave their quarters."
"Why did you go to the manor house to eat oil-cakes?
The Master said, "If the Abbot pardons Miaozong, then Miaozong will dare to deliver a message. Dahui said, "I pardon you; try to say something.
The Master said, "Miaozong also pardons the Abbot. Dahui said, "What about the oil-cakes? The Master gave a shout and departed.
The fame of this [monk] spread in all directions.
Layman Zhang Jiucheng (the Junior Grand Secretary), a successor of Master Dahui Zonggao of Mount Jing, was known as the "Immaculate Layman" (Wugou Jushi).
Before he had passed the imperial examinations, while conversing with a guest about Yang Yi, the Duke Wen, and Lü Gong, the Weiming...
Among the eminent scholars of his time, those who achieved such refined and subtle mastery all attained it through the study of Chan. He then felt a deep admiration for this path.

Having heard that Master Chan-shi Baoyin Chuming’s lineage of the Way descended from Daotong and resided at Jingci Monastery, he went there immediately to inquire about the essentials of entering the Way.
Chuming said: "This matter requires nothing more than not abandoning it from moment to moment; after a long period of pure cultivation, when the time comes, [enlightenment] will manifest of itself."

Nevertheless, he entered into realization. Furthermore, [the Master] brought up the story of Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree” to have him reflect upon it from time to time. After a long while, the official had no realization;
he took his leave and went to visit Chan Master Qing of Shanquan. The official asked, "This matter is within the lot of every person; each and every one is perfectly accomplished."
"Is it so? Qing replied, "Yes. The official asked, "Why is it that I have no point of entry? Qing took a string of prayer beads from his sleeve and showed them to him, saying, "Whose are these?
The official looked up and down, unable to respond. Qing then put the beads back into his sleeve and said, "If they were yours, you would have taken them;
as soon as you engage in discursive thought, they are no longer yours. The official was struck with awe. Not long after, he passed away.

While staying at the Su family residence, one night while using the toilet, he investigated the "Pine Tree" koan. Upon hearing the croaking of frogs, he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse:
"A single frog’s croak on a moonlit spring night, Shatters heaven and earth; all share one family. At such a moment as this, who can understand?
Xuan Sha suffered aching feet atop the ridge. The following morning, he went to visit Chan Master Fayin Yi.

The Master’s words were quite in accord with his capacity. It happened to be the anniversary of his private memorial service, so he went to the Mingjing Hermitage to make offerings to the assembly of monks.
When the presiding monk, Chan Master Weishang, saw him, he extended his hand. The Master gave a shout. Weishang struck the Master on the cheek.

The Master stepped forward, and Weishang said, "How can you, Mr. Zhang, the School Registrar, slander the Great Prajñāpāramitā? The Master replied, "This is all my understanding reaches; what else would you have me do, Master?"
When Master Shang was about to cite the story of Mazu ascending the hall and Baizhang rolling up his mat to interrogate him, before he had even finished speaking, the Master pushed over the lectern.
Shang cried out, "Registrar Zhang has committed murder! The Master sprang up and asked a monk standing nearby, "What would you do?
The monk was at a loss. The Master struck him and turned to Shang, saying, "If the ancestors do not settle their own affairs, the calamity will fall upon their descendants."
Yunshang laughed heartily. The Master (Xuedou) offered this verse: "The circumstances of rolling up the mat are truly marvelous; When heard by those in all quarters, they all knit their brows.
The stand and tray were kicked over and people scattered like stars; A straightforward man has never been deceived. Yunshang replied: "From the start, his high price did not spare him;
In the midst of the hundred-battlefield, he brandishes his two brows. To seize the horns and break through the pass—do you understand? [He continued: "The dense thicket..."
In the forest, who would dare to deceive one another? In the *Guichu* year of the Xiangsheng era, [Wumen] was the preeminent among the scholars.
He again visited Chang at Dong’an. Chang said, "Fushan Yuanjian said: 'Even if you were able to enter the chamber of Fenyang, you have only reached the gate of Fushan;
you have still not seen the old monk. What do you say to this? Wumen shouted at his attendant monk, saying, "Why did you not answer him? The monk was at a loss for words.
The Duke struck a monk with his palm and said, "In a den of frogs, there truly is no dragon. In the autumn of the Ding-si year, Chan Master Dahui presided over Mount Jing;

scholars looked up to him as they do at the stars. When the Duke read his *Essentials of Speech*, he sighed, saying, "Now I know there are people in the School of the Patriarchs," and he held these words in high esteem, regretting that he had not yet met him in person.
Later, when the Duke served as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, he happened to meet the State Councilor.
Lord Liu invited Dahui to preach the Dharma at Tianzhu. Lord Liu went three times but did not meet him.

When Dahui finally returned the visit, Lord Liu received him with nothing more than formal greetings. Dahui, however, silently took note of this. Soon after, Dahui was granted a temple stipend and returned to his hometown.
Upon arriving at Jingshan, he discussed the principle of "investigating things" (*gewu*) with Official Feng and other gentlemen. Dahui said, "You only know of 'investigating things,' but..."
He did not know that there was an object to be investigated. The Duke was bewildered. Dahui laughed heartily. The Duke said, "Can you explain this to me?
Dahui replied, "Have you not seen it recorded in a minor collection of stories? There was a man of the Tang who plotted rebellion with An Lushan.

This man had previously served as the Governor of Langzhou, and a portrait of him was there. When the Emperor Minghuang visited Shu and saw it, he became enraged and ordered his attendants to draw their swords."

He struck the head of the statue. At that time, the Governor of Lang was residing in Shaanxi; suddenly, the head fell to the ground. Upon hearing this, the Master (Li Gong) immediately grasped the profound meaning.

He inscribed on the wall of the Abhedyaprāsāda Hall: "Zishao [Zhao Mengfu] held that the principle is in the object; Miaoxi [Dahui Zonggao] held that the object is governed by the principle. If you wish to know the 'One Thread,' it is simply two five-hundreds. Dahui then granted him his approval.
Later, while serving as Governor of Shaoyang, he encountered the calamity of his father’s death. Passing through Mount Jing, he provided a meal for the monks. Holding...

Jūn (Zhaozhou) was displeased; Dàhuì (Linji) discussed matters of state administration with him, whereupon Jūn exiled Dàhuì to Hénghuáng and ordered the Duke (Zhaozhou) to remain at home observing the mourning period.

When the mourning period ended, he was settled in Nán’ān. In the spring of the Bingzi year, he received imperial grace and returned north. While passing through Xīnggàn, Dàhuì happened to arrive there as well.
They traveled together by boat and engaged in intense discussions on the essentials of the School, never once mentioning past events. This is the oral transmission of the Yú family.
The record states: When Xian was descending from the Ling region, he accompanied his maternal uncle back to Xingan. Thereupon, they met Dahui; the uncle ordered him to pay his respects.
Xian said, "I have never bowed to monks. The uncle said, "You should simply question him. Xian knew that [Dahui] had once held a scroll [of scripture].
He then cited three sentences from Zisi’s *Zhongyong*: "What Heaven mandates is called nature; following nature is called the Way; cultivating the Way is called instruction.
He asked about these three phrases. Dahui replied, "Ordinary people do not know where their own original life-spirit (benming yuanchen) has descended."
Furthermore, how could one possibly drag good people into a fiery pit? The sages and worthies did not break through at the very first step.
Xian said, "Can you, Master, act as a sage or a worthy to break through for us? Dahui replied, "'The mandate of Heaven is called nature'—this is the Pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
'Following nature is called the Way'—this is the Perfectly Full Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). 'Cultivating the Way is called...'"

The Teaching is precisely the manifestation of a thousand, ten-thousand, or hundred-million transformation bodies. Xian was thus able to inform his maternal uncle, saying: "What words can you use when bowing?
Later, while stationed in Yongjia, in the autumn of the *dingchou* year, he requested leave from his post and took a detour to visit Dahui at Yuwang Monastery.
The following year, Dahui received imperial authorization to resume his leadership of Mount Jing; he went to visit the Master at Qingshan Monastery and said: "In my dreams, I always..."

[The Master] asked, "How is it with your recitation of the *Analects* and *Mencius*? Da-hui cited the *Awakening of Faith*: "Because of quiescence, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear therein, like images in a mirror.
The Master said, "Were it not for you, Senior Teacher, one would never hear such a discourse. He then composed a verse on Huanglong’s Three Barriers:

"My hand—how does it resemble the Buddha’s hand? All the patch-robed monks under heaven have no mouths. My feet—how do they resemble the ox’s feet? The whole world is covered in grass. The Buddha’s mouth—how does it resemble my mouth? I preach the Dharma for the sake of the great assembly."
Even if you were to suddenly lift up and walk away, you would still be running inside a ghost cave (you cannot hide it).
"How can my feet be like a donkey's?"—and yet you are stuck again by sticky glue. To turn over and head straight for Tuṣita Heaven is already to have been caught by that rat poison.
(Unable to spit it out: Every person has their own place of affinity for birth. Beneath the Iron Ring Mountains for several thousand years;
the three calamities reach as far as the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven. This donkey still remains right by the side (having mastered its efforts).
The Layman Wu Weiming, Censor-in-Chief (Dharma heir of Jingshan Gaofeng).
The layman Wu Weiming, whose courtesy name was Yuanshao, had long studied under Chan Master Zhenxie Le.
He attained the samādhi of self-enjoyment as his ultimate realization. Later, he visited Dahui at the Yangyu Hermitage and entered the room with the assembly. Dahui...
He brought up the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan to question him. As the official was about to answer, Dahui struck him with his bamboo staff;
the official had no reply and subsequently remained to seek instruction. One day Dahui said to him, "There is no need to display your cleverness;
you must simply 'crack' and 'break through'—only then can you confront birth and death. If you merely display your cleverness, what end will there ever be?"

He took his leave. While traveling along the road at Yanping, he suddenly attained sudden enlightenment. He wrote several verses in succession and sent them to Dahui, all concerning matters previously discussed in the master’s quarters.
One verse said: "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing; The entire body is a set of golden chain-bones.
Zhaozhou personally saw Old Nanquan, Who could explain that Zhenzhou produces radishes. Dahui then spoke a verse in response.
The Commentary states: His entire body is a single set of golden chain-bones, fit to serve as a model for humans and devas.
If you wish to recognize this little fellow Linji, he is none other than the "white-handed thief" of those bygone days.
The Layman Huang Yanjie of Mensi (Dharma heir of Jingshan Daokao).
The layman Huang Yanjie of Mensi, whose courtesy name was Jiefu and pen-name Miaode, had his doubts suddenly severed beneath Dahui’s single shout.
Dahui bestowed his robe upon him. He once raised the story of Shoushan’s bamboo stick; when he reached the point where [Yexian] drew near...
[The Master] previously seized [the staff], broke it, and threw it down the steps, saying, "What is this? Shoushan said, "Blind.
The Official said, "When Miaode reaches this point, he is utterly incapable. However, I do remember a quatrain I once composed on wax plum blossoms, which says:
'If one intends to chew the wax at the branch tip, The startled fragrance resembles that of orchids. Deep within the heavy snow of the village ahead, Do not mistake them for mountain plums.'"
Chan Master Tanhua of Tiantong (Dharma Heir of Long of Huqiu):
Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua of Tiantong in Mingzhou was the son of the Jiang family of Qizhou. Initially, he relied upon Chan Master Sui of Shuinan, where he first tasted the flavor of the Dharma.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes, engaging in spirited debate with various elders; there were none with whom he did not reach accord.
He went to Yunju to pay his respects to Chan Master Yuanwu. Upon seeing him, Yuanwu gave him a forceful and penetrating exhortation. When [Yuanwu] entered Sichuan, he directed him to visit Zhangjiao.
When Zhangjiao moved to Huqiu, the Master attended him on his travels. Before half a year had passed, he suddenly realized the Great Matter. He then went to call upon Ciyun;

subsequently, he shared the teaching seat at Lianyun and opened the Dharma at Miaoyan. Later, he was transferred to various great monasteries. During the days he resided at Guizong, [he... the Great...
Dahui was at Mei Yang. There was a monk who transmitted a set of instructional sayings by the Master (Foyan).

When Dahui saw them, he praised them with great fervor. Later, he sent a verse to him, saying: "Severing all paths atop the First Peak of the Golden Wheel, A thousand demons and a hundred monsters have hidden their tracks.
In recent years, I have received a true report: It is said that the authentic lineage of Yangqi has been restored. Such was the depth of his esteem.
Chan Master Shi Yi of Jingci (Dharma heir of Yuyang Yu):
Chan Master Shi Yi of Shui'an at Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Ma family of Wuzhou. At the age of sixteen, he donned the monastic robes.
He first visited Chan Master Xuefeng Huizhao. Huizhao presented him with the koan of "Hiding the body leaves no trace" and questioned him about it.

After several days, the Master finally attained realization and offered this verse: "The body hidden leaves no trace, yet there is nothing further to hide; The whole person is without reliance, and thus they meet face-to-face."
The ancient mirror does not trouble itself to reflect; thin mist and fog moisten the autumn light.
Huizhao examined him, asking, "Ultimately, where is the place where one hides the body without leaving a trace? The Master said, "Aha.
Huizhao asked, "Since there are no tracks or traces, why should one not hide the body? The Master said, "The stone tiger swallows the wooden goat. Huizhao deeply approved of this.
Chan Master Wuan Faquan of Daochang Monastery in Anji Prefecture (Dharma heir of Yuyang Yu).
He was the son of the Chen family of Gusu. Having long relied upon Fozhi, he attained realization.
Every time he entered the room, Fozhi asked him about the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature. The Master was unable to respond.

One day, hearing a monk cite the verse of the Fifth Patriarch which says, "Zhaozhou’s drawn sword," he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "The drums and pipes resound as I bare one shoulder;
Incense mists from the imperial towers drift onto the boat from Yizhou. Sometimes I go barefoot, playing with the bright moon, Treading it through until it is shattered."
Tian of the Waves of the Five Lakes.
Chan Master Huitong Qingdan (Dharma heir of Daopei Tai).
Chan Master Huitong Qingdan of Tanzhou was a native of the Yan family of Pengzhou. Initially, he crossed the mountain passes and arrived at Deshan. There he encountered...
Taixu ascended the hall. He cited Zhaozhou, who said: "The old woman of Mount Tai has already been thoroughly exposed for you.
Tell me, where does the meaning lie? After a long silence, he said: "Gathering yellow leaves from the ground, one pushes white clouds out into the mountains.
Upon hearing this, the Master was suddenly enlightened. The following day, he entered the room. Deshan asked: "Previously, Baizhang said that not falling into cause and effect..."
For what reason did he fall into the wild fox body? Later, when Baizhang did not obscure cause and effect, for what reason was he released from the wild fox body?
The Master said: "It would be better to bury him alive in a pit."
Chan Master Zhong’an of Lingyan (Dharma Heir of Daopei Tai).
Chan Master Zhong’an of Lingyan in Lizhou was a bhikṣu from his youth. In his prime, he traveled among the lecture halls of various monasteries.

Later, he visited Yuanwu at Jiangshan, where Foxing served as the head of the assembly (zuoyuan). The Master questioned him and immediately grasped the essential meaning. When Foxing took up residence at De... [text continues]
Shan sent his teacher to Zhongfu to deliver a letter of succession. Yuanwu asked, "You have traveled a thousand li to come; you have not disgraced our ancestral tradition.
The public case is already established—how do you communicate it? The teacher replied, "Presented face-to-face, there is no evasion.
Yuanwu said, "This is Deshan’s. Which one is yours, Venerable Sir? The teacher replied, "How could there be a second person? Yuanwu said, "Back!"
"Later, what about this? The Master presented the letter. Yuanwu smiled and said, "A master Chan practitioner naturally has his place. The Master said, "I entrust it to Jiangshan.
Next, he went before the Sangha Hall and, holding the letter, paid his respects to the Head Seat (Shouzuo). The Head Seat asked, "Xuan Sha’s blank paper—where does this come from?
The Master replied, "For a long time I have kept this essential point hidden; I did not strive to speak of it hastily. Today I pay homage."
[The letter] is presented. I hope you will deign to take a look. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) then gave a shout. The Master said, "An adept Head Seat. The Head Seat shouted again.
The Master struck him with the letter. As the Head Seat hesitated, the Master said, "If one does not understand three, eight, and nine, one cannot help but brood in silence."
The Master struck him again with the staff and said, "Receive it! At that time, Yuanwu and Foyan were watching. Yuanwu said, "My Head Seat has been struck to death.
Foyan said, "It is like two official horses kicking each other; what evidence is there for that? The Master said, "What need is there to speak of 'official horses kicking each other'?
This is precisely the treading of dragons and elephants. Yuanwu called the Master over and said, "I have five hundred..."
The Head Seat said, "Venerable Sir, why did you strike him? Yuanwu replied, "The Master must also receive a beating.
Yuanwu looked at Foyan and stuck out his tongue. Foyan said, "Not yet. He then turned to the Master and asked, "Empty-handed, holding a hoe;
walking, riding a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. What is the meaning of this?"
The Master bowed deeply and said, "What I have offered is entirely the truth. Foyan smiled and said, "So, you are truly a person of this house.
Later, he went to see Master Wuzu Zizhou and presented a letter from his dharma-kinsman. Wuzu asked, "What does it say in the letter?
The Master replied, "Its patterns and colors are already manifest. Wuzu asked, "Ultimately, what does it say? The Master replied, "Brandishing it in the open sun."
Baofu said, "Come closer. [Baofu] added, "Do you not recognize a few characters here? The Master said, "Do not feign defeat.
Wuzu looked at his attendant and asked, "Where is this monk from? [The attendant] replied, "This senior monk has previously been in the Master’s assembly."
The Fifth Patriarch said, "I am surprised that you are so slippery-headed. The Master replied, "I have been treated with dullness by the Abbot.
Thereupon, the Fifth Patriarch placed the letter over an incense burner and fumigated it, saying, "Namo Samantabhadra. The Master stepped forward and merely snapped his fingers.
The Fifth Patriarch then opened the letter. When he returned to De Shan, both Foguo and Foyan each composed a verse to see him off.
Not long after this, the seat at Lingyan became vacant. Monks submitted petitions requesting that the Master take up residence as abbot, and he consequently accepted the Dharma-duty.
As for Chan Master Xingji of Guoqing (the dharma heir of Yuanfa of Huguo):
Chan Master Jiantang Xingji of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou was a native of that prefecture. His surname was Yang, and his talent surpassed that of the Confucian scholars.
At the age of twenty-five, he abandoned his wife and children to study the supramundane Dharma. Later, upon seeing this hermitage, he attained a profound realization in secret.

He went forth to serve at Guanshan, where for seventeen years he lived alone, tilling the soil with a knife and sowing by fire. He once composed a verse that said: "The hearth-fire is out and the traveler’s bag is empty;
The snow falls like willow blossoms as the year draws to a close. I have gathered discarded hemp to patch my worn robe. Not... [the text continues].
Aware that his body was dwelling in solitude, he would often say to others, "I am still not yet settled; how could I take my pleasure in the mountain life?

One day, while observing a tree being felled as it fell to the ground, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. The obstruction that had long weighed upon his chest dissolved completely, like ice melting away.
Not long after, he received an invitation from Jangzhou to the Yuan-t'ung monastery, whereupon he said, "My Way is about to be put into practice."
He then joyfully took up his staff and departed. Ascending the seat, he preached the Dharma, saying: "The Perfect Penetration does not open a pharmacy for the living;
it sells nothing but the heads of dead cats. Who knows which one, free from calculation, will take a bite and have cold sweat pour down their entire body?
In the meditation hall, he would often hold up the handle of a broom and ask the students: "Vague like the handle of a broom; faintly resembling a red [broom]."
Regarding the "Spotted Snake," the assembly all offered interpretations, yet none were in accord with the truth. A monk requested further instruction, and the Master showed him this verse:

"Vaguely like the handle of a broom, Resembling a red-spotted snake; If one does not realize the patience of non-arising beneath the staff, One will fail to recognize one's father when the moment arrives.

On the first day of the eighth month in the Jihai year of the Chunxi era, he manifested a slight illness. He took up his brush to bid farewell to the Prefectural Governor, Mr. Zeng, and by midnight, he wrote this verse:
He addressed the assembly, saying: "An iron tree blossoms; a rooster lays an egg. At seventy-two years, the cradle rope breaks.
He cast down his brush and entered nirvana.
This was the Venerable Jue'a (the Dharma heir of Lingyin Yuan).
Master Jue’a was the son of the Teng family in the kingdom of Japan. He received the tonsure at the age of fourteen and was ordained as a full bhikṣu;
he became renowned for his mastery of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. At twenty-nine, a merchant returning from the Central Kingdom spoke of the flourishing state of the Chan school.
Jue’a was stirred by this and, accompanied by his dharma-brother Jinqing, sailed across the sea to arrive here. Carrying incense in his sleeve, he paid homage to Master Fohai of Lingyin.

When the Buddha-Hai asked him about his arrival, Jue-A immediately wrote down the answer. He further wrote: "In my country there is no Chan school; we only lecture on the sūtras and śāstras of the five schools.
Our sovereign has no surname or clan name, but is titled the Golden Wheel King (Cakravartin). He changed the era name to Jiaying.

Having abdicated the throne, he left the household life with the name Xingzhen; he is forty-four years old. He has commanded his seven-year-old son to receive the succession, and it has now been five—"
[The Emperor] decreed: "There shall be no requirement for monks to submit offerings upon ordination; however, those whose exegesis of the teachings is eminent shall be granted [honors].

We, [the undersigned], in deep admiration of the reputation of Master Yuan of the Sagely Court, have come specifically to the *zhàngshì* (abbot’s quarters) to pay our respects. We pray that you will transmit the seal of the mind (*xīnyìn*) so as to ferry us across the perilous strait of delusion.

Furthermore, as for the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. They transcend all marks and transcend all words, yet we employ provisional words to manifest them. This is Zen.
"How do you, Master, provide instruction? Foghai replied, "Sentient beings have deluded perceptions; they see Buddhas and they see worlds.
Jue'a asked, "From what cause does ignorance arise? Foghai struck him. Jue'a then requested Foghai to ascend the seat to resolve his doubts.
The following autumn, he took leave to travel to Jinling. Upon reaching the banks of the Changlu River, he suddenly attained great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of a drum.
Only then did he come to understand the intent behind the Buddha-ocean’s outstretched hand.
Regarding the Inner Secretary Layman Zeng Kai (a dharma successor of Lingyin Yuan):
the Inner Secretary Layman Zeng Kai, whose courtesy name was Tianyou, had long studied under Yuanwu and subsequently traveled between the gates of Dahui.
It has been some time since [this occurred]. In the *Xinwei* year of the *Shaoxing* era, Fohai was appointed to Guangxiao Temple in Siqu.
Master [Wuzu] and the layman Chaoran Zhao visited him and asked, "What is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
Fohai replied, "The lantern, the pillar, the cat, and the dog. The Master said, "Why is it that praise brings joy while disparagement causes distress? Fohai replied, "Serve..."
"Have you ever seen a true teacher (kalyāṇamitra)? The official replied, "I have been seeking instruction for thirty years; how can you say I have not seen one?
Fohai said, "See him where there is joy; see him where there is affliction. As the official hesitated, Fohai let out a thunderous shout and struck him with a *kei*.
The Duke prepared to respond. Fohai said, "He who opens his mouth is not he. The Duke was bewildered. Fohai called out to him, "Where has the Minister gone?
The Duke suddenly attained realization and nodded his head. He then spoke this verse: "Alas, the blind donkey! A pestilence to the monastic groves.
With one roar that shakes the earth, the celestial mechanism is leaked. If anyone further asks what the meaning is, pick it up..."
Fuzi said, "I would cut it right at the handle. Fohai remarked, "That only achieves one peg. The Layman Ge Tan, Prefectural Governor.
His courtesy name was Qianwen and his style name was Xinzhai. In his youth, he passed the highest imperial examinations. He devoted himself to the joy of Chan meditation.

He was a dharma successor of Lingyin Yuan. The Layman Ge Tan, Prefectural Governor. His courtesy name was Qianwen and his style name was Xinzhai. In his youth, he attained the highest degree. He took pleasure in the cultivation of Zen.
He first visited Chan Master Wuan Quan to seek guidance. Wuan instructed him to investigate the saying, "This very mind is Buddha. After a long time, he had no realization.
He requested, "Master, what expedient means can you provide so that I may gain entry? Wuan replied, "Layman, you are truly insatiable.
Subsequently, Fohai came to reside at Jianchi, and the Master followed him there. Fohai then brought up the instruction previously given by Wuan.
"Please explain these words for the sake of the assembly. The Buddha-ocean (the Master) expounded upon them, saying:

"Mind is Buddha, eyebrows trailing the ground; neither mind nor Buddha, two eyes staring wide. Amidst the butterfly dream, home is ten thousand li away; the nightingale on the branch, the moon at the third watch.
He stayed for ten days before returning. One day, he raised the phrase: "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing," and suddenly—
Nevertheless, he suddenly attained clarity. The verse says: Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor yet any thing; Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, the mountain looms high.
In the midst of the brilliant sunshine, he turns his body upside down; The wild fox leaps into the golden-haired lion’s den.
Wu’an approved of this, immediately sent a letter and the verse to present to Fohai, who replied: "This matter cannot be fully expressed by paper and brush. Layman, you must come to see me."
"You must have heard something," [he said]. He then went back to Tiger Hill (Hǔqīu).

Fohai welcomed him, saying, "Your realization, Layman, is sufficient to enter the realm of the Buddhas, yet you have not yet attained entry into the realm of Māras. The Master continued to pay him profound respects without ceasing.

Fohai assumed a solemn countenance and said, "Why do you not say, 'The golden-haired lion leaps into the den of the wild fox'? Thereupon, the Master gained a deep and thorough understanding. He once asked various...
Chan said: "A husband and wife are fighting; they call upon their son to serve as witness. Now tell me: does he bear witness for his father, or does he bear witness for his mother?

Master Huian added these comments: "A small emergence meets a great encounter. In the sixth year of the Chunxi era, while serving as Governor of Linchuan, in the eighth year he was stricken by illness.
One night, he suddenly asked for a brush and wrote this verse: "Beating the drum within the vast ocean."
Hearing the bell atop Mount Sumeru, the karmic mirror suddenly shattered. Turning his body, he emerged into the void and summoned his subordinates, showing them [the mirror] and saying:
"Life and death are like day and night; there is nothing strange about this. If one speaks from the perspective of the Way,"
"How can there be birth and death? If you interpret it in terms of birth and death, you are far removed from the Way. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Bāoyìn of Biefēng at Jìngshān (a successor of Huízàng Mínghuì):
Chan Master Bāoyìn of Biéfēng at Jìngshān in Lín’ān Prefecture was the son of the Lí family of Jiāzhōu. He followed Dēishān Qīng...
He had already attained realization prior to receiving full ordination. After his ordination, he studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*, mastering their teachings.
He then left them to rely upon Miyin at Mount Zhongfeng. One day, Miyin raised a case concerning a monk who asked Yantou, "What is it like when arising and ceasing do not stop?
Yantou rebuked him, saying, "Who is it that arises and ceases? The Master was immediately awakened; Miyin nodded in approval. When Yuanwu returned to Zhaojue, Miyin...
He sent the Master to visit him, and consequently followed the assembly into the room. Yuanwu asked, "How did the sages of antiquity receive people?
The Master held up his fist. Yuanwu said, "That is what I, this old monk, use.
What is it that the sages of antiquity use? The Master struck him with his fist. Yuanwu also raised his fist and crossed them; they laughed heartily and stopped. [Later...]
He went to Mount Jing to visit Dahui. Dahui asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From West Sichuan.
Dahui said, "Before you have even left Jianmen Pass, I shall give you thirty blows of the staff! The Master said, "It would not be fitting for me to trouble the Master by rising to greet him.
Dahui was pleased and swept out his quarters to welcome him.
Chan Master Huifang of Chuan, Wenshu’s Dharma Heir.
Chan Master Huifang of Chuan, Tanzhou, was the son of the Xu family of that prefecture. He studied the Way under Chan Master Dao at Dayue.
Before long, the temple was converted into a Shenxiao Palace. While traveling south along the Xiang River on a merchant vessel, he heard a person on the bank using his native dialect shouting, "Naa!
At this, he attained realization. He immediately spoke a verse: "A single cry from the heart of the river at Mian— Only now do I realize my lifelong vow.
After many years of parting, we meet again; The myriad sages all return to the same source."
As they traveled along the way, there was Zen Master Wenshu Siye (a dharma successor of Wenshu Dao) of Wenshu [Temple] in Changde Prefecture.
In his previous life, he had been a butcher. One day, while in the midst of slaughtering a pig, he suddenly attained a profound realization.
Having thoroughly penetrated the source of the mind, he immediately abandoned his worldly labors to become a bhikṣu. He composed a verse, saying: "Yesterday was the heart of a yakṣa;
today is the face of a bodhisattva. Between the bodhisattva and the yakṣa, there is not even a single thread’s distance.

He went to see Mañjuśrī, who asked, "When you were just slaughtering the pig, what did you see that led you to shave your head and go on pilgrimage? The Master then made the gesture of brandishing a butcher's knife.
Mañjuśrī shouted, “This butcher! Go to the hall for practice! The Master then descended and went to the hall.
Layman Pan Lianggui, a *Dai-zhi* (Court Gentleman of the Second Class), a successor of Fodeng Xun, was a layman whose courtesy name was Yirong.
At the age of forty, he turned his mind toward the ancestral gate; wherever he went, he hung [his robe].

Baozhi went to visit various masters in succession. Later, he followed Fodeng, but after a long time, they did not reach accord. He therefore complained, saying, "I simply wish to know what it is like at the moment of death.
Fodeng said, "What an excellent envelope! Keep it for future use; you have not yet resolved this matter."
"I should not have left later. Suddenly, he changed the envelope, and I was at a complete loss as to how to rectify it.
The Master (Fodeng) then asked about Nanquan’s story of killing the cat: "I have been contemplating this for a very long time, yet I still have not fully penetrated it.
I beg the Venerable One’s compassion. Fodeng said, "You are merely preoccupied with understanding someone else's cat; you do not realize that you have lost your own."
The Dog. Under these words, Gong was as if awakened from a drunken stupor.
Chan Master Shouyuan of Wuweishan (a successor of Letan Mingfa):
Chan Master Shouyuan of Su’an at Wuweishan in Hanzhou was a native of that prefecture. His secular surname was Shi. At the age of thirteen, he fell ill.
Next, he went to Master Nengchan Yimujianhui at Yiqi. Having received full ordination, he left the Gorges and arrived at Baofeng.
There he encountered Baofeng ascending the hall, where Baofeng cited Yongjia: "The single moon universally appears in all waters; the moons in all waters are subsumed within the single moon."
Upon hearing this, the Master was relieved and attained realization.
Chan Master Yungju Desheng (dharma heir of Longxiang Gui):
Chan Master Yungju Wuan Desheng of Nankang Commandery was the son of the He family in Hanzhou. He went to visit Wenshu Dao.
A Zen master asked about the essential point of the Buddha-dharma. Mañjuśrī showed him this verse:
"The Khitan broke into the Persian camp, Seized the precious jewel, and sold it in the village. The destitute beggar at the crossroads Has a bag of elegance hanging from his waist."
The Master was about to respond when Mañjuśrī said, "Do not err. The Master withdrew and studied for three years before finally grasping the essential meaning.

He went to see Fóxìng, but his faculties did not accord with the master's. He then traveled to Fúmián and went to Gǔshān to pay his respects, where he immediately asked: "The National Teacher’s statement regarding not crossing the stone gate—"
"What is the meaning of this? Zhuan’an responded with a shout: "Idle talk! The Master immediately attained realization.
Chan Master Huizun of Luoshan (dharma heir of Longxiang Gui):
Chan Master Huizun of Luoshan Luan, Tongzhou. A native of Fuzhou, surnamed Zheng, he traveled extensively to study under various masters.
In his later years, he relied upon Zhuan’an at Donglin. Not long after, Zhuan’an retired from his duties.
The Master then visited Gao’an Wu, Nanhua Bing, and Caotang Qing, all of whom recognized and appreciated his potential. When Zhuan’an moved to Qianyuan in Min, the Master returned there to visit him.

Zhuan-an asked, "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when conceptualization changes, the essence becomes distinct. Without lingering in the prison of long-term intellectualizing, bring forth a single phrase of the Way.
The Master was suddenly enlightened and spoke this verse: "Pressed out until my whole body is a mouth, What prevents me from reviling the rain and scolding the wind?
Last night, a fierce tiger in the village ahead Bit to death the great beast of the southern mountain. Zhuan-an nodded in approval.
Chan Master Zhongji Shanan (Dharma heir of Yunju Wu).
Chan Master Zhongji Shanan of Fuzhou was a native of Yanling. He had traveled back and forth between Longmen and Yunju for many years without attaining any realization.
One day, while he was engaged in communal labor selecting vegetables, Gao’an suddenly threw a cat into the Master’s lap.
As the Master was about to deliberate, Gao’an lunged at his chest and kicked him down. Thereupon, the Great Matter was clearly realized.
This was Zen Master Ziyuan of Yunju (the dharma heir of Yunju Wu) in the Nan-kang Prefecture.
Zen Master Ziyuan of Yunju Puyun was the son of the Ong clan of Mianzhou; he left the monastic enclosure and traveled south.
Having visited various great venerable masters in succession, he finally went to Longmen. One day, while in the corridors, he had an awakening upon seeing a painting of a foreigner.
That night, he reported this to Gao’an, who cited a verse by Fayan: "On his head he wears a sable-fur hat; at his waist he hangs a horn-whistle.
His words do not allow others to understand them; they must be translated by one who knows him. Gao’an then held up a torch and showed it to him, saying: "I..."
I have finished translating for you. Thus, the Great Dharma was clearly understood. He presented a verse, saying:
"The sounds and languages of foreign lands are inexhaustible, Yet beneath Qiyun Pavilion, they were all at once penetrated. The gateway of the mouth is vast and boundless;
It has swallowed the thorny chestnut of Yangqi. Gao’an sent the Master to rely upon Foyan. Foyan said to him, "My Way is heading East."
Chan Master Shouren of Changlu (Dharma heir of Wugu Xing).
Chan Master Shouren of Qie’an at Changlu in Zhenzhou was a native of Shangyu in Yue. He relied upon Xuetang at Wugu, where he heard a general discourse [on the Dharma] which said:
"The way our fellow practitioners nowadays apply themselves to their practice is just like learning archery: first one must steady one's feet."
Later, he practiced that method. Although he had no conscious intent, because of his long practice, every arrow he shot hit the mark.

He let out a shout and said, "The arrow is being released right now! Look, look! The Master involuntarily threw himself down, making a gesture of dodging the arrow, and suddenly attained great enlightenment.

Shouzuo Ran of He Mountain (dharma heir of Daochang Bian). A native of Gusu, he served Zhengtang for a long time. On one occasion during his entry into the room, Zhengtang asked, "Why does a cat especially love to catch mice? Ran replied, "When the object is seen by its master, the eyes stand bolt upright. Zhengtang said, "Excellent! Later, when Ran was about to depart, Zhengtang asked him, "What is your ultimate destination? Ran replied, "The place where there is no road. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will know you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with being known. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will see you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with being seen. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will hear you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with being heard. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will speak to you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with speaking. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will act for you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with acting. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will give you food? Ran said, "I am not concerned with eating. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will clothe you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with wearing clothes. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will dwell with you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with dwelling. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will accompany you? Ran said, "I am not concerned with companionship. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your teacher? Ran said, "I am not concerned with having a teacher. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your disciple? Ran said, "I am not concerned with having a disciple. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your fellow practitioners? Ran said, "I am not concerned with fellow practitioners. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your patrons? Ran said, "I am not concerned with patrons. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your donors? Ran said, "I am not concerned with donors. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your benefactors? Ran said, "I am not concerned with benefactors. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your enemies? Ran said, "I am not concerned with enemies. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your friends? Ran said, "I am not concerned with friends. Zhengtang said, "If you go to that place, who will be your kin? Ran said, "I am not concerned with kin. Chan Master Ji of Dongshan (a successor of Master Lin of Daochang) was the Chan Master Ji of Dongshan in Linjiang Commandery.
Through Li Chaoling, he became acquainted with his nephew, the Layman Xianglin, the Duke Xiang.
Li Yin went to visit him and asked, "When household bandits trouble people, what then? The Master said, "Who is the household bandit?
Li raised his fist. The Master said, "The bandit’s own body has been revealed. Li said, "Do not try to deceive me.
The Master said, "The evidence is right here. Li was speechless.
The Seventeenth Generation under Nanyue (the Thirteenth Generation under Linji):
Chan Master Tanmi of Jingci, of the Lin’an Prefecture Jingci Monastery (Dharma heir of Jiaozhong Guang).
He was the son of the Lu family of Tiantai. Having studied the Tiantai teachings, he renounced them...
Dahui attended at Mount Jing, where he visited Xuechao Yi and Ciana Yuan. He entered Min Province and stayed at both Dongxi Chan and Xi Chan monasteries, yet no realization arose.
He went to Jiaozhong in Quannan to serve as the *yuezong* (manager of communal affairs); upon resigning from that post, he returned to his former quarters.

While casually discussing the karmic conditions of Xiangyan striking the bamboo, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. He composed a verse and presented it to Jiaozhong, who then cited the words of Xuansha: "Xuansha had not yet reached the ultimate."
When questioned, he was never at a loss for words. Jiaochong said to him, "You may now go see Miaoxi.
He then took his leave and went to Mei Yang, where he served diligently for four years under Chan Master Yanchong of Jingci (the dharma heir of Yan of Donglin).
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Sheng family of Yuqian. He first studied under Dayu Hongzhi and Zhengtang Dayuan;
later, he heard Donglin say to the assembly, "In this place of mine, there is nothing else that is mysterious or wondrous."
"There is only a soup of wood shavings and rice with iron nails; chew on them as you please. The Master secretly rejoiced at these words and went directly to pay his respects.

He set forth his insights and understanding, to which Donglin replied, "According to your way of seeing, you are sitting right within the realm of reflective awareness. The Master remained in doubt and could not yet resolve it.

He cast away everything he had previously attained all at once. One day, hearing a monk cite Nanquan’s saying, "People of this age see this single stalk of flowers as if in a dream," he silently experienced an awakening and remarked, "Striking the grass is only intended to startle the snake."
The next day, he entered the room. Donglin asked, "Where was it that Yantou secretly revealed his meaning?
The Master said, "Today I have caught this old thief red-handed. Donglin said, "The very life of Master Bodhidharma rests in your hands.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, Donglin suddenly struck him a punch straight to the chest. He was instantly awakened, so much so that sweat poured down his back; he simply nodded his head.
He said to himself, "Linji said, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much. Could this possibly be empty talk? He then presented a verse, saying:
"To act for others, one must act to the very end; to kill, one must see blood. Deshan and Yantou—ten thousand miles, a single bar of iron.
Donglin approved of this.
Chan Master Zhizhen Cici (Dharma Heir of Yan of Donglin):

Chan Master Zhizhen Yuan’an Cici of Wuzhou was a native of Tongchuan. His secular surname was Li. While frequenting lecture halls, he listened to a discourse on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*).
Upon reaching the passage, "The four elements are each separate; where, then, does this illusory body reside? Ultimately, it has no substance," [he attained realization].
"It is truly identical to an illusion. Thereupon, he attained an awakening and composed a verse, saying:
"A single bright pearl is here within me; when touched or moved, it emits light that shakes the earth. He presented this to various lecturers, but none were able to understand it.

Returning home, he presented it to his own teacher, who then questioned him with the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature. The teacher said, "Even if you have [recited] it hundreds of thousands of millions of times..."
Upon reviewing this, it was found that the verse had not been produced. His master considered this disrespectful and rebuked him, ordering him out.

The Master then traveled south and took up residence at the Yuan Tong Monastery on Mount Lu. At that time, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Preceptor; when he entered the room for the assembly, he raised the following kōan:
"A monk asked Yunmen, 'When one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha, what then? Yunmen said, 'The Buddha is also dust. As soon as the Master heard these words, he let out a shout.
Pointing his finger at his chest, he said, "The Buddha is also dust. The Master then recited a verse: "Push aside the dust to see the Buddha; the Buddha is also dust.

Question finished, answer finished—turn yourself around right here and now. I urge you to drink one more cup of wine: once you have passed the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friend left behind.
He also recited a verse on the Samādhi of Dust-to-Dust: "Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket—the Kunlun who discerns jewels."
Sitting at the bottom of the abyss, each speck of dust climbs upward to Mount Sumeru. A clear-eyed Persian laughs and snaps his fingers. He laughs and snaps his fingers;
a pure breeze rises upon the coral branches. Wan-an deeply approved of this.
Chan Master An Yong of Gushan (Dharma Heir of Xichan Xu).
Chan Master Mu’an An Yong of Gushan, Fuzhou, was the son of the Wu family of Min County. He visited Lan’an at Yunmen.
One day, upon entering the inner quarters, Lan’an said: “I do not ask about words; I do not ask about wordlessness. The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while.”
He was unable to approach the World-Honored One for a long time. Subsequently, [Lan’an] gave a shout, whereupon [the monk] attained sudden enlightenment.
He prostrated and said, "Had it not been for today’s question, how could I have lost the opportunity before my eyes? Lan’an granted him approval.
The Hermit Master Anfen of Jianmen (Dharma Heir of Xichan Xu).
The Hermit Master Anfen of Jianmen in Nanjian Prefecture was a youth who, along with Mukan, studied under Anguo.

Later, he relied upon Lan’an, yet had not yet attained deep realization. He took his leave to visit Daie at Jingshan; while traveling along the riverbank, he gazed up in reverence at the imperial palace.
Hearing the Street Official shout, "The Minister is coming! he was suddenly and completely enlightened. He composed a verse, saying:
"For many years this matter has hung upon my breast; I have questioned all quarters, yet my eyes remained unopened. Now, at this moment, liver and gall are utterly shattered— A single cry:
'The Minister comes upon the river! He then went straight back to Xichan Monastery. Lan’an welcomed him and bestowed upon him the *kāṣāya*.
The Daoist Ruler No. 13 of Wuzhou (Dharma Heir of Kaiyan Qian).
The Daoist Ruler No. 13 of Mount Xianzhou in Jianning Prefecture frequently questioned various Chan masters regarding his own affairs.

When Kaiyan returned and settled in a thatched hut to the left of the mountain, the Daoist went there to serve him. On the eighth day of the third month in the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era, at night—
Suddenly awakened, he composed a verse and presented it to Kaishan, saying: "Originally there was no seam or crack; Upon being touched, it immediately radiates light.
Since it is a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, Why need one use it to shoot at sparrows? Kaishan replied: "When the 'spat' sound breaks through, true joy and ease arise;
Birth-and-death, the mundane and the sage—all sink into equanimity. Laughing 'he-he' beneath Mount Xianzhou, I shall not fail the expectations we shared."
Formerly, there was the Zen Master Mian Xianjie of Tiantong in Qingyuan Prefecture (a dharma heir of Tiantong Hua).
He was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou and traveled extensively to study under various spiritual teachers.
Later, he visited Ying’an at Mingguo in Quzhou. Ying’an was solitary and rigid, difficult to approach, and the Master frequently encountered scoldings from him.
One day, Ying’an asked, "What is the True Dharma Eye? The Master immediately replied, "A broken sandalwood bowl. Ying’an nodded his head in approval.
Minister Li Hao, Lay Practitioner (Dharma heir of Tiantong Hu).
Minister Li Hao, lay practitioner, styled De-yuan and nicknamed Zheng-xin. In his youth, he read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as if visiting an old home;
he cherished it in his heart and never forgot it. Later, while serving in office, he visited Mingguo Temple and devotedly entered the master’s room. Ying’an struck him with his staff...
Xiong asked, "After you die, Elder, where will you go? The official was startled and broke into a cold sweat. Ying’an shouted at him to leave. The official withdrew to practice further meditation;
within ten days, he had finally ascended to the inner sanctum. He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Kangchao, saying:
"The gate has the shop of Sun Bin; The home retains the wife of Gan Zhi. Sleeping at night and rising early— Who awakens, and who is deluded? Ying’an [received it].
Yuan’an praised him as excellent. There was also a seller of rouge who had likewise long studied under Ying’an and prided himself greatly on his realization.
Yuan’an presented him with this verse: “Without applying red powder, one is naturally elegant; Often, practitioners of Chan stop short at this point.
Only after penetrating the snares of past and present Does one come here to receive a blow of the fist.”

Chan Master Youquan of I’an at Huazang in Changzhou was a native of the Qi family in Qihua, Lin’an. At the age of eighteen, he...
Chan Master Fozhi Yuyu was at Lingyin Monastery, where Wuan served as the First Seat.

In the meditation hall, Wuan questioned him regarding the principle of "establishing all dharmas from the ground of non-abiding. After a long time, the Master attained realization and replied: "Sewing a needle in the dark."

As he exhaled air from his ears, Wuan approved him and secretly transmitted the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) to him. Once, while sitting in meditation through the night until dawn, the one who distributed the gruel arrived;

the Master forgot to open his alms bowl. A neighboring monk touched it with his hand, and the Master was awakened to realization. He composed a verse, saying: "A pitch-black *k'un-lun* [giant] holds a fishing rod;
The ancient sail is hoisted high as it descends the turbulent rapids. Amidst the shadows of reeds, he plays with the bright moon, Drawing forth..."
The blind turtle was caught on the fishing boat. Fozhi once asked him, "When the mind encompasses the vast void and its measure spans the *sāhasra* world-system, what then?
The Master said, "The great ocean does not harbor a corpse. Fozhi patted his seat and said, "This son shall one day occupy this seat;
he will go about scolding the Buddhas and reviling the Patriarchs. From then on, the Master concealed his talents and became even more reclusive, traveling about...
He traveled through the regions of Lake Hu, River Xiang, and Zhejiang for several decades. He attended upon Ying’an at Guizong and studied under Dahui at Jingshan.
When Wuan resided at Daochang, he invited the Master to share his seat and preach the Dharma; thus, his reputation became widely known.

Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui (Dharma heir of Baizhang Hai).
Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui in Tanzhou was the son of the Zhao family of Fuzhou. At the age of twenty-three, he traveled to Jiangxi to visit Baizhang.
Upon first seeing him, Baizhang granted him permission to enter the inner quarters, and he subsequently became the foremost among those engaged in study. While standing in attendance, Baizhang—
Baizhang asked, "Who is there? The Master replied, "It is I. Baizhang said, "Is there any fire in the hearth? The Master stirred it and said, "There is no fire.
Baizhang rose from his seat and stirred deeply, finding a small amount of fire. He held it up to show him and said, "You say there is none."
"What about this? At these words, the Master attained awakening and paid his respects, explaining what he had understood. Baizhang said, "This is merely a temporary crossroads. As the Sūtra says:
'If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.

When the time and season arrive, it is like suddenly awakening from a dream or suddenly remembering what was forgotten; only then do you realize that your own property is not obtained from another. Thus, the Patriarch...
He said, "Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and there are no dharmas. It is simply the absence of delusion.
The minds of ordinary people and sages are equal; the original mind-dharma has been complete from the very beginning. Since you are now thus, protect and maintain it well yourself.
The next day, he went into the mountains with Baizhang to perform manual labor. Baizhang asked, "Did you bring fire? The Master replied, "I brought it. Baizhang...
[The Master] asked, "Where is it? The Master then picked up a piece of firewood, blew on it twice, and handed it to Baizhang.

Baizhang said, "Like an insect gnawing through wood. (Jingshan Gao said: "Had Baizhang not had these subsequent words, he would have been deceived by the head cook. Chushi Qi said: 'Baizhang, however, because of those subsequent words, was seen through by others;

he brought the head cook along with him in following the heterodox and pursuing the evil. Fortunately, Tianning has no such trouble. You all who come here, what are you looking for? One blind man leading a crowd of blind men, pulling each other into a pit of fire. With his staff, [Dayang] drove them all away at once.)
Sima Touduo came from Hunan and said to Baizhang, "Recently, while in Hunan, I found a mountain named Daming.
It is the place where a spiritual teacher of fifteen hundred people resides. Baizhang said:
"Can an old monk like me dwell there? The head monk said, "It is not a place for the Master to reside.
Baizhang asked, "Why? The head monk replied, "The Master is a man of bone; that place is a mountain of flesh. Even if he were to dwell there, his followers would never exceed a thousand.
Baizhang asked, "Is there no one among my assembly who could dwell there? The head monk said, "I shall observe them all first. At that time, Huilin Jue was...
Regarding the first seat: Baizhang ordered his attendant to invite [the monk] there and asked, "What kind of person is this?

The *dhūta* practitioner coughed once and walked several paces. The *dhūta* said, "Not him. Baizhang again ordered the master to be summoned; at that time, the master was serving as the steward (*diànzuò*).
Upon seeing him, the *dhūta* said, "This is truly the master of Mt. Huishan. That night, Baizhang...
He summoned the Master into his room and instructed him, saying: "My karmic conditions for transformation are fulfilled here. Mount Gui Shan is a magnificent realm;
you should reside there to succeed my lineage and extensively guide future students. When Hualin heard this, he said, "I, this humble one, am merely the head cook (Dianzuo) among the assembly;
how can I take charge as abbot? Baizhang replied, "If you can utter a single phrase that transcends the ordinary before the assembly, I shall grant it to you."
The Abbot pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "You must not call this a 'water pitcher. What would you call it?
Hualin replied, "It cannot be called a wooden stump. Baizhang then asked the Master [Hualin], who kicked over the pitcher and walked out.
Baizhang laughed and said, "The First Seat has lost the mountain to you. Thereupon, the Master went to that mountain. This was Mount [Yunju].
The cliffs were precipitous and remote, devoid of human habitation; he kept company with monkeys and apes and sustained himself on acorns and chestnuts. For five or seven years, no one came at all.
The Master thought to himself, "I am originally a monastic administrator whose purpose is to benefit others. Since there is now a total absence of visitors, how can my own virtue be of any help?
He immediately abandoned his hermitage, intending to go elsewhere. As he reached the mountain pass, he saw snakes, tigers, wolves, and leopards crossing his path in every direction.
While on the road, the Master said, "You various beasts, do not block my path. If I have a karmic affinity with this mountain, you may each disperse;
if I have no such affinity, there is no need for you to move. I am merely passing through."
"Eat as much as you wish. Having said this, the insects and tigers dispersed in all directions. The Master then returned to his hermitage.
Before a full year had passed, the monk An (also known as Lan’an), accompanied by several other monks, arrived from Baizhang to assist the Master.
An said, "I shall serve as the steward for the Master. When we have five hundred monks, we will not prepare congee regardless of the season; instead, we shall simply dismiss them."
Below the mountain at Meigai, the local residents subsequently joined forces to construct a Buddhist monastery. The regional commander Li Jingrang submitted a memorial naming it Tongqing Temple.
The Prime Minister Pei Xu once consulted [the Master] on the profound mysteries; consequently, practitioners of Chan from all over the world flocked there like spokes converging on a hub.
[The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The mind of a man of the Way is simple and straightforward, free of artifice. It has no back and no front; it is without..."

With a mind free from deceit and falsehood, at all times, one’s seeing and hearing remain ordinary and straightforward, without further artifice. Nor is it necessary to close one's eyes or block one's ears;
it is sufficient simply that the mind does not cling to objects. The sages of antiquity spoke only of the faults and afflictions on the side of turbidity.
If one is free from such numerous evil thoughts, emotional attachments, perceptions, and habitual tendencies, it is like autumn water—stilled, clear, and pure.
Being limpid and unimpeded, he is called a man of the Way and is also named a man of no affairs. At that time, a monk asked:
"For one who has attained sudden enlightenment, is there still further cultivation? The Master said: "If one truly awakens to the source, they know for themselves;

'cultivation' and 'non-cultivation' are dualistic extremes. Now, although those with the initial resolve may, through conditions, attain a sudden awakening to the principle in a single thought-moment,"

There still remain the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless, vast eons that have not yet been suddenly purified. One must teach them to purify and eliminate the flowing consciousness of present karma;
this is precisely what cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is. There can be no other dharma to teach them how to practice and advance toward [enlightenment]. They enter into principle through hearing.

When one hears that the principle is profound and subtle, the mind becomes naturally luminous and clear, no longer dwelling in the realm of delusion. Even if there are hundreds or thousands of wondrous meanings, they may be emphasized or suppressed as the occasion demands;
this is truly like putting on one's robes while already seated, having attained the ability to provide for oneself through one’s own understanding.

To state the essential point: within the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is admitted; yet within the gateway of the myriad practices (*saṃskāra*), not a single dharma is abandoned. If it were merely a single blade...
Entering directly, the sentiments of both ordinary people and sages are exhausted; the essence reveals true permanence. Principle and phenomena are non-dual—this is the Buddha of Suchness.
Yangshan asked, "If hundreds of thousands of millions of objects come at once, what do you do? The Master said, "Blue is not yellow; long is not short.
All dharmas each abide in their own place; it is no concern of mine. Yangshan bowed. Yangshan.
A question was asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master pointed to a lantern and said, "A truly fine lantern.
Yangshan said, "Is this not it? The Master said, "What is this? Yangshan said, "A truly fine lantern.

The Master said, "Indeed, you do not see. (Xueyan Qin’s verse says: "Bringing it forth face-to-face and entrusting it to him; clearly, this meaning has no east or west. His wrist has the strength to hold a thousand-jun weight.")
"Who says his whole body is mud and cement? One day, the Master said to the assembly, "So many people here have attained the Great Functionality, yet they have not attained the Great Utility.
Yangshan repeated these words and asked the hermitage master below the mountain, "What is the meaning of the Master saying this?
The hermitage master replied, "Try raising it again and see. As Yangshan was about to raise it once more, he was kicked over by the hermitage master. Yangshan—
Shangu returned and recounted this to the Master. The Master laughed loudly, "He-he! While the Master was seated in the Dharma Hall, the storehouse head struck the wooden fish.
The fire-head attendant threw down his fire-tongs and clapped his hands, laughing loudly. The Master said, "There is such a person among the assembly."
He then summoned him and asked, "How is it with you? The fire-tender replied, "I did not eat my gruel, so I am hungry;
that is why I am joyful. The Master nodded his head. While picking tea, the Master said to Yangshan, "All day long I have been picking tea;
I hear only your voice, but I do not see your form. Yangshan shook the tea tree. The Master said, "You have attained only its function, not its essence."
[Shishuang] attained his essence. Yangshan asked, "I wonder, how about the Master? The Master remained silent for a long while. Yangshan said, "The Master has only attained the essence;
he has not attained the function. The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows. Yangshan said, "The Master shall take these blows;
to whom shall I give my blows? The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows. (Shoushan Nian said: "Now, as for being a man of the Way...")

A true master must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma before they can succeed. At that time, had it not been for Baizhang, one would have been left to lean on a fence and grope along a wall. Baoci said: "Tell me, where exactly does the fault lie? Langye Huijue said: "At the fifth watch, rising even earlier than dawn, there are still travelers on the road at night.

He also said: "Had it not been for Baizhang, we would have ended up breaking into Caizhou. Baiyun Shouduan said: "Father and son meet; their spirits accord. Their sharp wits exchange blows; the pecking and the hatching occur simultaneously. Even so, how can one ultimately express the perfect integration of essence and function?

Baizhang’s giving his son thirty blows was simply a matter of the circumstances of raising a child. Jiangshan Zhengqin said: "When Mr. Zhang first becomes friends with Mr. Li, he waits to fine Mr. Li."

A single cup of wine; I was instead punished with a cup by Master Li. "A fine hand displaying its skill among fine hands. Lian of Yüquan said: "Even if one were to achieve the perfect integration of essence and function, what can be done? One has already missed the mark head-on. Let us stop for now at 'missing the mark.

But as for 'giving you thirty blows'—what then? "Three cups of wine to brighten the young lord’s face; a single branch of flowers to adorn the beauty’s hair. [Ascending the hall: A monk came forward and said, "I request the Master to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
The Master said, "I have already exhausted myself thoroughly for your sake. The monk bowed. (Later, someone brought this up to Xuefeng Cun. Xuefeng said:)

The ancients possessed such a heart of compassionate intimacy. Xuansha Zhiyan said, "Master Shanshou has missed the point of the ancients. When Xuefeng heard this, he asked Xuansha, "In what way did I, this old monk, miss the point of the ancients?

If there were no lightness or heaviness, then at that very moment, had the monk seen this, would he have understood whether the Dharma-body can preach the Dharma or not? Had he then immediately turned his steps back toward the abbot’s quarters—would this not have been an extraordinary feat by a master, sparing the monks of the world from further censure and disparagement?

Chan Master Xiangyan Zhixian of Dengzhou was a native of Qingzhou. During his time at Baizhang, he was naturally sharp and quick-witted.
He was unable to attain realization through Zen meditation. Upon the passing of Baizhang, he went to study under Guishan.
Guishan asked him, "I have heard that while you were with your late master Baizhang, you would answer ten when asked one, and a hundred when asked ten.

This is merely your cleverness, sharp wit, intellectual understanding, and conceptual consciousness—the very root of birth and death. Before your parents were even born, try to utter a single word. The Master was struck by this.

Upon being asked this single question, he was immediately left in a state of total bewilderment. Returning to his quarters, he took up the texts he had studied throughout his life and sought, from beginning to end, for even a single phrase with which to respond;
yet in the end, he could find none. He then sighed to himself, saying, "A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger.
He repeatedly requested that Guishan explain it to him, to which Guishan replied, "If I were to explain it to you, you would later come to curse me. Guishan said: "I have spoken."
"This is mine; it shall never concern you. The Master then took all the texts he had studied throughout his life and burned them, saying, "In this life I shall not study the Buddha-dharma.
I will instead become a simple monk who prepares porridge and rice, so as to spare my mind from toil."
He then wept as he took his leave of Mount Mushi and traveled directly to Nanyang. There, beholding the remains of National Teacher Huizhong, he settled down to stay.
One day, while clearing away grass and wood, he happened to toss aside a piece of tile and stone; it struck a bamboo stalk and produced a sound. Suddenly, he attained awakening.

He immediately returned to bathe and burn incense, bowing from afar toward Mount Mushi and praising him, saying: "The Master’s great compassion exceeds that of my own parents. Had I [understood] at that time..."
"Explain this to me; how could there be such an event as today? Thereupon he spoke in verse: "A single blow causes all that was known to be forgotten;

No further cultivation or maintenance is required. Every movement reveals the ancient path; One does not fall into the trap of silent stillness. Nowhere is there a trace to be found; Within sound and form lies majestic deportment.
Those who have realized the Way in all directions All say this is the highest capacity. When Guishan heard this, he said to Yangshan:
Mount San said, "This disciple has attained thorough penetration. Yangshan said, "This is merely the product of mental scheming;

it was composed through the activity of the conscious mind. Wait until I have personally examined him myself. Later, when Yangshan saw the Master, he said, "The Master praised you for having realized the Great Matter.

A bright moon fills half the window, and a harmonious atmosphere pervades. At such a time as this, tell me: do Guizong and Jingshan still have a chance to meet? Let us set aside whether they see each other or not. But consider this: when this monk asks in such a manner, does he possess the eye?

Guo asked, "What is long? The Master said, "Not even a thousand sages can measure it. He asked, "What is short?
